t: In responders, monthly migraine days decreased markedly and significantly across all three treatment months compared to baseline.
Even non-responders (by the >50% criterion) showed a statistically significant, though smaller, decrease in monthly migraine days with treatment.
Across the full cohort, headache intensity during remaining attacks did not change significantly with treatment.
In responders, headache intensity decreased significantly at months 1 and 3 compared to baseline.
In non-responders, headache intensity did not change significantly with treatment.
Photophobia incidence during attacks decreased significantly across all 3 treatment months in the full cohort.
In non-responders, photophobia incidence did not decrease significantly with treatment.
Across the full cohort, phonophobia incidence did not change significantly with treatment.
In responders, phonophobia incidence was significantly reduced at months 1 and 3.
Nausea incidence during attacks did not change significantly with treatment in the full cohort, responders, or non-responders.
At baseline, phonophobia and yawning as premonitory symptoms were reported significantly more often by future responders than future non-responders.
The incidence of headache following premonitory symptoms decreased substantially more in responders than non-responders after galcanezumab treatment.

Premonitory symptom-to-headache incidence decreased far more in super-responders than super non-responders, supporting a dose-dependent relationship between migraine frequency reduction and premonitory symptom reversal.

Irritability and cognitive impairment as premonitory symptoms leading to headache improved with galcanezumab only in responders, not in non-responders, distinguishing them from most other premonitory symptoms.
Visual and sensory aura-to-headache incidence was reduced by treatment in both responders and non-responders, while speech aura improved only in responders.

Aura-to-headache incidence was reduced by galcanezumab in super-responders but showed no effect in super non-responders, suggesting the drug's effect on aura is secondary to reduction in migraine frequency.
The number of migraine triggers followed by headache decreased substantially more in responders than non-responders after galcanezumab treatment.
Trigger-to-headache incidence dropped much more in super-responders than in super non-responders, following the same dose-dependent pattern seen with premonitory symptoms.

Not drinking enough, menses, and being too hot as triggers improved with galcanezumab only in responders, distinguishing them from 8 other triggers that improved in both responders and non-responders.
Menses, weather changes, and certain odors as triggers were minimally or completely unaffected by galcanezumab treatment across all four response groups.
Super non-responders were significantly older and had a longer duration of migraine history than super-responders, suggesting cumulative pain exposure affects treatment responsiveness.

Unlike other premonitory symptoms, headache following neck stiffness/pain was reduced only in non-responders and super non-responders (not in responders/super-responders), suggesting neck pain may not be a classical centrally-mediated premonitory symptom.

Of 46 completers, 58% were classified as galcanezumab responders (≥50% MMD reduction), 24% as super-responders (≥70% reduction), 42% as non-responders (<50% reduction), and 17% as super non-responders (<30% reduction).

The authors propose that galcanezumab's reduction of premonitory symptoms and triggers is secondary to its reduction of the magnitude and duration of meningeal nociceptive signaling reaching the brain over time, rather than direct central CGRP blockade.
Super non-responders were significantly older and had a longer migraine disease duration than super-responders.
The incidence of headache following irritability and cognitive impairment decreased after galcanezumab only in responders, not in non-responders.
Seven of the nine most common premonitory symptoms showed reduced headache incidence after galcanezumab in both responders and non-responders.

In super non-responders, headache incidence after neck stiffness was the only premonitory symptom not improved, while all other 8 symptoms improved; conversely neck stiffness improved in super non-responders but not super-responders.
Headache onset following visual and sensory aura decreased after galcanezumab in both responders and non-responders, whereas speech aura-related headache decreased only in responders.
In super non-responders, headache incidence after visual, sensory, or speech aura was not reduced by galcanezumab, unlike in super-responders.
Eight of eleven common migraine triggers showed reduced headache incidence after galcanezumab in both responders and non-responders, while three triggers improved only in responders.

In super non-responders, six triggers remained unaffected by galcanezumab that improved in super-responders, two triggers (letdown after stress, food/wine) improved in both groups, and three triggers (weather, odors, menses) were unaffected in either group.

The authors propose that neck pain reduction by galcanezumab reflects peripheral neutralization of CGRP in deep neck structures rather than central reversal of meningeal nociceptive hyperexcitability, since neck stiffness improved in non-responders and super non-responders but not classical premonitory symptoms.
Galcanezumab was administered at 120 mg per month, with an initial 240 mg loading dose, over a 3-month treatment period in high-frequency episodic and chronic migraine patients.
Prior evidence of a hyperexcitable visual cortex in migraine patients is proposed as the common mechanistic basis for light acting as a trigger, a premonitory symptom, and an ictal symptom.

The authors propose that even a mild (30-50%) reduction in monthly migraine days is sufficient to partially reverse pain-induced hyperexcitability of neurons that generate premonitory symptoms and triggers.
The findings support lowering the clinical threshold for defining treatment response from a ≥50% reduction to a ≥30% reduction in monthly migraine days.
Overall, 30.4% of participants were diagnosed with migraine aura, with similar rates of visual, sensory, and speech aura subtypes between responders and non-responders.

In super non-responders, seven of nine premonitory symptoms (cognitive impairment, photophobia, irritability, fatigue, stress/nervousness, dizziness/vertigo, nausea) were completely unaffected by galcanezumab treatment.
In super-responders, galcanezumab decreased headache occurrence preceded by all premonitory symptoms except neck stiffness.
Ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block was effective in 90.7% of chronic migraine patients at 1-month follow-up.
The effective rate of SGB for chronic migraine declined to 82.5% at 2-month follow-up.
The effective rate of SGB for chronic migraine was 71.1% at 3-month follow-up.
Among responsive patients at 3-month follow-up, 95.7% benefited from repeated stellate ganglion blocks.
Patients who responded to repeated SGB treatment at 3 months received a significantly greater number of blocks than non-responders.
Comorbid anxiety or depression was found to be a negative predictor of SGB treatment effectiveness at the 3-month follow-up.
Ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block was associated with an overall adverse event rate of 9.3% in chronic migraine patients.
No serious complications occurred with ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block; all adverse events observed were transient.
Hoarseness was reported as the most common adverse event following ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block.
A systematic review pooling 19 studies (11,324 patients) found that 18% (range 4-32%) reported muscle pain three months after COVID-19 infection.
The same systematic review found that 10% (range 1-21%) of patients reported headache three months after COVID-19 infection.
A German three-district survey of PCR-confirmed COVID-19 patients found 15.8% reported muscle/joint pain and 9.1% reported headache three months post-infection.
A systematic review of 18 studies (8591 COVID-19 survivors) reported a 26% prevalence of muscle and joint pain one year after infection.
In a Danish study of ICU survivors, 25.5% reported joint pain one year after critical illness related to COVID-19.
In the same Danish ICU survivor study, 21.3% reported muscle pain one year after critical illness.
Up to 10% of affected patients report ongoing work incapacity at seven to twelve months after acute COVID-19 infection.
In a Norwegian population-based study of 70,000 participants, the adjusted relative risk of chest pain 12 months after COVID-19 infection was 6.7 compared to persons without COVID-19.
The same Norwegian study found an adjusted relative risk of 1.8 for headache 12 months after COVID-19 infection compared to uninfected persons.

The Norwegian study found an adjusted relative risk of 1.7 for joint pain at 12 months, with a confidence interval crossing 1, indicating no statistically significant difference from uninfected persons.
In a Kuwaiti study, 26.4% of 121 patients reported new-onset headache (bifrontal/temporal) three months after acute COVID-19, resolving within one month in only 5% of those affected.
In a systematic review, female sex and disease severity were each identified as risk factors for persistent post-COVID symptoms in three of ten studies examining predictors.
In the German Förster study, female sex, disease severity, and comorbidities were predictors of post-COVID-19 symptoms.

In a Spanish study, 45% of COVID-19 survivors reported persistent musculoskeletal pain eight months after acute infection, and 75% of those affected reported that the pain was not present before infection.
In the Spanish study, female sex was a risk indicator for post-COVID-19 musculoskeletal pain with an odds ratio of 1.35.
Prior musculoskeletal pain was a risk indicator for post-COVID-19 musculoskeletal pain with an odds ratio of 1.55.
Headache at hospital admission was the strongest risk indicator among those assessed for post-COVID-19 musculoskeletal pain, with an odds ratio of 1.87.
The neuroinvasive capacity of SARS-CoV-2 is proposed as a key mechanism of neurological symptoms including headache, via activation of the trigeminovascular system and glia.
Axonal degeneration of motor and sensory nerves in the context of septic multiorgan failure underlies critical-illness polyneuropathy in severe COVID-19 patients.

Persistent systemic inflammation, muscular deconditioning from hospitalization/lockdown-reduced activity, and altered central pain processing due to stress are proposed contributors to post-COVID musculoskeletal pain.
German statutory health insurance claims data showed a 40% incidence of new-onset headache three months after PCR-confirmed COVID-19, compared to 23% in matched controls without COVID-19.

A prospective Dutch population-based study comparing pre- and post-infection symptom measurements with matched non-infected controls found that only 12.7% of symptoms reported after COVID-19 could be attributed to the infection itself.

In a prospective US cohort, pre-infection depression, anxiety, subjective stress, and loneliness were associated with a 1.3- to 1.5-fold increased risk of post-COVID symptoms and functional impairment one year after infection.
In the German COVIDOM cohort study, both the intensity of acute-phase symptoms and the degree of personal resilience predicted the extent of symptoms 6-12 months after infection.

As of the guideline update, no long/post-COVID treatment options (pharmacologic or non-pharmacologic) are yet supported by randomized controlled trials, though over 787 studies are registered in the NIH database.

A multimodal internistic-psychosomatic rehabilitation program combining behavioral-therapy-oriented psychotherapy with individually adapted, gradually increasing exercise therapy is being evaluated in a multicenter study since February 2022.
The guideline states that long/post-COVID pain is frequently associated with fatigue and cognitive impairment, and that these often occur together as a symptom complex.

The guideline recommends validated self-report instruments for assessing chronic pain severity in long/post-COVID, including the Brief Pain Inventory, the German Pain Questionnaire, the Fibromyalgia Symptom Questionnaire, the Kiel Headache Questionnaire, and the DN2 for neuropathic pain.
The neuroinvasive capacity of SARS-CoV-2 is considered a key mechanism of neurological symptoms including headache, via activation of the trigeminovascular system and glia.
Critical-illness polyneuropathy following septic multiorgan failure is attributed to axonal degeneration of motor and sensory nerves.
Muscle and joint pain after intensive care treatment can be explained by muscular imbalances/deficits and contractures.

Persistent systemic inflammation, muscular deconditioning (from hospitalization and reduced physical activity due to lockdown measures), and altered central pain processing due to stress from contact restrictions and psychological symptom burden may contribute to musculoskeletal pain.

A German statutory health insurance claims-data study found the incidence of new-onset headache at 3 months was 40% after PCR-confirmed COVID-19 compared to 23% in an age-, sex- and comorbidity-matched control group without COVID-19.

In a Dutch prospective population-based study comparing pre- and post-infection symptom measurements with matched uninfected controls, only 12.7% of the symptoms reported by people after COVID-19 could be attributed to the infection itself.

In a prospective American cohort study, baseline (pre-infection) depression, anxiety, subjective stress, and loneliness were associated with a 1.3- to 1.5-fold increased risk of post-COVID symptoms and impairments in daily life one year after COVID-19.
In the German population-based COVIDOM study, both the intensity of acute-phase symptoms and the degree of personal resilience predicted the extent of symptoms 6-12 months after infection.

A multicenter study evaluating a multimodal internal medicine-psychosomatic interdisciplinary rehabilitation program, combining behaviorally oriented disorder-specific psychotherapy with individually adapted, gradually progressive exercise therapy, has been underway since February 2022 with no reported outcomes yet.

For nociplastic pain (fibromyalgia-like complaints), the guideline recommends non-pharmacological approaches such as aerobic training and psychotherapeutic methods as primary treatment, with central pain modulators (some tricyclic antidepressants, SNRIs, gabapentinoids) as pharmacological options.

The guideline recommends validated self-report psychometric instruments to assess chronic pain severity, including the German version of the Brief Pain Inventory, the German Pain Questionnaire, the Fibromyalgia Symptom Questionnaire for multilocular muscle/joint pain, the Kiel Headache Questionnaire for headache, and the DN2 for neuropathic pain.
In oligodendroglial extracellular vesicles, pS129-alpha-synuclein concentration increased in the order HC<PD<MSA and was significantly higher in both PD and MSA compared with healthy controls.
In neuronal extracellular vesicles, pS129-alpha-synuclein concentrations decreased numerically in the order HC>PD>MSA but this difference was not statistically significant.

The oEV:nEV pS129-alpha-synuclein concentration ratio increased in the order HC<PD<MSA, with most MSA samples showing a ratio >1, but the PD group was roughly evenly split above and below 1, giving only moderate group separation compared to the total alpha-synuclein ratio.

Average total tau concentration in both neuronal and oligodendroglial EVs was significantly lower in the MSA group compared with HC and PD, consistent with the scarce tau pathology known in MSA, and this remained significant after adjusting for age.
Total tau concentrations in nEVs and oEVs were similar between the HC and PD groups.
Differences between nEV and oEV tau concentrations were statistically insignificant within HC, PD, and MSA groups, suggesting that measuring tau in one EV type is sufficient.

pT181-tau was detectable in only 6 of 76 neuronal and oligodendroglial EV lysates from HC, PD, and MSA samples, indicating that at current assay sensitivity this analyte is not useful for distinguishing among the groups.
Serum NfL concentration was significantly lower in the PD group compared with HC and MSA groups, even after adjusting for age.

The lower NfL concentration in PD and MSA compared to HC was observed specifically in female samples but not in male samples, consistent with a prior report finding this effect significant only in females.

Adding oEV pS129-alpha-synuclein concentration to a model with nEV alpha-synuclein, oEV:nEV alpha-synuclein ratio, and total EV concentration improved diagnostic separation among HC, PD, and MSA groups, with AUCs of 0.874 for PD vs HC, 0.993 for MSA vs HC, and 0.936 for PD vs MSA.
Adding serum NfL to the pS129-alpha-synuclein-containing diagnostic model did not improve separation among HC, PD, and MSA groups.
Adding oEV total tau concentration to the base diagnostic model did not significantly improve model predictions for separating HC, PD, and MSA.
Adding serum NfL to a model containing oEV tau improved diagnostic predictions, increasing the AUC for HC vs PD separation from 0.633 to 0.720, though the improvement was borderline significant.

Across all groups combined, total alpha-synuclein concentration in both nEVs and oEVs correlated positively with oEV pS129-alpha-synuclein but not with nEV pS129-alpha-synuclein; this correlation was not observed in the control group alone.
In the PD group specifically, both nEV and oEV alpha-synuclein concentrations correlated positively with oEV pS129-alpha-synuclein.
In the MSA group specifically, both nEV and oEV alpha-synuclein concentrations correlated positively with oEV pS129-alpha-synuclein.

None of the measured EV biomarkers (alpha-synuclein, pS129-alpha-synuclein, tau, NfL) correlated with disease duration or disease progression as assessed by UPDRS-III, UMSARS, or Hoehn and Yahr scale.
During the ictal phase of migraine, patients showed lower SDNN and LF heart rate variability than healthy controls, with lower HRV correlating with greater pain intensity.

24-hour ECG in migraine patients showed decreased SDNN, RMSSD, and HF compared to controls, especially among those with aura during the night period, indicating parasympathetic hypofunction with sympathetic predominance.
Newly diagnosed migraine patients showed decreased SDNN and RMSSD and higher mean heart rate compared to age-matched healthy controls, consistent with decreased vagal modulation.
Among 421 participants completing online questionnaires and cognitive tests, memory deficits were associated with fatigue or mixed symptom profiles following COVID-19.
In a retrospective study of 271 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, higher resting HRV (SDNN) predicted greater survival among patients aged 70 and older, suggesting a protective role for vagal activity.

Among 17 COVID-19 patients monitored with daily ECG, a drop of more than 40% in SDNN within 72 hours preceded a CRP surge of 50% or more in 10 of 12 affected patients, indicating HRV decline predicted acute inflammation.

A study of 50 individuals with prior COVID-19 infection compared to 50 healthy controls found decreased time-domain and frequency-domain HRV measures, indicating persistent HRV abnormality after COVID-19.
In the Copenhagen Holter Study of 678 healthy participants aged 55-75, lower nighttime SDNN strongly predicted future stroke development even after adjusting for known stroke risk factors.
Among 5,308 patients with transient ischemic attack or minor stroke, higher baseline SDNN predicted reduced neurological disability and reduced stroke recurrence at 90 days.
In 884 stroke-free Cardiovascular Health Study participants, two HRV measures—CV% and SLOPE—significantly improved prediction of clinical stroke risk score.
In 11 epilepsy patients, mean heart rate, LF/HF ratio, and SD2/SD1 increased during the 5-10 minutes preceding seizure onset, suggesting these HRV features could help predict seizures.
Analysis of 238 temporal lobe seizures from 41 patients found that decreased RR interval and pNN50 helped identify the pre-ictal state in 90% of patients and 41% of seizures.
A meta-analysis of 2,086 patients with anxiety disorders and 2,294 psychiatric-free controls found that lower HF and time-domain HRV measures were associated with anxiety disorders.
A meta-analysis of 37 publications found consistent low vagal activity, characterized by decreased HF and increased LF, associated with stress.

In schizophrenia patients, respiration exerted weaker influence on heart rate while heart rate more strongly influenced respiration compared to controls; first-degree relatives showed a similar but attenuated pattern, suggesting a genetic component to cardiorespiratory coupling.
In a large Brazilian civil-servant cohort, reduced HF-HRV was associated with impaired executive function (trail-making B performance), mediated by insulin resistance and subclinical atherosclerosis.
In young male participants, higher SDNN was associated with better resistance to food temptation and higher ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity during dietary decision-making.
Higher heart rate variability was associated with decreased impulsivity, which may indirectly help individuals resist social media overuse.

Older adults with high resting HRV were more likely to avoid gazing at angry faces than those with low HRV, suggesting greater emotional regulation ability with a positivity effect that emerges with aging.

Greater resting RMSSD was associated with stronger amygdala-medial prefrontal cortex connectivity across age groups, while amygdala-ventrolateral PFC connectivity was linked to RMSSD only in younger adults.
Higher RMSSD was linked with greater functional connectivity from bilateral ventromedial PFC in young adults and from bilateral posterior cingulate cortex across all age groups.
Ultra-low frequency HRV was positively associated with MoCA cognitive scores and negatively associated with cardiovascular risk score in adults with cardiovascular risk factors.
Patients who progressed from MCI to dementia with Lewy bodies showed lower HRV (SDNN, RMSSD, LF, HF) and worse visuospatial and executive function than those who progressed to Alzheimer's disease.
Cognitive impairment (MMSE below 24) was more prevalent among elderly women with lower HF HRV.

In amnestic MCI, a blunted postural increase in normalized low-frequency HRV was related to episodic memory and hippocampal/insular atrophy, while in non-amnestic MCI, LF increase related to cerebrovascular burden and executive function, suggesting distinct autonomic mechanisms between MCI subtypes.

MCI participants showed smaller postural increases in normalized LF and smaller decreases in normalized HF when moving from supine to standing compared to healthy controls, despite no baseline HRV differences.

In cognitively healthy elderly with pathological CSF amyloid/tau levels, HRV (RR and LF) decreased from resting to a task-switching challenge, indicating a hyperactive sympathovagal response, despite no baseline HRV differences between groups.

HRV (pNN50) decreased acutely after mild traumatic brain injury/concussion in young athletes, recovering by about 3 weeks, with higher acute middle cerebral artery blood velocity linked to higher HRV and better cognitive scores at follow-up.
Migraine patients during the ictal stage showed lower SDNN and LF than controls, reflecting parasympathetic dysfunction that correlated negatively with pain intensity.

24-hour ECG analysis showed decreased SDNN, RMSSD, and HF in migraine patients compared to controls, especially those with aura during nighttime, supporting parasympathetic hypofunction with sympathetic predominance.
Newly diagnosed migraine patients showed decreased SDNN and RMSSD along with higher mean heart rate compared to age-matched controls.
An online survey found that memory deficits were associated with fatigue or mixed symptom presentations following COVID-19.
Higher resting SDNN predicted greater survival among hospitalized COVID-19 patients aged 70 and older, supporting a protective role of vagal activity.
A drop of more than 40% in SDNN within 72 hours preceded a C-reactive protein surge of 50% or more in most of a small cohort of COVID-19 patients, suggesting HRV decline predicts acute inflammation.
During the ictal (attack) phase, migraine patients showed lower SDNN and LF than controls, indicating parasympathetic dysfunction that correlated with greater pain intensity.

24-hour ECG recordings showed migraine patients, especially those with aura, had decreased SDNN, RMSSD, and HF at night compared to controls, supporting parasympathetic hypofunction with sympathetic predominance.
Newly diagnosed migraine patients showed decreased SDNN and RMSSD along with higher mean heart rate compared to age-matched healthy controls.
In an online survey and cognitive testing of 421 participants, memory deficits were associated with fatigue or combinations of symptoms following COVID-19.
Among hospitalized COVID-19 patients aged 70 and older, higher resting HRV (SDNN) predicted greater survival.
Weekly daily ECG monitoring in COVID-19 patients showed that a drop in SDNN of over 40% within 72 hours preceded a CRP inflammatory surge in most cases, suggesting HRV can predict acute inflammation.

Individuals with a history of COVID-19 infection showed decreased HRV in both time domain (SDNN, RMSSD) and frequency domain (LF, HF) measures compared to healthy controls, indicating persistent HRV abnormality after COVID-19.
In the Copenhagen Holter Study, lower nighttime SDNN strongly predicted future stroke development in healthy older participants, even after adjusting for known stroke risk factors.
Among patients with TIA or minor stroke, higher baseline SDNN predicted reduced neurological disability and reduced stroke recurrence at 90 days.
In stroke-free elderly participants from the Cardiovascular Health Study, two HRV measures (CV% and SLOPE) significantly improved stroke risk prediction beyond the clinical CHS stroke risk score.
In epilepsy patients, mean heart rate, LF/HF ratio, and SD2/SD1 increased in the 5-10 minutes preceding seizure onset, suggesting these HRV features could help predict seizures.
Analysis of temporal lobe seizures showed that decreased RR interval and pNN50 helped identify the pre-ictal state in the majority of patients and a substantial proportion of seizures.

A meta-analysis found that patients with anxiety disorders had lower HF and time-domain HRV measures than psychiatrically healthy controls, suggesting decreased vagal activity underlies elevated cardiovascular risk in anxiety.
A meta-analysis of 37 publications found that psychological stress is consistently associated with low vagal activity, characterized by decreased HF and increased LF.

Schizophrenia patients showed weaker influence of respiration on heart rate but stronger influence of heart rate on respiration compared to controls, with first-degree relatives showing similarly stronger heart-rate influences, suggesting a genetic component to this autonomic coupling abnormality.

Central-autonomic-network analysis showed schizophrenia patients had stronger respiratory and cardiac influences on central (EEG) activity and stronger central influences on vascular activity compared to controls.

Using a strict MARS-D cutoff (maximum score of 25), 32.8% of cluster headache patients versus 22.0% of migraine patients were classified as adherent, a difference that did not reach statistical significance.
A significantly larger proportion of cluster headache patients than migraine patients reported never having stopped taking prescribed headache medication.
Migraine patients cited concern about side effects as a reason for stopping medication significantly more often than cluster headache patients.
Among cluster headache patients on prophylactic medication, verapamil was the most commonly used, best-tolerated, and most effective agent.
In cluster headache patients, positive expectations of medical treatment were significantly correlated with medication adherence, with a large effect size.
In migraine patients, trust in the doctor and treatment concept was significantly correlated with medication adherence, though with a small effect size.
Coping was statistically significantly but negligibly associated with adherence in migraine patients.
Self-efficacy scores were significantly higher in cluster headache patients than in migraine patients.
Coping scores were significantly higher in cluster headache patients than in migraine patients.
Mental comorbidity (depression symptom severity) did not differ significantly between cluster headache and migraine patients, nor between adherent and non-adherent subgroups.
Cluster headache patients were predominantly male while migraine patients were predominantly female, a highly significant sex distribution difference between the two headache groups.
Migraine patients had significantly longer disease duration than cluster headache patients.
Medication adherence was comparable between patients with chronic and episodic cluster headache.
Headache-related impairment (HIT-6) did not significantly influence treatment adherence in either cluster headache or migraine patients.

No individual MARS-D item (forgetting, altering dose, stopping temporarily, skipping doses, taking less than instructed) showed a statistically significant difference in response frequency between cluster headache and migraine patients.
Using the more permissive MARS-D sum score approach instead of a strict cutoff, there was no statistically significant difference in adherence between cluster headache and migraine patients.
Citing phase 3 trial data, discontinuation rates for galcanezumab were higher in migraine than in cluster headache across both episodic and chronic subtypes.
Higher degree of nociplastic pain, as measured by the Fibromyalgia Survey Score, was associated with greater pelvic pain severity.
Higher degree of nociplastic pain was associated with greater frequency of pelvic pain.
Higher degree of nociplastic pain was associated with greater interference of pelvic pain with daily life.
Higher degree of nociplastic pain was associated with greater tenderness on pelvic myofascial examination.
Each additional point on the Fibromyalgia Survey Score increased the likelihood of high-impact pelvic pain by 7%.
Degree of nociplastic pain was a stronger predictor of pain outcomes than the presence of endometriosis in the same models.
Opioid use was a stronger predictor of worse pelvic pain outcomes than nociplastic pain (FM Survey Score) in the multivariable models.
The presence of endometriosis was a weaker predictor of pelvic pain outcomes than degree of nociplastic pain across all models.
Degree of nociplastic pain was independently associated with pelvic pain severity, frequency, and impact even after accounting for endometriosis, surgical history, age, and BMI.
Patients with generalized ligamentous laxity (GLL) were identified using a Beighton score cutoff of 4 or greater.

FAIS patients with generalized ligamentous laxity treated via periportal capsulotomy with capsular closure achieved 2-year patient-reported outcome improvements in pain, function, and quality of life that were statistically similar to matched FAIS patients without laxity treated without capsular closure.

Patients with generalized ligamentous laxity (GLL) undergoing hip arthroscopy with periportal capsulotomy closure showed a HOOS-Symptoms score improvement (26.3±24.0) similar to that of matched non-GLL patients (20.6±18.1) at 2 years.
GLL patients had a HOOS-Pain improvement (29.8±20.4) comparable to non-GLL patients (24.4±9.0) after arthroscopic FAIS treatment at 2 years.
GLL patients had a HOOS-ADL improvement (24.9±18.4) similar to non-GLL patients (22.0±19.9) after arthroscopic FAIS treatment at 2 years.
GLL patients had a HOOS-Sports improvement (43.6±26.1) comparable to non-GLL patients (33.1±29.8) after arthroscopic FAIS treatment at 2 years.
FAIS patients with generalized ligamentous laxity showed HOOS Quality-of-Life score improvements at 2 years comparable to matched patients without joint hypermobility.
Both the GLL and non-GLL cohorts achieved minimal clinically important differences (MCID) on each HOOS subscore at similarly high rates.

Overall, patients with generalized ligamentous laxity undergoing FAIS surgery with capsular closure had outcomes equivalent to normal-laxity patients treated without capsular closure, supporting the safety and efficacy of this tailored surgical approach for hypermobile patients.
Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel COL5A1 variant, c.488G>A p.(Gly163Asp), described as a frameshift mutation, in a patient diagnosed with classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient presented with a distal aortic dissection extending through the left common iliac artery, a rare vascular complication in classical EDS.
Physical examination showed generalized joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 4 out of 9, supporting a joint hypermobility diagnosis per Brighton criteria.
The patient's complete blood count showed mild thrombocytopenia, with secondary causes ruled out.
Genetic testing of family members showed that the patient's mother also carried the same COL5A1 variant.

The authors note that only one prior case in the literature reports co-occurrence of transposition of the great arteries with vascular EDS, raising the possibility that the patient's congenital cardiac defect and connective tissue disorder share a common vascular mechanism.

The patient reported a 10-year history of chronic back and hip pain, easy bruising, and episodes of palpitations, dizziness, and light-headedness, consistent with autonomic and musculoskeletal symptom burden in cEDS.
24% of fibromyalgia patients (56/233) tested positive for antinuclear antibodies, most at low titre.
14.1% of fibromyalgia patients (33/233) were seropositive for myositis-specific or myositis-associated antibodies, with MSA in 9% and MAA in 6%.
Anti-Mi2 was the most common myositis-specific antibody found (13 patients), but only 3 of these patients were ultimately diagnosed with idiopathic inflammatory myopathy.
After one year of follow-up, 7 of the 233 fibromyalgia patients were ultimately classified as having probable idiopathic inflammatory myopathy.
Primary Sjögren's syndrome was diagnosed in 5 of 233 fibromyalgia patients via objective glandular impairment testing, despite none reporting sicca symptoms at baseline.
ANA positivity was significantly associated with the presence of myositis-associated antibodies but not with myositis-specific antibodies.
Elevated muscle enzymes (CPK, LDH, transaminases) were not significantly associated with MSA or MAA seropositivity in fibromyalgia patients.
Positivity for myositis-specific antibodies was significantly associated with a definite diagnosis of connective tissue disease.
Positivity for myositis-associated antibodies was significantly associated with a definite diagnosis of connective tissue disease.
ANA positivity was significantly associated with a definite diagnosis of connective tissue disease.
Widespread Pain Index, Symptom Severity Score, and tender point counts were significantly higher in female fibromyalgia patients than in male patients.
Clinical severity measures (WPI, SSS, TP count) were similar between fibromyalgia patients who were seropositive versus seronegative for MSA/MAA.

The distribution of myositis-associated antibodies in fibromyalgia patients differed from that reported in a large healthy population study, with anti-Pm/Scl being the most common rather than anti-Ro52kD.
One fibromyalgia patient with persistently elevated CPK was classified as having probable statin-induced myopathy, with clinical and serological improvement after statin discontinuation.
One fibromyalgia patient was diagnosed with transthyretin amyloidosis, confirmed by abdominal fat pad excisional biopsy.
Four fibromyalgia patients were diagnosed with axial spondyloarthritis based on specific MRI findings.
Thyroid dysfunction (5 hyperthyroidism, 4 hypothyroidism) was identified in 9 fibromyalgia patients during the study.
A definite connective tissue disease diagnosis was made in 12 of 233 fibromyalgia patients (5.2%) during the study period.
Two fibromyalgia patients seronegative for MSA/MAA were classified as probable polymyositis based on proximal weakness, elevated CPK, and electromyography findings.
Nine fibromyalgia patients were positive for antisynthetase antibodies, but only two (anti-PL7 and anti-PL12 positive) were ultimately diagnosed with idiopathic inflammatory myopathy.
There was no statistically significant gender difference in seropositivity for ANA, MSA, or MAA among fibromyalgia patients, though male patients trended higher for ANA and MAA.
Two fibromyalgia patients developed inflammatory arthritis and mildly elevated CPK during follow-up and were classified as undifferentiated connective tissue disease.
Female fibromyalgia patients had significantly higher Widespread Pain Index, Symptom Severity Score, and Tender Point counts than male patients.
Anti-Pm/scl was the most common MSA/MAA in the FM cohort at a much higher proportion than reported in a large healthy-population study.
Anti-RNP positivity was more common in FM patients than reported for healthy individuals in a large reference cohort.
All FM patients seropositive for anti-Ro52kD were subsequently diagnosed with primary Sjögren's syndrome due to glandular impairment.
A prior study by Gau et al. found that fibromyalgia patients have approximately twice the risk of subsequently developing primary Sjögren's syndrome.
Fibromyalgia is reported to occur in about 31% of patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome.

About one-third of fibromyalgia patients reporting sicca syndrome were found seropositive for a pSS-associated autoantibody in a prior study, whereas none of the current cohort's patients reported sicca symptoms.

Across studies, patients showed a sustained heart rate increase after cardioneuroablation, persisting for at least 2 years, consistent with impaired parasympathetic stimulation of the heart.
Heart rate variability was reduced after cardioneuroablation, persisting for at least 2 years, indicating impaired parasympathetic stimulation of the heart.
Cadaver neuroanatomical studies show that most cardiac cholinergic (vagal) fibres access the heart through the posterior and anterior right atria.
Functionally, the right vagus nerve predominantly innervates the sinoatrial node while the left vagus nerve predominantly affects the atrioventricular node.

The superior paraseptal ganglionated plexus (SPSGP), located at the junction of the interatrial septum and superior vena cava, is the final common pathway of right vagal innervation to the sinoatrial node, while the inferior paraseptal ganglionated plexus (IPSGP), near the proximal coronary sinus, is the final common pathway of left vagal innervation to the AV node.

Periprocedural complications of CNA are likely underreported; by analogy, complication rates for comparable right/left atrial ablations (atrial flutter/focal atrial tachycardia and atrial fibrillation) are 1.4-2% and 2-3% respectively.

HSAN III results from an autosomal recessive mutation on chromosome 9q causing IKBKAP deficiency, which reduces expression of elongator complex protein 1 (ELP-1).
Intraneural microelectrode recordings from the common peroneal nerve showed that functional muscle spindle afferents are absent in individuals with HSAN III.

Recordings from the ulnar nerve in the upper limb similarly showed no spontaneous or stretch-evoked muscle spindle afferent activity in HSAN III, in contrast to the rich activity seen in healthy controls.
Spontaneous bursts of muscle sympathetic nerve activity with dominant cardiac rhythmicity were absent in HSAN III, likely due to loss of baroreceptor negative feedback.

Tonic activity of post-ganglionic sympathetic axons (increasing with emotional stress) and evocable muscle pain via intraneural stimulation were preserved in HSAN III, indicating that unmyelinated motor and sensory axons supplying muscle are not lost.

Multi-unit and single-unit recordings from cutaneous fascicles showed that low-threshold myelinated tactile afferent physiology is essentially normal in HSAN III despite the loss of muscle spindle afferents.
Psychophysical testing suggests that C-tactile afferents, which mediate affective touch, are absent or greatly reduced in HSAN III.

HSAN III is associated with reduced density of unmyelinated cutaneous sensory axons, which accounts for the greatly elevated temperature and pain thresholds, while myelinated cutaneous afferents and unmyelinated sympathetic efferents are apparently normal in density.
Using passive joint-angle matching at the knee, patients with HSAN III performed poorly compared with healthy controls, whereas patients with cerebellar ataxia performed well.
Proprioceptive matching error at the knee was positively correlated with the degree of ataxia (Brief Ataxia Rating Score) in HSAN III patients but not in patients with cerebellar ataxia.
Unlike HSAN III, HSAN type IV does not exhibit ataxia, retains functional muscle spindles, and has normal proprioception.

Applying elastic tape across the knee joint to increase cutaneous tensile strain dramatically improved proprioceptive matching accuracy in HSAN III patients with the worst baseline acuity, restoring performance to within normal limits.
Unlike at the knee, proprioception was normal at the elbow in HSAN III and elastic taping had no effect on elbow joint-angle matching.
On the Purdue Pegboard precision-grip test, patients with HSAN III scored much lower than controls, with noticeable difficulty picking up and inserting objects.

Applying elastic tape to the hand, wrist, elbow and shoulder did not improve precision manual dexterity task performance in HSAN III, indicating increased cutaneous input cannot substitute for muscle spindle loss in this task.

A mouse model with reduced ELP-1 protein shows absent H-reflexes and loss of muscle spindle afferent neurons in the dorsal root ganglia, recapitulating many features of HSAN III including progressive gait ataxia, postural disturbance and kyphoscoliosis.

The major HSAN III mutation causes variable tissue-specific skipping of exon 20 in the IKBKAP transcript, reducing IKAP/ELP-1 protein levels, with the lowest expression occurring in the central and peripheral nervous system.
Correction of the IKBKAP exon 20 splicing deficit rescues the disease phenotype in a mouse model of HSAN III.
Scoliosis is a common feature of HSAN III, suggesting that muscle spindles in the axial musculature are also absent in this condition.

Mild, self-limited exacerbations of back pain occurred less frequently with anthroposophic eurythmy therapy (3 cases) than with yoga (7 cases) or physiotherapy (25 cases) in the low back pain RCT.
In postpolio syndrome patients, anthroposophic therapies added to either placebo or an experimental transdermal gel produced significant improvements in pain symptom scores with large effect sizes.
Use of the experimental transdermal gel combined with anthroposophic therapies improved quality of life and resilience in postpolio syndrome patients.

Rhythmical massage according to Ita Wegman significantly improved pain intensity compared with control in patients with dysmenorrhea, while other outcomes and comparisons (biofeedback, usual care) showed no significant differences.

In a nonrandomized comparative study of 86 low back pain patients, both anthroposophic and conventional therapy groups improved substantially in symptoms and physical health, with the anthroposophic group showing greater gains in mental health, general health, and energy at 12-month follow-up.
At 24-month follow-up, patients with chronic low back pain receiving anthroposophic treatment showed sustained improvements in symptoms, back function, and quality of life.

In an abstract-only study of 30 back pain patients treated with Arnica planta tota Rh D3, significant improvements occurred within the initial 6-day treatment period for all patients; benefits were maintained in those who continued treatment for 3 months, but symptoms returned in patients who discontinued.

In 41 fibromyalgia patients treated with Hepar Magnesium D10 over 10 weeks, Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores improved by at least 20% in 41.5% of patients at 5 weeks and 50% of patients at 10 weeks, with a medium effect size at 10 weeks.

In a real-world pre-post study of 45 migraine patients receiving anthroposophic medications, eurythmy, art therapy, and rhythmical massage, physician- and patient-rated migraine intensity and certain quality-of-life scale items significantly improved at 6-month follow-up, with improvements sustained at 24 months.

In the migraine study, adverse events were reported in 3% (n=1) of patients taking anthroposophic drugs compared with 9% (n=3) of patients taking nonanthroposophic drugs, with no serious adverse events.

In the low back pain comparative study, adverse reactions occurred in 15% (5/34) of patients treated with anthroposophic medicine compared with 11% of patients in the conventional therapy group, with no serious adverse events.

Across the included studies, AM therapies for chronic pain conditions were associated with considerable symptom reduction and predominantly large effect sizes on pain outcomes in five studies, with no notable adverse effects, though this may partly reflect underpowered studies or publication bias.
A multiple regression analysis adjusting for age showed that a higher number of AOC1 risk alleles was significantly associated with a higher (worse) FIQ score in women with fibromyalgia.
When compared as categories based on number of risk alleles, FIQ scores approached but did not reach statistical significance, with the highest scores in patients carrying 5-6 risk alleles.

Categorizing patients by deficient DAO activity (at least one risk allele) versus normal DAO activity (zero risk alleles) showed no significant association with sleep quality, atopic dermatitis, migraine, GI disorders, allergies, or intolerances.
Women with a higher number of AOC1 risk alleles had greater intensity of dry skin (an atopic dermatitis feature) than those with only two risk alleles.

Participants with the highest number of AOC1 risk alleles had lower stool consistency (looser stools) on the Bristol scale compared to those with a single risk allele or normal DAO activity, who tended toward constipation.
No changes in the frequency of gastrointestinal disorder symptoms were observed according to the number of AOC1 risk alleles.
In this fibromyalgia cohort, the minor allele frequencies for the four AOC1 variants were 31.5% (rs10156191), 10% (rs1049742), 32.5% (rs1049793), and 27% (rs2052129).

Although each AOC1 SNP individually was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, partial linkage disequilibrium among the four SNPs was suspected, since combinations of DAO-deficiency risk alleles occurred more frequently than expected from individual genotype frequencies.

Prior studies examining the same AOC1 variants in migraine patients found that rs10156191 was associated with migraine only in women, with a notably strong but statistically non-significant trend, and no association observed in men.

Experimental oral administration of 75 mg pure liquid histamine provoked immediate and delayed symptoms, including diarrhea, flatulence, and headache, in 50% of healthy women with no history of food intolerance.
A cited prior study found that the prevalence of DAO deficiency, based on the same AOC1 SNPs examined here, was close to 75% among women with fibromyalgia.

Among all FIQ items, only the item assessing inability to work showed a significant difference by risk allele category, but this result was considered unreliable due to the small number of patients who were employed.
9.6% of the studied collegiate football players had a Beighton score of 4 or greater, meeting the definition of generalized joint hypermobility (GJH).
The mean Beighton score across the 73 football players was 1.4, with a score of 0 being the most common result.
The overall number of musculoskeletal issues per athlete over the 2-year period did not differ significantly between athletes with and without GJH.
Athletes with GJH had significantly fewer hip-related musculoskeletal issues than athletes without GJH.
Athletes with GJH had significantly fewer wrist-related musculoskeletal issues than athletes without GJH.
Athletes with GJH appeared in significantly fewer games over the 2-year period than athletes without GJH.
The mean number of seasons completed did not differ between the GJH and no-GJH groups.
There were no significant differences between the GJH and no-GJH groups in mean number of injuries, injuries per game, injury treatments received, or days unavailable.
The proportion of athletes who underwent surgery did not differ significantly between the GJH and no-GJH groups.
Beighton score, GJH rate, and BMI differed significantly according to player position.
Quarterbacks demonstrated the highest mean Beighton score and GJH rate of any football position.
No offensive or defensive linemen demonstrated GJH, and this position had the lowest mean Beighton score.
Hamstring injury rate differed significantly by player position, with linebackers having the highest rate and linemen having none.
The number of musculoskeletal injuries was positively correlated with the number of games an athlete played.
Mean Beighton score by player position showed a non-significant inverse correlation with mean body mass index by position.
The prevalence of GJH in this collegiate football cohort was lower than previously reported in a general healthy male college student population.

In the HARVEST cohort of 1245 people with untreated hypertension, orthostatic hypertension was present in only 0.7% of participants when defined using the mean of two visits, and no participant met criteria on all three study visits.
The magnitude of the systolic blood pressure increase upon standing was inversely correlated with supine blood pressure.
Participants with a white coat effect (elevated office blood pressure but normal 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure) had a lower prevalence of orthostatic hypertension than those without this effect.
Orthostatic hypertension was more prevalent among participants whose blood pressure normalized over follow-up (2.1%, 8 of 286) than among those who remained hypertensive (0.25%, 2 of 794).

Mechanistic studies suggest that increased sympathetic responses drive orthostatic hypertension in younger individuals, whereas increased vascular stiffness underlies orthostatic hypertension in older patients.
Hypovolemia may predispose to sympathetic overactivation, which in turn can contribute to orthostatic hypertension.

Orthostatic hypertension has also been described in younger individuals with other hyperadrenergic conditions such as postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS), which is considered a distinct entity from essential hypertension.
Among the 15 female patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, teratomas (mostly ovarian) were found in 13, indicating a strong link between underlying neoplasm and disease in women.
Delirium and seizures were the two most common events leading to presentation among Southeast Asian patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
Male patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis showed a stronger predilection for early seizures and insomnia compared to female patients.
Female patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis were about four times more likely than males to develop movement disorders or have an underlying neoplasm.
Patients with dysautonomia required a longer ICU stay (beyond 14 days) than those without, but their 1-year outcomes did not differ.
One male patient with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was found to have an underlying biliary neuroendocrine tumour.
None of the SEA anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis patients experienced clinical relapse at 1-year follow-up.
Nearly two-thirds of patients had favourable functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale 0-2) at 1-year follow-up.
Although patients with dysautonomia required ICU stays longer than 14 days, their 1-year outcomes did not differ from patients without dysautonomia.

At three months after switching from erenumab to fremanezumab, 25.6% (10/39) of treatment-refractory chronic migraine patients achieved at least a 30% reduction in monthly migraine days and were classified as responders.
Median monthly migraine days significantly decreased from baseline through month 3 and month 6 of fremanezumab treatment.
The median number of headache-free (crystal clear) days per month increased progressively during fremanezumab treatment.
Painkiller intake and HIT-6 disability scores were significantly reduced at the last follow-up on fremanezumab.
Fremanezumab-related side effects, generally mild, were reported in approximately one-fifth of patients across follow-up timepoints, with one discontinuation due to an injection site reaction.
Among patients who were non-responders at month 3 and continued treatment, over a third became responders by month 6, indicating a subgroup of delayed responders.
After six months of treatment, a total of 35.9% of patients responded to fremanezumab, with the majority of these achieving at least a 50% reduction in monthly migraine days.
One-third of patients remained sustained responders to fremanezumab at long-term follow-up (up to 18 months).
The vast majority of patients had already failed onabotulinumtoxinA before erenumab, underscoring the treatment-refractory nature of the cohort.
Prior evidence cited by the authors indicates that interictal plasma amylin levels are elevated in patients with chronic migraine, suggesting involvement of amylin receptor pathways.

Cited experimental evidence shows that infusion of the amylin analogue pramlintide induced migraine attacks in a proportion of patients similar to CGRP infusion, implicating amylin receptors in migraine pathogenesis.
The proportion of patients using concomitant migraine preventatives alongside fremanezumab remained stable (approximately half) from baseline through last follow-up.
Using electrical stimuli, self-reported habituation to pain was reduced in migraine patients at the trigeminal area but not at the tibial region.
Multiple studies using laser-evoked potentials reported reduced habituation of the N2–P2 amplitude in migraine patients compared with controls.

A large observer-blinded longitudinal study using advanced statistical models found no group differences in N2–P2 amplitude habituation between migraine patients and controls, contrary to earlier smaller studies.
LEP amplitudes did not differ between chronic tension-type headache patients and healthy controls, but migraine patients showed reduced habituation compared to CTTH patients.
Menstrual phase affected the amount of habituation to pain in both migraine patients and healthy controls.
Reduced N2–P2 habituation over time in migraine patients was accompanied by increased functional connectivity between the thalamus and somatosensory areas, an effect not seen in controls.
Early studies using pressure or electrical stimuli found no self-report differences in habituation between chronic low back pain patients and controls.
Using an 8-day heat paradigm, CLBP patients and controls showed similar long-term habituation and within-session sensitization, with no group differences in related brain activity.
In painful radiculopathy patients, LEP habituation was reduced compared with controls, but this effect was not apparent for subjective pain ratings.
Using a detailed event-related fixed-interval area (ERFIA) analysis with multilevel modeling, reduced habituation to pain was found in CLBP patients specifically 340-460 ms post-stimulus.

Hollins et al. (2011) found no group differences in habituation or sensitization to heat pain between fibromyalgia patients and controls, though both groups showed an adaptation phase, a within-run sensitization phase, and habituation over runs.
De Tommaso et al. (2011) reported reduced habituation of the N2, P2, and N2–P2 amplitudes (but not N1) in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Fibromyalgia patients with comorbid migraine or sensory deficits showed a more pronounced reduction in pain habituation than fibromyalgia patients without such comorbidities.
In fibromyalgia, reduced habituation to pain was correlated with pain at tender points, and patients with reduced habituation reported greater widespread pain.
Reduced habituation of the N2–P2 or P2 EEG components in fibromyalgia patients was related to reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density.
In migraine patients, reduced trigeminal-area habituation to pain was correlated with migraine attack frequency.
Changes in somatosensory and parietal cortex activity correlated with migraine attacks per month, while orbitofrontal activity correlated with disease duration.
Disease duration correlated with reduced N2–P2 amplitude habituation differences between migraine phases, though habituation did not correlate with days until the next attack.

In medication-overuse headache patients, N2–P2 amplitude habituation was partially restored after 6 weeks in those who clinically improved following acute medication withdrawal, suggesting medication overuse aggravates central sensitization.
Preventive topiramate treatment normalized N1 amplitude habituation in migraine patients but had no effect on N2–P2 amplitude habituation.
Treatment with a ketogenic diet improved habituation of electrical evoked potentials in migraine patients, though no comparison to a no-diet control group was available.

OnabotulinumtoxinA treatment was effective for reduced N2–P2 habituation in the trigeminal area in migraine patients, with greater effectiveness in those with more severe reduced habituation at baseline.
A similar study using electrical stimuli failed to replicate the effect of onabotulinumtoxinA on habituation to pain in migraine patients.
Early short-term studies using pressure or electrical stimuli found no self-reported habituation differences between chronic low back pain patients and controls.
CLBP patients and controls showed similar long-term habituation to pain and similar within-session sensitization using an 8-day heat pain paradigm.
No differences in brain activity related to habituation were found between CLBP patients and controls, either across days or within sessions.
In patients with painful radiculopathy, laser-evoked potential habituation was reduced compared to controls, though this was not reflected in pain ratings.
Using event-related fixed-interval area analysis, reduced habituation to pain was found in CLBP patients specifically at 340 to 460 ms post-stimulus.
High temporal resolution analysis of LEP signals in radiculopathy patients had limited applicability due to poor data quality.
Fibromyalgia patients and controls both showed adaptation, sensitization, and habituation phases to heat pain with no group differences in habituation or sensitization.
EEG analyses showed reduced habituation of the N2, P2, and N2-P2 amplitudes in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, but not for the N1 amplitude.
Follow-up studies from the same laboratory replicated reduced habituation of the N2-P2 amplitude in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Fibromyalgia patients with comorbid migraine or sensory deficits showed a more pronounced reduction in pain habituation than fibromyalgia patients without comorbidities.
Habituation to pain on the thigh (N2 component) and foot (P2 component) did not differ between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
Burning mouth syndrome patients showed reduced brain activity habituation in the dACC, bilateral ventral MCC, left PCC, and cerebellum over repeated thermal stimuli, an effect not seen in controls.
Temporomandibular disorder patients did not show habituation differences compared to either healthy controls or fibromyalgia patients.
In cardiac syndrome X, reduced habituation was found after laser stimulation, more apparent at the chest than the hand for self-report and N2-P2 amplitude.
In chronic pancreatitis patients, reduced habituation of pain ratings and N2-P2 amplitude was shown, more pronounced with chest (pancreatic-area) stimulation than forearm.

Spinal cord injury patients with central neuropathic pain showed reduced habituation of pain ratings and contact heat-evoked potentials compared to both healthy controls and SCI patients without neuropathic pain.
Other studies found no differences in habituation of CHEPs or pain ratings between SCI patients with and without neuropathic pain, contradicting an earlier positive finding.
In complex regional pain syndrome, neither heat pain ratings nor pinprick ratings showed reduced habituation or differences compared to healthy individuals.
Both the presence of chronic pain and hypervigilance independently affected EEG habituation signal at several time latencies, despite no group differences in pain ratings.
Reduced habituation to pain in fibromyalgia was correlated with pain at tender points, and patients with reduced habituation showed greater widespread pain.
A correlation between reduced N2 amplitude habituation and self-reported depressive symptoms in fibromyalgia patients was not replicated in a larger-scale study.
An association was reported between habituation to pain and self-reported daily activity in fibromyalgia patients.
Reduced habituation of the N2-P2 or P2 EEG component was related to reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density in fibromyalgia patients.
Reduced habituation at the trigeminal area was correlated with migraine attack frequency.
Changes in somatosensory and parietal cortex activity correlated with migraine attacks per month, while orbitofrontal activity correlated with disease duration.
Disease duration was correlated with reduced habituation between migraine phases based on the N2-P2 EEG amplitude.
Habituation to pain did not correlate with the number of days until the next migraine attack.
In medication-overuse headache patients, N2-P2 amplitude habituation was partially restored after 6 weeks in those who clinically improved following acute medication withdrawal treatment.
In medication-overuse headache patients who clinically improved after acute medication withdrawal, habituation of the N2-P2 laser-evoked potential amplitude was partially restored after 6 weeks.
Preventive treatment with topiramate normalized the N1 amplitude habituation pattern in migraine patients but did not affect N2-P2 amplitude habituation.
Treatment with a ketogenic diet improved habituation of electrical evoked potentials in migraine patients, although no comparison to a non-diet control group was available.
OnabotulinumtoxinA treatment was effective at improving reduced habituation to pain, but only when stimulation was applied at the trigeminal area.
OnabotulinumtoxinA treatment was more effective in migraine patients who had more severely reduced habituation at baseline.
A similar study using electrical stimuli did not replicate the onabotulinumtoxinA effect on habituation seen with other stimulation methods.
A pilot study reported that Erenumab, an anti-CGRP receptor antibody, affected the initially reduced habituation of the N2 amplitude in migraine patients.
In fibromyalgia patients, habituation to pain was correlated with pain reported at tender points.
Fibromyalgia patients with reduced habituation to pain showed greater widespread pain.

De Tommaso et al. (2011) reported a correlation between reduced habituation of the N2 amplitude and self-reported depressive symptoms in fibromyalgia patients, but this was not replicated in a larger-scale study.
An association was reported between habituation to pain and self-reported daily activity levels in fibromyalgia patients.
Reduced habituation of the N2-P2 EEG component was reported to be related to reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density in fibromyalgia patients.
In fibromyalgia patients with reduced distal intra-epidermal nerve fiber density, the P2 EEG component amplitude increased over time (sensitization) rather than habituating.
Reduced habituation at the trigeminal area was correlated with migraine attack frequency.
Changes in brain activity in the somatosensory and parietal cortex were correlated with the number of migraine attacks per month.
Orbitofrontal cortex activity was correlated with migraine disease duration.
Disease duration was correlated with reduced habituation of the N2-P2 amplitude between migraine phases.
Habituation to pain did not correlate with the number of days until the next migraine attack.

Patients with burning mouth syndrome showed reduced fMRI brain activity in the dACC, bilateral ventral MCC, left PCC, and cerebellum over the course of four repeated thermal stimuli, indicating habituation, which was not observed in controls.

In contrast to burning mouth syndrome patients, healthy controls showed increased posterior cingulate cortex brain activity over the course of repeated thermal stimuli, indicating sensitization rather than habituation.
Patients with temporomandibular disorder did not show habituation differences compared to either healthy controls or fibromyalgia patients.

In patients with cardiac syndrome X, reduced habituation was shown after laser stimulation for both self-report ratings and the N2-P2 amplitude, more apparent when stimulating the chest than the hand.
In chronic pancreatitis patients, reduced habituation for pain ratings and the N2-P2 amplitude was more pronounced with stimulation at the chest (pancreatic area) than at the forearm.

One study found reduced habituation to pain in spinal cord injury patients with central neuropathic pain for both pain ratings and contact heat-evoked potentials compared to both healthy controls and SCI patients without neuropathic pain.
Two other studies reported no difference in habituation of contact heat-evoked potentials or pain ratings between spinal cord injury patients with and without central neuropathic pain.
In patients with complex regional pain syndrome, neither heat pain ratings nor pinprick ratings showed reduced habituation or differences compared to healthy individuals.

In a mixed chronic pain sample, both the presence of chronic pain and the degree of hypervigilance independently affected habituation of the EEG signal at several time latencies, despite no group differences being found in pain ratings.
An fMRI study in healthy participants using the dopamine D2 receptor antagonist haloperidol provided evidence for a role of dopamine in habituation to pain.
A review of genetic and molecular mechanisms of habituation identified 258 genes as possible drug targets.

GABA release was shown to increase as a result of short-term habituation to an olfactory stimulus in Drosophila, supporting a link between GABA-neurotransmission and habituation of CNS cellular processes.
Estrogen concentrations were reduced in female migraineurs compared to controls during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.
No differences were found in overall progesterone levels between female migraineurs and controls.
No differences were found in testosterone levels between male migraineurs and controls.
Early diurnal cortisol concentrations were elevated in both female and male migraineurs compared to controls, suggesting HPA axis dysregulation.
No differences in heart rate variability (HRV) were found between female or male migraineurs and controls.
Syncope is common across the lifespan, with about 40% of people experiencing at least one episode and syncope accounting for up to 3% of emergency department visits.
In POTS, syncope appears no more frequent than in the general population and, when it occurs, is usually vasovagal syncope.

The number and rhythmicity of jerking movements differ between syncope and tonic-clonic seizures, with syncope typically showing fewer than 10 arrhythmic jerks versus more than 20 rhythmic jerks in seizures.
Recovery of consciousness after syncope typically occurs within about 10 seconds, although fatigue or sleepiness can persist for hours afterward.

Reflex (vasovagal) syncope involves vagally-mediated cardioinhibition causing sinus slowing that may include asystole usually lasting less than 20 seconds; this response decreases with age but is very common in childhood and likely ubiquitous in toddlers with VVS.
Asystole occurring during reflex syncope is not a cardiac emergency, and there is no evidence that it is associated with poor prognosis.
Vasovagal syncope is by far the most common form of paediatric syncope, with a peak age of onset around 15 years; its likelihood decreases thereafter but rises again after age 60.
Vasovagal syncope occurs about twice as often in female as in male adolescents.
Syncope recurs in at least one third of patients with vasovagal syncope, with attacks varying widely in presentation and frequency.

Initial orthostatic hypotension is diagnostically defined by a systolic BP decrease greater than 40 mmHg and/or diastolic BP decrease greater than 20 mmHg within 15 seconds of standing, detectable only with beat-to-beat monitoring.
Initial orthostatic hypotension occurs in its fully developed form in 15-20% of paediatric syncope cases and in attenuated form in approximately 50% of all children.

Chronic classical orthostatic hypotension is rare in children, suggesting that vasovagal syncope and initial orthostatic hypotension are more likely causes of syncope during standing in paediatric patients.
Very rapid ventricular tachycardia, as seen in many channelopathies, causes syncope if it lasts more than 3-5 seconds.
Syncopal episodes lasting less than 30 seconds with spontaneous return to sinus rhythm and no recall of onset suggest an arrhythmic cause.
Tonic-clonic seizures typically involve 20-100 repetitive jerking movements, distinguishing them from syncope by number.
Psychogenic pseudosyncope and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures are suggested by frequent episodes (many per week or daily), long attacks (>10 minutes), and consistently closed eyes.
Both psychogenic pseudosyncope and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures occur mainly in adolescence and young adulthood and are more frequent in females than males.
Pallid and cyanotic breath-holding spells (including reflex anoxic seizures/VVS in infants) both typically begin at approximately 10 months of age.

Nonpharmacological measures (increased water/salt intake, bolus water ingestion, counter-manoeuvres such as leg-crossing) are the mainstay of therapy for iOH and VVS, but none has been proven effective specifically in children.
Conventional blood pressure devices are too slow to capture the rapid haemodynamic changes of initial orthostatic hypotension, requiring specific beat-to-beat monitoring for accurate diagnosis.

Heart rate patterns differentiate reflex syncope from orthostatic hypotension: heart rate is low in reflex syncope but high or normal in orthostatic hypotension, whereas blood pressure is low in both.
Hair grooming syncope and stretch syncope are situational reflex syncope subtypes that preferentially occur during adolescence.
In ictal asystole, cortical seizure activity triggers asystole, causing a typical focal seizure to abruptly end in a fall with complete unconsciousness resembling syncope.
Hair grooming syncope and stretch syncope (induced by stretching arms and neck upwards and backwards) are situational forms of reflex syncope that preferentially occur in adolescence.
Initial orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed when systolic BP falls more than 40 mmHg and/or diastolic BP falls more than 20 mmHg within 15 seconds of standing.
Initial orthostatic hypotension occurs in fully developed form in 15-20% of paediatric syncope cases and in attenuated form in roughly half of all children.
Chronic classical orthostatic hypotension is rare in children, and when present its causes mirror those in adults, including medication effects, type 1 diabetes and hypovolemia.
Syncope occurring while supine is a cardiac danger sign because it suggests circulatory standstill, unlike reflex syncope and orthostatic hypotension which are usually alleviated by lying or sitting.
Syncope during or just after exercise is a danger sign for arrhythmic or structural cardiac disease, and exercise stress testing is considered essential in evaluation.
A family history of unexpected death before age 40 suggests inherited cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia and should always be asked about during syncope evaluation.
An ECG is essential in syncope evaluation because many cases of cardiac syncope occur in existing but previously undetected structural heart disease.
Very rapid ventricular tachycardia, as seen in many channelopathies, causes syncope if it lasts more than 3-5 seconds, typically without warning prodrome.
When arrhythmic syncope episodes last less than 30 seconds, patients appear immediately normal and ask 'What happened?' without recall of onset, a pattern suggestive of an arrhythmic cause.
Loss of consciousness due to arrhythmia that is terminated by resuscitation should be termed 'aborted sudden cardiac death' rather than syncope, since the underlying causes and implications differ.

Arrhythmic syncope in children and adolescents is often genetic, with inherited arrhythmia syndromes showing specific triggers: startle (loud noise or cold water on the face) in long QT syndrome, sudden fever onset in Brugada syndrome, and exercise/excitement in catecholaminergic polymorphic VT or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.

In children, structural causes of cardiac syncope include aortic stenosis, coarctation of the aorta, anomalous coronary arteries, tetralogy of Fallot and transposition of the great arteries, while primary pulmonary hypertension and cardiomyopathy present more commonly in adolescence.
Syncope is the most common cause of misdiagnosed epilepsy, which can lead to unnecessary and futile anti-epileptic medication.
Tonic-clonic seizures typically involve 20-100 repetitive jerking movements, and a lateral tongue bite is a specific sign, distinguishing them from syncope.

In ictal asystole, cortical seizure activity triggers asystole, causing a focal seizure to suddenly end in a fall with complete unconsciousness resembling syncope; this can occur at any age but only in a fraction of a patient's seizures.
Syncope in infants can rarely trigger a tonic-clonic seizure, termed an 'anoxic epileptic seizure'.

Strong clues for psychogenic pseudosyncope or nonepileptic seizures include frequent episodes (many per week or daily), long attacks lasting more than 10 minutes, and consistently closed eyes, with blood pressure and heart rate typically high rather than low and normal EEG/cerebral blood flow during spells.

Psychogenic pseudosyncope and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures are more frequent in females than males, typically occur in adolescence and young adulthood, and patients with PPS often also have vasovagal syncope while patients with PNES frequently also have epileptic seizures.

Video-EEG is considered the gold standard for diagnosing psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, while tilt testing with video-EEG, heart rate, blood pressure or cerebral perfusion recording is used for psychogenic pseudosyncope.

Reflex anoxic seizures, despite the misleading name, are cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope with asystole in infants and toddlers evoked by unpleasant or surprising stimuli; the ESC guidelines recommend the term 'VVS in infants' instead.

Breath-holding spells are classified as pallid or cyanotic based on facial colour during the attack, both typically starting around 10 months of age; pallid breath-holding is synonymous with reflex anoxic seizures (VVS in infants), whereas cyanotic breath-holding spells involve an involuntary respiratory reflex causing secondary circulatory impairment.

Nonpharmacological measures such as increased water and salt intake, bolus water ingestion before risk situations, and physical counter-manoeuvres like forceful leg crossing are the mainstay therapy for vasovagal syncope and initial orthostatic hypotension, though none has been formally proven effective in children.
Chest discomfort and palpitations are common in adolescents with syncope, possibly related to hyperventilation, and are unreliable discriminators for cardiogenic syncope.
Postsyncopal fatigue, sleepiness and headache are common after vasovagal syncope.

A retrospective chart review of patients treated for hyperfunctional facial lines or dystonias who also had headache disorders found that onabotulinumtoxinA appeared to be a promising treatment for migraine.

An internal analysis showed that onabotulinumtoxinA's pain-relieving effect was only weakly correlated with reduction in muscle resistance to passive movement, supporting a direct antinociceptive action independent of muscle relaxation.

Nociceptive free nerve endings in muscle contain substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide, providing an anatomical rationale for a direct effect of onabotulinumtoxinA on afferent sensory signaling relevant to pain and migraine.

Botulinum toxin type A injections given for hemifacial spasm were observed to decrease facial sweating, consistent with the toxin's known blockade of postganglionic sympathetic cholinergic fibers innervating sweat glands.
Bhatia and colleagues reported successful reduction of sialorrhea using botulinum toxin type A injections into the parotid gland in four patients with neurological disease.
A human study showed that botulinum toxin type A injections significantly reduced rhinorrhea for up to 4 weeks compared with placebo in patients with intrinsic (parasympathetically-driven) rhinitis.

Finzi and Wasserman reported in 2006 that onabotulinumtoxinA injection into glabellar frown lines improved symptoms of major depressive disorder, invoking the facial feedback hypothesis linking facial expression and emotion.
Benefits of onabotulinumtoxinA for depression were subsequently confirmed in three double-blind, placebo-controlled studies and in an Allergan phase 2 trial.

Using fMRI, Hennenlotter and colleagues found that reducing facial muscle feedback via botulinum toxin type A injection attenuated amygdala activation and its coupling with other emotion-related brain regions.
Kim and colleagues found that botulinum toxin type A attenuated amygdala activity in response to angry faces.
In an animal model, injection of onabotulinumtoxinA into the epicardial fat pads suppressed vagally mediated atrial fibrillation.

A human study found that intraoperative administration of onabotulinumtoxinA into the cardiac fat pads did not meet its primary endpoint (time to >30 seconds of in-hospital postoperative atrial fibrillation), although treatment decreased the duration of the first-episode atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery.
A case report described resolution of vaginismus symptoms following onabotulinumtoxinA pelvic floor injections in a woman whose condition had contributed to marital breakdown.
