Dykstra and colleagues were, in 1988, the first to inject onabotulinumtoxinA into patients with detrusor sphincter dyssynergia, an approach that eventually led to its use for overactive bladder.

Clark and Berris described a patient with facial asymmetry from unilateral facial nerve paralysis who achieved relief from asymmetry after contralateral frontalis muscle injection with onabotulinumtoxinA, without ptosis or other adverse events.
During spontaneous migraine attacks, functional connectivity between the primary somatosensory/motor cortices and the posterior insula was decreased bilaterally compared to the interictal period.

Lower functional connectivity between the sensorimotor cortex and posterior insula, present in both ictal and interictal sessions, was associated with patients who typically experience longer migraine attacks.
78% of surveyed EDS/HSD patients reported a formal or suspected diagnosis of dysautonomia, the most commonly reported comorbidity.
69% of surveyed EDS/HSD patients reported a formal or suspected diagnosis of anxiety.
67% of surveyed EDS/HSD patients reported a formal or suspected diagnosis of migraine.
66% of surveyed EDS/HSD patients reported a formal or suspected diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome.
65% of surveyed EDS/HSD patients reported a formal or suspected diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome.
58% of surveyed EDS/HSD patients reported a formal or suspected diagnosis of depression.
On average, respondents reported having 6.6 of the 10 most common EDS/HSD-related comorbidities either formally diagnosed or suspected, indicating a high overall comorbidity burden.
Nearly all (94%) of respondents reported that their EDS/HSD-related symptoms negatively affected their ability to work, attend school, or participate in preferred recreational activities.
The average longest time respondents waited for a diagnosis of EDS/HSD or a related disorder was 17.2 years.

Nearly all (95%) of respondents reported experiencing medical trauma or medical gaslighting, defined as providers discounting or minimizing symptoms or inappropriately attributing them to psychosocial causes.
Over half (56%) of respondents said their experiences with medical trauma/gaslighting caused them to avoid or put off medical care, with an additional 11% avoiding care as much as possible.
Nearly half (49%) of respondents were dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with their current local medical support for EDS/HSD symptoms.
The majority (82%) of respondents found it somewhat difficult, difficult, or very difficult to access quality care for their EDS/HSD condition.

Despite 99% of respondents believing provider collaboration was important to outcomes, 63% were dissatisfied with the collaboration among their current or past providers, with 22% 'very dissatisfied.'

Nearly all respondents (95%) said they would utilize a proposed Chicagoland EDS/HSD collaborative center within one to two years of its availability, with 82% describing themselves as 'very likely' to do so.

Just over half (55%) of respondents had accessed complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) or integrative care in the last five years, and 90% expressed interest in using such services at a future center.
Physical therapy showed very high past utilization (78%) and future interest (92%) among respondents.
Despite 74% having private insurance, 30% of respondents spent $10,000 or more on EDS/HSD-related healthcare costs in the preceding year, and 9% spent more than $20,000.

Sixty-eight percent of respondents had a formal diagnosis of hEDS or HSD, with an additional 20% having a suspected EDS/HSD diagnosis, illustrating substantial diagnostic uncertainty in this population.
Childhood (pre-pain) motion sickness susceptibility scores differed significantly across the seven groups in an ANCOVA controlling for sex and anxiety.
Individuals with fibromyalgia syndrome reported significantly higher childhood (pre-pain) motion sickness susceptibility than pain-free controls, with scores 83% higher.
Migraine sufferers showed 47% higher childhood motion sickness susceptibility scores than controls, but this did not reach statistical significance after correction.
Low back pain patients showed 27% higher childhood motion sickness susceptibility than controls, not statistically significant.
Neck pain patients showed 48% higher childhood motion sickness susceptibility than controls, not statistically significant.
Whiplash-associated disorder patients showed 58% higher childhood motion sickness susceptibility than controls, close to but not reaching significance.

Rheumatoid arthritis patients (used as an additional control group) showed 42% higher childhood motion sickness susceptibility than pain-free controls, not statistically significant, though noted as a potential vestibular confound.
Adult (current) motion sickness susceptibility scores did not differ significantly between groups after adjusting for sex and anxiety.
Migraine patients showed nearly double (94% higher) adult motion sickness susceptibility scores than controls, a difference that narrowly missed statistical significance.

Rheumatoid arthritis, low back pain, neck pain, and whiplash-associated disorder groups showed 33-81% higher adult motion sickness susceptibility scores than controls, none reaching statistical significance.
Anxiety scores were weakly but significantly correlated with both childhood and adult motion sickness susceptibility scores.
Females reported significantly higher current adult motion sickness susceptibility scores than males, though the sex difference was not significant for childhood scores.
Among pain-free controls, age was not associated with either childhood or adult motion sickness susceptibility scores.
Similar reductions in monthly headache days were observed in patients under and over 65 years old, suggesting age does not predict response to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
In a pooled patient-level analysis of 1410 migraine patients (ESTEEMen), response to erenumab did not differ between male and female patients.
No difference in mean MHD reduction was seen between pre- and post-menopausal patients treated with CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Being employed rather than unemployed increased the odds of being a responder to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
A negative family history of migraine was associated with decreased likelihood of response to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2) was a negative predictor of response to CGRP(-R) mAbs in chronic migraine patients.
A negative association between obesity and treatment response was also seen in another cohort, but did not reach statistical significance in multivariable analysis.
Super-responders were more likely to have unilateral pain than non-responders, though the difference was not statistically significant.
Unilateral pain was more frequent among 3-month responders and was associated with a significantly greater reduction in monthly headache days than bilateral pain.
Both unilateral fixed and unilateral alternating pain were associated with higher likelihood of responding to CGRP(-R) mAbs, independent of other associated variables.
One study found a nonsignificant univariable association between unilateral pain and response rate.
The combination of unilateral pain and allodynia predicted a ≥50% response in chronic migraine patients.
Patients with cranial autonomic symptoms had a significantly higher reduction in monthly headache days at 12 weeks than those without.
Presence of vomiting during migraine attacks was positively associated with a ≥75% reduction in monthly headache days after 3 months of CGRP(-R) mAb treatment.
Patients with moderate photophobia (vs. none) tended to respond better to CGRP(-R) mAbs, though this did not reach significance in multivariable analysis.
Absence of all accompanying symptoms (nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia) predicted nonresponse to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
No difference in response rates was found between migraine with and without aura.

Pathologically heightened sensitivity fulfilling the definition of cephalic allodynia, measured by quantitative sensory testing in the interictal phase, was strongly associated with less than 50% reduction in monthly migraine days after 3 months of treatment.
Interictal extra-cephalic allodynia measured by quantitative sensory testing was also associated with less than 50% reduction in monthly migraine days after 3 months of treatment.
A higher heat pain threshold (lower thermal sensitivity) predicted good response to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Presence of allodynia as a clinical symptom was associated with nonresponse after 3 months of CGRP(-R) mAb treatment.
Pooled analysis of four studies showed migraine patients with daily headaches were significantly more likely to be nonresponders to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
A favorable response to triptans for acute migraine treatment was associated with a good response to CGRP(-R) mAbs, with a pooled odds ratio of 2.66 across studies.
One study found medication overuse at baseline predicted a ≥50% response to CGRP(-R) mAbs, an association not replicated in other studies which generally found MO decreased response likelihood.
In Schoenen et al., 86.7% of migraine patients with daily headaches were nonresponders to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
The number of monthly headache or migraine days at baseline alone did not show a significant relationship with response rate to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Baseline migraine burden scores such as HIT-6 and MIDAS showed an unclear relationship with response to CGRP(-R) mAbs, with most odds ratios not reaching significance.
A favorable response to triptan acute medication was associated with a good response to CGRP(-R) mAbs, with a pooled OR of 2.66.

Frattale et al. hypothesized that in patients with good triptan response, CGRP is the main mediator generating and maintaining migraine attacks, whereas in triptan non-responders other pain mediators not targeted by CGRP(-R) mAbs may predominate.

In most studies, presence of medication overuse at baseline decreased the likelihood of achieving ≥50% response to CGRP(-R) mAbs, though most individual odds ratios were not statistically significant.
In contrast to most studies, Vernieri et al. found that medication overuse at baseline was predictive of a ≥50% response to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
A greater number of previous preventive medication failures was associated with a decreased likelihood of responding to CGRP(-R) mAbs, with a pooled OR of 0.83 per additional failure.
Patients with psychiatric comorbidities in general were less likely to respond to CGRP(-R) mAbs, with a pooled OR of 0.56.
Comorbid depression specifically was associated with a decreased likelihood of responding to CGRP(-R) mAbs, with a pooled OR of 0.51.
Personality disorders and a greater number of serious stressful events were associated with treatment response failure to CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Lovati et al. found non-responders scored higher on disinhibition, anhedonia, depressivity, and distractibility on the PID-5 questionnaire compared to full-responders.
In Driessen et al., response rate to fremanezumab was not significantly different in subgroups with major depressive disorder or generalized anxiety disorder.
Vernieri et al. found comorbid gastroesophageal reflux disease indicated a predisposition to treatment failure with CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Ihara et al. found that a history of immuno-rheumatological disorders was linked to treatment failure with CGRP(-R) mAbs.
Non-responders to erenumab and fremanezumab had higher baseline mean flow velocities in both middle cerebral arteries on transcranial Doppler compared to good responders.
Alpuente et al. found that higher baseline salivary CGRP levels were independently associated with treatment response to erenumab in patients with episodic migraine.
De Vries Lentsch et al. did not find an association between baseline serum CGRP-like immunoreactivity and reduction in monthly migraine days with CGRP(-R) mAb treatment.
Zecca et al. found the RAMP1 rs7590387 genetic variant was less frequent in patients with ≥75% response compared to non-responders, though significance was lost in multivariable analysis.

In a post hoc analysis of a randomized clinical trial, obese patients (class I and II) receiving 100 mg eptinezumab did not show a ≥50% responder rate superior to placebo, but a higher 300 mg dose achieved more than 10% separation from placebo in both obesity classes.
In phase II and III randomized clinical trials of fremanezumab and galcanezumab, baseline weight or obesity (even BMI >30 kg/m2) did not influence treatment outcomes.
Migraine patients with depressive symptoms had higher salivary CGRP levels independent of monthly headache days, suggesting a separate pathology contributing to treatment failure.
MrgprB2 Cre tdTomato reporter expression overlapped almost completely with the mast cell marker avidin in mouse meninges, confirming MrgprB2 expression on meningeal mast cells.
MrgprB2-expressing meningeal mast cells were located in close proximity to peripheral nerve endings within the meninges.
Flow cytometry showed the majority of c-kit+FcεRI+ meningeal and peritoneal mast cells were MrgprB2-expressing.

MrgprB2 knockout mice showed significantly reduced Compound 48/80-induced mechanical facial hypersensitivity compared to wild-type mice in both sexes, indicating MrgprB2 mediates this migraine-like pain response.
PACAP1-38 activated MrgprB2 expressed in HEK293 cells with an EC50 in the low micromolar range.
PACAP1-38 activated human MRGPRX2 expressed in HEK293 cells with an EC50 in the low nanomolar range, roughly 170-fold more potent than at MrgprB2.

PACAP1-38 activated a significant percentage of WT connective tissue mast cells, but this activation was completely absent in MrgprB2-/- mast cells, demonstrating MrgprB2 dependence of PACAP1-38-induced mast cell activation.

Dural application of PACAP1-38 significantly increased mechanical facial hypersensitivity in WT mice compared to baseline, while MrgprB2-/- male and female mice showed significantly reduced hypersensitivity compared to WT.
PACAP1-38 dose-dependently induced β-hexosaminidase release from WT human LAD2 mast cells expressing MRGPRX2, but not from MRGPRX2-knockout LAD2 cells.
In humanized transgenic mice, PACAP1-38 significantly activated peritoneal mast cells expressing MRGPRX2 (X2+) compared to control mice lacking MRGPRX2 expression (X2-).
Dural application of PACAP1-38 significantly increased mechanical facial hypersensitivity in humanized MRGPRX2+ (X2+) mice compared to control X2- mice, in both males and females.
PACAP1-38 was more potent at inducing mechanical hypersensitivity via MRGPRX2 than via MrgprB2, with the equivalent dose producing a 50% greater increase in humanized MRGPRX2+ mice.
Loss of MrgprB2 significantly attenuated but did not completely abolish PACAP1-38-mediated migraine-like pain, suggesting additional receptors (e.g., PAC1R, VPAC1, VPAC2) may also contribute.
Standing tests appear to lack sufficient diagnostic reliability to identify all adolescents who have postural tachycardia syndrome.
Apomorphine, a dopaminergic agonist, further enhanced nitroglycerin-induced mechanical allodynia in the in vivo rat migraine model.
Apomorphine increased brainstem c-Fos expression induced by nitroglycerin, reflecting enhanced trigeminovascular neuronal activation.
Apomorphine increased CGRP concentrations in trigeminal ganglion and brainstem in the nitroglycerin-induced migraine model.
The combination of haloperidol and ondansetron reduced basal CGRP release in the in vitro hemiskull preparation, while other drug combinations had no effect.

Haloperidol, a pure D2 receptor antagonist, appeared more effective than metoclopramide in reducing migraine-related parameters in both dopaminergic activation- and nitroglycerin-induced migraine-like conditions.
Plasma levels of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a vasodilator and marker of trigeminal inflammation, are increased in migraine patients.
Migraine prevalence differs by sex, affecting 17% of women and 6% of men.
In China, migraine prevalence was estimated at about 9.3% as of 2012.
In a single-blind trial, topical lavender oil applied at migraine onset reduced attack severity significantly more than placebo.
A higher proportion of patients in the lavender group were total or partial responders compared with placebo.
A greater proportion of lavender-treated patients showed improvement in associated migraine symptoms compared with placebo.
A three-month randomized controlled trial found that prophylactic lavender reduced the frequency and severity of migraine attacks.
In animal models, lavender reduced inflammation and neuropathic pain via effects on peripheral and central opioid and cannabinoid type-2 receptors.
In an animal model of renal ischemia/reperfusion injury, lavender oil improved antioxidant enzyme activity, reduced lipid peroxidation, and markedly lowered TNF-alpha and IL-1beta concentrations.
Linalyl acetate in lavender oil exerts anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting NF-kB activation.
Lavender caused dilation of rabbit carotid arteries in an experimental study.
In diabetic rats, low-concentration intraperitoneal linalyl acetate increased acetylcholine-related aortic vasodilation.
A 28-day combination of Lavandula angustifolia and Citrus bergamia essential oils improved quality of life, particularly among emergency and critical care nurses.
Human cell line studies indicate lavender oil has estrogenic and antiandrogenic properties, relevant to considerations of allergy in adults.
A significantly smaller proportion of patients with generalised joint hypermobility (GJH) returned to sport within two years after ACL reconstruction compared with patients without GJH.
There was no significant difference between GJH and non-GJH groups in the proportion of patients who returned to their pre-injury activity level (RTP) within two years of ACL reconstruction.
There was no significant difference in the time to return to sport between the GJH and non-GJH groups.
There was no significant difference in the time to return to pre-injury activity level between the GJH and non-GJH groups.
At the time of return to pre-injury activity level, patients with GJH had lower quadriceps strength symmetry (limb symmetry index) than patients without GJH, though the effect size was small.
At the time of return to sport, there was no statistically significant difference between GJH and non-GJH groups in muscle function tests or patient-reported outcomes.

Apart from quadriceps strength LSI, there were no further statistically significant differences between GJH and non-GJH groups in muscle function tests or patient-reported outcomes at the time of return to pre-injury activity.
Among patients who returned to sport, knee hyperextension was far more prevalent in the GJH group than in the non-GJH group.
Among patients who returned to sport, the GJH group had a significantly greater proportion of women than the non-GJH group.
Among patients who returned to pre-injury activity level, patellar tendon autografts were used more often for ACL reconstruction in the GJH group than in the non-GJH group.

An ad-hoc analysis stratifying return-to-sport rates by patient sex and by graft choice showed no statistically significant difference, suggesting the lower RTS rate in GJH patients is not simply explained by sex or graft type.
Among patients who returned to sport, those with GJH were significantly younger than those without GJH.
Female sex was less predominant among NDPH patients (62.6%) than among T-CDH patients (73.3%).
About 38% of NDPH patients had an identifiable precipitant for their headache, most commonly an influenza-like viral illness.
A minority of NDPH patients (6.3%) reported a thunderclap headache at onset.
NDPH patients had significantly lower rates of nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, motion sensitivity, cranial autonomic symptoms, and aura symptoms compared to T-CDH patients.
NDPH patients were more likely to have strictly unilateral headache, while T-CDH patients more often had both unilateral and bilateral headache presentations.

By phenotype alone, 64% of NDPH patients met ICHD-3 criteria for chronic migraine, 28% for chronic tension-type headache, and 9% for neither, compared with 84%, 10%, and 4% respectively in the T-CDH group.

Joint hypermobility disorder diagnosis was unexpectedly more common in T-CDH patients than in NDPH patients, suggesting hypermobility is a predisposing factor for chronic headache in general rather than specific to NDPH.
Medication overuse was far less common in NDPH (15.6%) than in T-CDH (42.1%).
There was a trend for acute treatments including NSAIDs and triptans to be less effective in NDPH than in T-CDH.
Dosulepin (doselupin) was the most effective preventive treatment trialed in NDPH, with 45.6% of patients experiencing at least a 30% improvement.
Response to most oral preventive treatments was poor in both NDPH and T-CDH, with fewer than 20% of patients achieving even a 30% improvement with many treatments.

K-means cluster analysis of 337 NDPH patients identified three subgroups differing by age, sex, headache severity, migrainous symptoms, and trigger burden: an older male, less severe cluster; a predominantly female, severe, low-migrainous-symptom cluster; and a predominantly female, high-migrainous-symptom, high-trigger cluster.
Among the three NDPH clusters, cluster 3 (high migrainous symptoms/high triggers) had a significantly greater proportion of patients responding to any acute treatment than clusters 1 and 2.

Anxiety and depression scores measured by HADS did not differ significantly between NDPH and T-CDH groups, and diagnosed depression and anxiety were both slightly less common in NDPH, arguing against NDPH having a greater psychological basis than other chronic daily headache.
Cardiovascular autonomic testing (CAT) established a definitive cause of syncope in 79% of patients with previously unexplained syncope, while 21% remained without a diagnosis.
Vasovagal syncope (VVS) was the single most common CAT diagnosis, present in 42% of patients.
Complex syncope, defined as ≥2 concomitant diagnoses (CSS, VVS, OH) during testing, was found in 16% of patients, establishing it as a distinct, clinically useful diagnostic category.
Orthostatic hypotension (OH) was diagnosed in 10% of patients with unexplained syncope.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was identified as the cause of syncope in 4% of patients evaluated by CAT.
Carotid sinus syndrome (CSS) was diagnosed in 4% of patients with unexplained syncope.
Psychogenic pseudosyncope (PPS) was diagnosed in 2% of patients with unexplained syncope.
Immediate orthostatic hypotension (iOH) was present in only 1% of patients with unexplained syncope.
Vasovagal syncope prevalence peaked around age 20 and decreased steadily with increasing age.
The frequency of negative CAT was relatively even across the 20–50-year age group but slightly higher in the 60–70-year age group.
Complex syncope prevalence showed a bimodal age distribution, with a small peak at age 20–25 years and a larger peak at 70–75 years.
Orthostatic hypotension prevalence increased with age, peaking around age 70.
POTS and psychogenic pseudosyncope (PPS) prevalence were both highest around age 20 years.
Carotid sinus syndrome prevalence increased with age and was highest around age 75.

A range of clinical and demographic factors, including older age, higher supine systolic blood pressure and heart rate, absence of prodromes, hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery disease, were univariate predictors of a negative CAT result.
Older age at first syncope was an independent predictor of negative CAT, with 8% higher odds per 10-year increment.
Higher supine heart rate was an independent predictor of negative CAT, with 12% higher odds per 10 b.p.m. increase.
Absence of prodromal symptoms was the strongest clinical predictor of negative CAT, associated with 48% higher odds.
A history of hypertension was an independent predictor of negative CAT, with 45% higher odds.
A history of diabetes was an independent predictor of negative CAT, with 82% higher odds.
A history of heart failure was an independent predictor of negative CAT, with 98% higher odds.
A history of coronary artery disease was an independent predictor of negative CAT, with 51% higher odds.
Supine systolic blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, although significant on univariate analysis, were not significant independent predictors of negative CAT after adjustment for age and gender.
Patients with negative CAT were significantly older than VVS patients (median age 54 vs. 40 years).
Patients with negative CAT reported prodromes significantly less frequently than VVS patients (44% vs. 59%).

Reported palpitations, orthostatic dizziness, and supine syncope did not significantly differ between negative CAT and VVS patients, and traumatic syncope injuries showed only a non-significant tendency toward being more frequent in the negative CAT group.

A prior meta-analysis of 38,843 patients found that unexplained syncope was associated with a 13% increase in all-cause mortality compared with controls, with a stronger association in older, diabetic, and/or hypertensive patients.
The AI-based diagnostic model achieved high overall diagnostic performance across headache subtypes on the internal test dataset, with micro-average accuracy of 93.7%.
The model showed particularly strong diagnostic performance specifically for migraine, with a sensitivity of 88.8% and a c-statistic of 0.89.
In the clinic-based dataset used to build and validate the model, migraine was by far the most common diagnosis, comprising nearly 80% of the 6058 patients.
Aerobic exercise training showed low certainty evidence of a clinically relevant reduction in mobility difficulties at the end of the intervention in people with fibromyalgia.
Mixed exercise training showed low certainty evidence of a clinically relevant reduction in mobility difficulties at the end of the intervention in people with fibromyalgia.
Ten included Cochrane reviews were methodologically assessed with AMSTAR-2, with one rated moderate quality, seven rated low quality, and two rated critically low quality.

At an average follow-up of 24 weeks, mixed exercise training and cognitive behavioural therapies showed low certainty, clinically relevant evidence for reducing mobility difficulties in fibromyalgia patients.

Mixed exercise training showed low certainty, clinically relevant improvement in health-related quality of life at an average follow-up of 24 weeks, with NNTB values ranging from 5 to 11 for a 15% MCID.
Dropout rates for any reason did not differ between active non-pharmacological interventions and controls, except for biofeedback and movement therapies.
All systematic reviews reported that adverse event reporting was inconsistent across the analysed studies, with very low certainty evidence overall.
The overview identified 181 randomised or quasi-randomised trials totaling 11,917 participants across ten eligible Cochrane reviews, with an average trial size of 66 participants.
Survey respondents with migraine reported greater pain relief from full doses of classical psychedelics than from conventional medication.
Microdoses of psychedelics achieved significantly better pain relief than conventional medication among respondents with migraine.
Respondents with fibromyalgia reported better pain relief with full-dose psychedelics compared to conventional medication.
Microdoses of psychedelics produced pain relief comparable to conventional medication in fibromyalgia (one of the three non-migraine categories with comparable relief).
Full-dose psychedelics were reported to give better pain relief than conventional medication in arthritis and tension-type headache, with microdoses providing comparable relief in these conditions.
Survey respondents with migraine reported significantly better pain relief from psychedelic microdoses than from conventional medication.
Among fibromyalgia patients, psychedelic microdoses achieved pain relief comparable to conventional medication.
Among arthritis patients, psychedelic microdoses achieved pain relief comparable to conventional medication.
Among tension-type headache patients, psychedelic microdoses achieved pain relief comparable to conventional medication.

Women with generalized joint hypermobility had a higher proportion of pelvic girdle pain in early pregnancy (47.1%) than women without GJH (32.6%), but the adjusted association was not statistically significant.
In late pregnancy, PGP prevalence rose in both groups and no significant association remained between GJH and PGP.
At 9 months after childbirth there was no significant association between GJH and PGP.

Women with the combination of generalized joint hypermobility and early-pregnancy BMI ≥25 kg/m2 had markedly increased odds of pelvic girdle pain in early pregnancy compared with women with normal joint mobility and BMI <25 kg/m2.

Women with generalized joint hypermobility had significantly higher odds of reporting greater pelvic pain intensity in early pregnancy than women without GJH (aOR 2.04), but this association was not significant at late pregnancy or 9 months postpartum.
A higher proportion of women with GJH reported pelvic girdle pain onset before the current pregnancy compared with women without GJH.
A lower proportion of women with GJH had pelvic girdle pain onset during the current pregnancy compared with women without GJH (borderline significance).
Among women with pregnancy-induced PGP, a higher proportion of those with GJH had onset in early pregnancy compared with women without GJH, though not statistically significant.
Using a Beighton score cut-off of ≥5/9, the prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility among pregnant women in this cohort was 9.6%.

The authors propose that relaxin, a hormone that peaks in the first trimester and promotes collagen remodeling and pelvic ligament relaxation, may make women with generalized joint hypermobility more vulnerable to pelvic girdle pain in early pregnancy, especially combined with high BMI.

Sensitivity analyses suggested a tendency for childbirth, early BMI ≥25 kg/m2, and pregnancy-induced PGP onset to increase the odds of pelvic girdle pain in women with GJH, but none of these associations reached statistical significance.
Compared with unaffected cohorts, vasovagal syncope patients show lower systolic BP, higher diastolic BP, and higher heart rate, suggesting reduced venous return and stroke volume as reflex triggers.
A genetic association study suggested that syncope patients may share genetic susceptibility to lower blood pressure and altered autonomic control of circulation.
Reflex syncope patients show higher anxiety levels compared with individuals with no previous loss of consciousness, suggesting anxiety is a component of the reflex-related phenotype.
Tilt-positive patients had lower systolic BP, diastolic BP, and heart rate compared with tilt-negative patients, independent of age and gender, implying reduced capacity to compensate for lower BP.
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is hypothesized to result from age-related autonomic dysregulation leading to a blunted sympathetic response.
Cardioinhibition (vagally mediated bradycardia/asystole) predominates in younger reflex syncope patients, while vasodepression (sympathetic withdrawal) is stronger in older patients.

In 163 patients with tilt-induced syncope, the early BP decrease was primarily due to low stroke volume with incomplete compensatory heart rate increase, while decreased peripheral resistance played only a minor, later role, and cardioinhibition emerged as an equally large but later determinant of the BP fall (~1 min before syncope).
A pronounced increase in circulating epinephrine and vasopressin, likely a compensatory response to hypotension, heralds the imminent vasovagal reflex during tilt testing.
Cerebral tissue oxygenation progressively decreases, independent of mean arterial pressure, in patients with spontaneous vasovagal reflex during passive tilt testing.

A subgroup of patients with sudden-onset cardioinhibitory syncope without prodromes (adenosine-sensitive syncope) shows a purinergic profile opposite to typical vasovagal syncope, with low plasma adenosine, low A2A adenosine receptor expression, or a dysfunctional genetic variant.
Twenty-four hour Holter monitoring is rarely useful for syncope diagnosis because symptoms usually do not recur during the monitoring period, giving a true diagnostic yield as low as 1-2%.

In syncope units, cardiac aetiology is diagnosed in 6-13% of patients, reflex syncope in 56-73%, orthostatic hypotension in 1-10%, psychogenic pseudosyncope in 1-2%, and the cause remains unexplained in 18-20% of cases.
A mean 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP below 105 mmHg in men and below 97 mmHg in women identifies patients with constitutional hypotension.
A mean 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP of 110 mmHg or less predicted a diagnosis of reflex syncope with 60% sensitivity and 70% specificity.

In a large multicentre comparison, one or more daytime systolic BP drops below 90 mmHg on ambulatory monitoring identified hypotensive susceptibility in reflex syncope with 91% specificity and 32% sensitivity (OR 4.6), while two or more drops below 100 mmHg achieved 84% specificity and 40% sensitivity (OR 3.5).

A meta-analysis of 55 studies including 4361 patients undergoing head-up tilt testing for suspected reflex syncope found positivity rates of 37% with passive tilt, 60% with isoproterenol, and 66% with nitroglycerine protocols.

In a randomized trial of 544 patients, the Fast Italian tilt protocol (10 min passive + 10 min nitroglycerine) yielded a similar positivity rate (57.8%) to the traditional protocol (62.4%), with similar distribution of cardioinhibitory, mixed, and vasodepressor responses, allowing time and cost savings.
In the absence of symptom reproduction, carotid sinus hypersensitivity was reported in 35% of asymptomatic older subjects, indicating poor specificity as a cause of syncope.

A meta-analysis of 5 randomized controlled trials in 660 patients with unexplained syncope found that initial implantation of an implantable loop recorder increased the relative probability of reaching a diagnosis 3.7-fold compared with a conventional diagnostic strategy, and was more cost-effective.

A meta-analysis of 4 studies in 1046 patients over 40 years old undergoing ILR implantation for severe recurrent likely reflex syncope found 36.6% had a diagnostic ECG event during follow-up (mean 13±10 months), of which 52% were asystolic events (mean duration 12.8±11.0 s) consistent with a reflex mechanism (sinus arrest 52%, AV block 20%, both 11%, undefined 16%).

A recent meta-analysis showed the electrophysiological study has a negative predictive value of only 70% for detecting eventual AV block when ILRs are used as reference, indicating insufficient accuracy.

Two randomized studies of empirical pacemaker implantation in patients with syncope and bifascicular bundle branch block found no benefit from pacing on secondary analyses of syncopal recurrence, alongside a significant rate of pacemaker-related complications.
A standardized education protocol for vasovagal syncope significantly reduced traumatic injuries and syncope recurrences in a pre-post comparison of 316 patients.

A meta-analysis of five randomized controlled trials found that initial implantation of an implantable loop recorder increased the likelihood of reaching a diagnosis in patients with unexplained syncope compared with a conventional diagnostic strategy.

In a meta-analysis of 4 studies involving 1046 patients over 40 years undergoing ILR implantation for severe, recurrent, likely reflex syncope, 36.6% had a diagnostic ECG event during follow-up, and 52% of these showed an asystolic event compatible with a reflex mechanism.

A large observational pre-post study of 316 patients with vasovagal syncope found that implementing a standardized patient education protocol significantly reduced traumatic injuries and syncope recurrences.
The first randomized open-label controlled trial of physical counterpressure manoeuvres showed a 36% relative risk reduction in syncope recurrence among patients able to recognize prodromes.

A meta-analysis of 11 trials (only 2 randomized) including 688 patients concluded physical counterpressure manoeuvres might prevent vasovagal syncope, but with a low level of evidence since none of the included studies were blinded or adequately controlled.
Six randomized controlled trials of beta-adrenergic blockers for prevention of vasovagal syncope were overall negative, and beta-blockers now have a limited role, if any, in VVS prevention.
In the randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind POST2 trial, fludrocortisone 0.2 mg daily significantly reduced the likelihood of syncope after 2 weeks of dose stabilization.

The randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind Prevention of Syncope Trial IV found that midodrine significantly reduced the relative risk of syncope recurrence, with a stronger effect after dose adjustment.
A meta-analysis found midodrine reduced the relative risk of vasovagal syncope recurrence, supporting its use as reasonable first-line medical therapy for reflex syncope.

Norepinephrine transporter inhibitors atomoxetine, reboxetine, and sibutramine reduced the likelihood of vasovagal syncope induction during tilt testing, and empirical use of atomoxetine and sibutramine was associated with reduced VVS, although high-level evidence is lacking.
Old, small studies of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for vasovagal syncope produced inconsistent results and did not reach sufficient evidence to be recommended by ESC guidelines.

An HV interval of 70 ms or greater, or induction of infra-Hisian block during atrial pacing, identifies patients with bifascicular bundle branch block who are at higher risk of developing atrioventricular block.

A recent meta-analysis showed that electrophysiological study has a negative predictive value of only 70% for detecting subsequent AV block when ILRs are used as the reference, indicating insufficiently accurate test characteristics.

Two randomized studies of empirical pacemaker implantation in patients with syncope and bifascicular block found no benefit from pacing on secondary analysis of syncopal recurrence, despite a significant rate of pacemaker-related complications.
In the ISSUE 3 randomized study, patients over 40 with recurrent asystolic syncope who received active DDD pacing had a significant reduction in syncope recurrences compared with sensing-only mode.

A meta-analysis found the estimated 3-year syncope recurrence rate after pacing was 2% in tilt-negative patients versus 33% in tilt-positive patients, with a positive tilt test being the only significant predictor of recurrence.

Two randomized controlled studies in patients over 40 with recurrent syncope and tilt-induced asystole reported significant benefit of closed-loop stimulation (CLS) pacing compared with sensing-only pacing.
A randomized, unblinded study of radiofrequency cardioneuroablation targeting cardiac ganglionated plexi reported high efficacy in preventing asystolic reflex syncope at 2-year follow-up.
The most common complication of cardioneuroablation is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, occurring in 6-20% of patients and sometimes requiring further treatment; its long-term safety remains unknown.
Two recent studies reported that yoga practice improves clinical outcomes and quality of life in patients with vasovagal syncope.

In a randomized clinical trial comparing ineffective pacemakers with ineffective beta-blockers for vasovagal syncope, pacemaker-treated patients did much better, illustrating that an invasive placebo was more effective than a non-invasive placebo.

Most patients in the control arms of randomized and observational vasovagal syncope trials do not faint during follow-up despite having fainted recurrently before enrollment, suggesting a substantial non-specific study/placebo effect.
A genetic association study suggested that syncope patients share genetic susceptibility to lower blood pressure and altered autonomic control of the circulation.
Reflex syncope patients show higher anxiety levels than individuals who have never experienced loss of consciousness, suggesting anxiety may be part of the reflex syncope phenotype.
Patients with a positive tilt test had lower systolic BP, diastolic BP, and heart rate than tilt-negative patients, independent of age and sex.
Older individuals have greater orthostatic tolerance than younger individuals because of higher systolic blood pressure providing a greater BP reserve.
The positivity rate of passive tilt testing decreases with advancing age, indicating older patients require stronger provocative stimuli to induce the syncope cascade.
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity may result from age-related autonomic dysregulation leading to a blunted sympathetic response.
Cardioinhibition typically predominates as the mechanism of reflex syncope in younger individuals, whereas vasodepression is the stronger mechanism in older age.

In a study of 163 patients with tilt-induced syncope, the early drop in blood pressure was caused by reduced stroke volume with incomplete compensatory increase in heart rate, while cardioinhibition emerged later as an equally important determinant of BP fall just before syncope.
A steep increase in circulating epinephrine and vasopressin precedes and heralds the onset of the vasovagal reflex during tilt testing, likely as a compensatory response to hypotension.
Cerebral tissue oxygenation progressively decreases during tilt testing in patients who develop spontaneous vasovagal reflex, independent of mean arterial pressure changes.

A subgroup of patients with sudden-onset cardioinhibitory syncope (complete AV block without prodromes) shows a purinergic profile opposite to vasovagal syncope, characterized by low plasma adenosine, low A2A adenosine receptor expression, or a dysfunctional genetic variant, termed adenosine-sensitive syncope.
Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring has a very low diagnostic yield in syncope, as low as 1–2%, because symptoms rarely recur during the monitoring period.

In syncope units, cardiac aetiology is diagnosed in 6–13% of patients, reflex syncope in 56–73%, orthostatic hypotension in 1–10%, and psychogenic pseudosyncope in 1–2%, with 18–20% remaining unexplained.
Mean 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP below 105 mmHg in men and below 97 mmHg in women identifies patients with constitutional hypotension.
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is found in 35% of asymptomatic elderly individuals in the absence of symptom reproduction, indicating poor specificity as a cause of syncope.

A meta-analysis found that electrophysiological study has a negative predictive value of only 70% for detecting eventual AV block when using ILR as the reference, an insufficiently accurate test characteristic.

Two randomized studies of empirical pacemaker implantation in patients with syncope and bifascicular block found no benefit for syncope recurrence in secondary analyses, along with a significant rate of pacemaker-related complications.
A standardized patient education protocol for vasovagal syncope significantly reduced traumatic injuries and syncope recurrences in a large pre-post observational study of 316 patients.
Increased fluid and salt intake may improve orthostatic tolerance in vasovagal syncope, but hydration alone does not appear sufficient to prevent symptoms.
In a small cohort of elderly hypertensive patients with confirmed vasovagal syncope, withdrawing or reducing antihypertensive therapy significantly reduced presyncope and syncope.
The first randomized open-label controlled trial of physical counterpressure manoeuvres showed a 36% relative risk reduction in vasovagal syncope recurrence.

A meta-analysis of 688 patients across 11 trials (only 2 randomized) concluded that physical counterpressure manoeuvres might be effective for prevention of vasovagal syncope, but with a low level of evidence since none of the trials were blinded or adequately controlled.
Physical counterpressure manoeuvres may be less effective in older patients and those with minimal prodromal symptoms because the manoeuvre is initiated too late.
Tilt training and stand training may not be effective for preventing vasovagal syncope, with poor long-term compliance and effectiveness.
Six randomized controlled trials of beta-adrenergic blockers for prevention of vasovagal syncope were, on the whole, negative, resulting in a class III (not recommended) designation.
In the placebo-controlled, double-blind Prevention of Syncope Trial II (POST2), fludrocortisone 0.2 mg daily significantly reduced the likelihood of syncope after two weeks of dose stabilization.

The Prevention of Syncope Trial IV, a randomized placebo-controlled double-blind trial, found midodrine significantly reduced relative risk of vasovagal syncope recurrence, with an even lower hazard ratio after dose adjustment.
A meta-analysis found midodrine reduced the risk of vasovagal syncope recurrence with a relative risk of 0.71.

The norepinephrine transporter inhibitors atomoxetine, reboxetine, and sibutramine reduced the likelihood of vasovagal syncope induction during tilt testing, and empiric atomoxetine and sibutramine use was associated with reduced VVS, though robust high-level evidence is lacking.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors were assessed in old, small studies with inconsistent results and did not reach sufficient evidence for inclusion in ESC guideline recommendations for vasovagal syncope.

In the ISSUE 3 randomized trial, patients over 40 with recurrent asystolic syncope or non-syncopal asystole >6s documented by ILR who received active dual-chamber (DDD) pacing had a significant reduction in syncope recurrence compared with sensing-only pacemakers.

A meta-analysis found the estimated 3-year syncope recurrence rate after pacing was 2% in tilt-negative patients versus 33% in tilt-positive patients, with a positive tilt test being the only significant predictor of recurrence.

Two randomized controlled trials in patients over 40 with recurrent syncope and tilt-induced asystole reported significant benefit of closed-loop stimulation (CLS) pacing compared with sensing-only (ODO) pacemakers.
A randomized, unblinded study reported high efficacy of radiofrequency cardioneuroablation targeting cardiac ganglionated plexi at 2-year follow-up for asystolic reflex syncope.
The most common complication of cardioneuroablation is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, occurring in 6-20% of patients and at times requiring further treatment.

In a randomized trial comparing (ineffective) pacemakers with (ineffective) beta-blockers for vasovagal syncope, patients receiving pacemakers fared much better, suggesting an invasive placebo was more effective than a non-invasive placebo.
Two recent studies reported that yoga improves outcomes and quality of life in patients with vasovagal syncope.
The title reports a case in which the antibiotic meropenem induced facial myoclonus, but no abstract or further detail is available to characterize the case.
A single 60-minute IV lidocaine infusion produced a response (≥50% reduction in pain intensity) in 80% of treatment-refractory patients, with 53% achieving complete resolution of head/facial pain.
Among responders to the first infusion, benefit lasted on average 9.5 weeks, with the majority (83%) benefiting for longer than 4 weeks.
In the six chronic SUNCT/SUNA patients, four (67%) responded to IV lidocaine with an accompanying 50% reduction in daily attack frequency.
Both chronic cluster headache patients responded to IV lidocaine, with an average benefit duration of 5 weeks.
All three trigeminal neuralgia patients responded to IV lidocaine, with an average duration of response of 10.7 weeks and at least a 50% reduction in daily attacks.
All three chronic orofacial migraine patients responded to IV lidocaine, showing an average 77% reduction in headache intensity lasting about 9 weeks.
The single patient with hemicrania continua did not respond to IV lidocaine treatment.

Six of 15 patients (40%) experienced at least one adverse event during the infusion, all mild and self-limiting, including peri-oral tingling, light-headedness, dull headache, limb numbness, dysgeusia, palpitations and tiredness.
All initial responders showed a sustained, similar magnitude of response to subsequent IV lidocaine infusions over time.
There was no statistically significant difference in duration of treatment benefit across the different diagnoses, though the study was likely underpowered to detect one.
Co-existing chronic migraine and fibromyalgia were present in five of the fifteen patients treated with IV lidocaine.
The treatment-refractory cohort had failed an average of 11.5 preventive treatments and 2.7 injectable or invasive treatments prior to IV lidocaine.
Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy had previously failed in five of the treatment-refractory patients prior to receiving IV lidocaine.

Lidocaine's anti-nociceptive effect is thought to be mediated by reversible blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels, which modulates peripheral and central sensitization implicated in headache and trigeminal neuralgia pathophysiology.

The lidocaine metabolite n-ethylglycine may prolong its anti-nociceptive effect via competitive inhibition of the glycine transporter GlyT1, increasing extracellular glycine and inhibiting ectopic sodium channel activation.
Lidocaine has anti-inflammatory properties that attenuate neutrophil activation and reduce serum concentrations of IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 and ICAM-1, mediators implicated in allodynia and hyperalgesia.
Generalized joint hypermobility (GJH), diagnosed by a Beighton score of 4 or more, was present in 20 of 84 (23.8%) patients with Hirayama disease.
HD patients with GJH had greater cervical-flexion range of motion than HD patients without GJH.
HD patients with GJH had greater cervical-extension range of motion than HD patients without GJH.
In the symptomatic-side abductor pollicis brevis, HD patients with GJH had greater single motor unit potential amplitudes than those without GJH.
In the less-symptomatic-side abductor pollicis brevis, HD patients with GJH had greater single motor unit potential amplitudes than those without GJH.
In the symptomatic-side abductor pollicis brevis, HD patients with GJH had lower motor unit numbers than those without GJH.
HD patients with generalized joint hypermobility had lower motor unit numbers in the less-symptomatic side abductor pollicis brevis muscle than those without hypermobility.
HD patients with generalized joint hypermobility had lower compound muscle action potential amplitude in the symptomatic-side abductor pollicis brevis muscle than those without hypermobility.
A mild negative correlation was found between motor unit number and cervical-flexion range of motion on the symptomatic side in HD patients.
A mild negative correlation was found between motor unit number and cervical-flexion range of motion on the less-symptomatic side in HD patients.
At 24 weeks, the neuron-derived extracellular vesicle phosphorylated-mTOR to total-mTOR ratio did not differ significantly between sirolimus- and placebo-treated MSA patients.
At 48 weeks, the neuron-derived extracellular vesicle phosphorylated-mTOR to total-mTOR ratio remained similar between sirolimus and placebo groups.
Neuron-derived extracellular vesicle total-mTOR, phosphorylated-mTOR, and their ratio were not associated with worsening on the Unified MSA Rating Scale.
Overall, the study concluded that oral sirolimus up to 6 mg/day did not engage brain mTOR pathways as measured by neuron-derived extracellular vesicle biomarkers.

The study proposes neuron-derived extracellular vesicle (NEV)-based biomarkers as a rational, minimally invasive approach for assessing target engagement of brain-directed therapeutics in clinical trials.
A phase II, placebo-controlled trial of the FcRn antagonist rozanolixizumab for severe fibromyalgia syndrome (NCT05643794) is recruiting in the UK, with no efficacy or safety data yet reported.
The authors encoded ICHD3 criteria using 103 prime numbers, generated 578 total encodings, and identified 99 pairs of logically contradictory characteristics.

After excluding logically contradictory characteristic pairs, the algorithm produced 253,842 unique dual-diagnosis composite-number profiles, which collapsed to 145 distinct logical dual diagnoses after removing duplicates.

Of the 145 logical dual diagnoses, 2 involved subset-relationship intersecting characteristics, 14 involved non-subset intersecting characteristics, and 129 (the majority) had non-intersecting characteristics.
The algorithm shows it is logically possible to diagnose migraine with aura concurrently with chronic tension-type headache and chronic migraine when aura occurs more than 15 days per month.

Cluster headache can be logically co-diagnosed with hypnic headache, and has a non-intersecting phenotypical relationship with migraine with aura, meaning both diagnoses can be satisfied without shared characteristics.

Citing de Coo et al., aura is estimated to be present in 7.0% of cluster headache diagnoses, from which the authors estimate migraine with aura can be co-diagnosed in approximately 7% of cluster headache patients.

Because cluster headache can be co-diagnosed with migraine with aura, the model implies it is theoretically possible to have a chronic migraine form of cluster headache co-occurring with migraine with aura when aura occurs ≥15 days/month.
A co-diagnosis between cluster headache and paroxysmal hemicrania is logically possible because cluster headache criteria are not defined by unresponsiveness to an indomethacin trial.
Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headaches can be logically co-diagnosed with primary sex headaches and primary stabbing headaches due to shared short-duration characteristics.
Based on Lobo et al.'s empirical study of NDPH phenotypes, co-diagnosis of tension-type headache in NDPH occurred in 8.8% of cases while co-diagnosis with chronic migraine occurred in 89.7% of cases.

Under strict ICHD3 definitions, it is logically impossible to diagnose new daily persistent headache concurrently with either migraine with or without aura, due to the exclusion of status migrainosus and the requirement that migraine attacks not be constant.

The model's finding that NDPH can be concurrently diagnosed with hemicrania continua, nummular headache, or thunderclap headache aligns with Rosen's prior clinical sub-classification of NDPH subtypes.

The model shows migraine without aura can be logically co-diagnosed with cold-induced headache, compression headache, or exercise headache, raising the question of whether stimulus-related headaches represent the same entity as migraine.

Post-traumatic headache represents approximately 4% of symptomatic headache disorders and, since its ICHD3 criteria share no characteristics with primary headache criteria, PTH can theoretically be concurrently diagnosed with any primary headache disorder.

Medication overuse headache has a prevalence of approximately 30-50% among patients seen at headache centers and, by ICHD3 definition, must always occur as a dual diagnosis with a pre-existing headache disorder occurring more than 15 days/month.

Episodic migraine (fewer than 15 days/month) cannot logically carry a concurrent diagnosis with medication overuse headache; therefore, an MOH diagnosis in migraine necessarily implies concurrent chronic migraine.

The prevalence of co-diagnosis arising from secondary headaches with a primary headache phenotype is estimated to range from 12.9% (tertiary headache center estimate) to 18% (WHO 2011 estimate) of all headache patients.
Greater deviation from an individual's typical monthly mean sleep duration the night before was a positive predictor of experiencing a migraine attack the following day.
A greater number of sleep interruptions the night before was a positive predictor of experiencing a migraine attack the following day.
Total hours slept the previous night did not predict whether a migraine attack occurred the next day.
Simply experiencing a migraine attack did not predict a change in total hours slept that same evening.
Greater self-reported pain intensity during a migraine attack was a positive predictor of increased total sleep duration that same evening.
A prior meta-analysis by the same research group found that migraine patients had poorer subjective sleep quality and reduced rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep compared with healthy controls.
App users self-reporting migraine attacks were predominantly female, mirroring the known female-predominant epidemiology of migraine.
Within the analytic sample, episodic migraine was far more prevalent than chronic migraine, precluding subgroup analysis by migraine chronicity.

Across all self-reported migraine attacks in the sample, throbbing or pulsating pain was the most frequently reported symptom, closely followed by photophobia, supporting that most reported headaches met migraine-like features.
Custom-made foot orthotics significantly reduced self-reported lower limb pain at 1 month compared to baseline, with further improvement by 3 months.
Most PedsQL health-related quality of life domains, including parent-reported emotional functioning, improved significantly at 1 month and were maintained or continued to improve at 3 months.
Self-reported social and school functioning did not significantly improve at 1 month but showed significant improvement compared to baseline by 3 months.
Fatigue scores (higher indicating fewer difficulties) improved significantly with custom orthotic use at 1 month and were maintained at 3 months.
Functional endurance capacity, measured by the six-minute walk test, improved alongside reductions in pain and fatigue and improvements in HRQoL following custom orthotic use.
The large majority of participants reported overall health improvement on the PGIC at 1 month, with all participants reporting improvement by 3 months and no participants reporting decline.

Custom-made orthotics were well tolerated with no serious adverse events; seven of 53 participants experienced minor, resolvable adverse events such as discomfort and blistering, all of which resolved by 3 months.

Weekly self-reported orthotic wear time increased significantly over the 12-week study period, with most participants wearing orthotics more than 20 hours per week from week 1 and more than 30 hours per week by week 11.
Generalised joint hypermobility is prevalent in approximately 34% of children and adolescents globally, with symptoms occurring in about one in five of these children.

A prior randomised controlled trial of 52 children with symptomatic generalised joint hypermobility found that modified prefabricated insoles worn for 12 weeks improved pain, physical health and function, stair ascent time, and transfer and basic mobility.
A small cohort study of 21 children with symptomatic generalised joint hypermobility found that prefabricated orthotics immediately improved gait patterns, though pain and fatigue were not assessed.

In adults with Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes, an observational cohort study found significant improvements in foot pain, functionality, fatigue and mental health-related quality of life after 3 months of custom-made orthotics.
Approximately 50% of human trigeminal ganglion neurons show CGRP immunoreactivity, indicating widespread CGRP expression in trigeminal sensory neurons relevant to migraine pathophysiology.
Up to 60% of human dorsal root ganglion neurons express CGRP mRNA, per a recent mRNA study.
In rodents, CGRP mRNA levels are 20 to 250 times lower in CNS structures such as the lateral medulla and midbrain/hypothalamus compared to the trigeminal ganglion.
CGRP levels in peripheral vasculature increased following intravenous nitroglycerin-induced experimental headache and during spontaneous migraine attacks with and without aura.
CGRP levels after migraine attacks decreased following sumatriptan treatment, coinciding with headache improvement.
Intravenous injection of CGRP into the peripheral vasculature of migraine patients caused a delayed headache with migrainous features, confirming a causal role for CGRP in migraine pathophysiology.
Rimegepant shows only 30-fold higher selectivity for the CGRP receptor than for the AMY1 receptor, illustrating cross-reactivity between gepants and amylin receptor signaling.

PET studies with the [C-11]MK-4322 tracer showed that after oral telcagepant administration only a small percentage was detected in cerebrospinal fluid relative to plasma, indicating minimal BBB penetration.

In primate and human brain regions, only supratherapeutic doses of telcagepant achieved moderate CGRP receptor occupancy, whereas clinically-relevant doses in healthy volunteers achieved low receptor occupancy.

A PET study found no evidence of central CGRP receptor occupancy after therapeutic doses of telcagepant in migraine patients during both ictal and interictal periods, arguing against a central site of gepant action being required for efficacy.

In rats with an uncompromised BBB, radiolabeled fremanezumab was detected in the dura, dural blood vessels, trigeminal ganglion, C2 dorsal root ganglion, sphenopalatine ganglion, and superior cervical ganglion, but not in central areas such as cortex, spinal trigeminal nucleus, thalamus, or hypothalamus.
Fremanezumab blocked CGRP-induced vasodilation in human meningeal arteries in vitro.
In a migraine rat model of cortical spreading depression, fremanezumab inhibited Aδ- but not C-type primary afferent meningeal nociceptors that innervate the cranial dura.
Translational EEG studies showed that abnormal visual cortical activity in migraine could be restored with galcanezumab treatment.
A functional MRI study showed that galcanezumab decreases hypothalamic activation.
A clinical study of erenumab in trigeminal neuralgia showed negative results, suggesting anti-CGRP mAbs may be selective for migraine and not effective for other cranial pain conditions.
Galcanezumab is FDA-approved for episodic cluster headache prevention, but its phase 3 RCT in chronic cluster headache did not meet the primary endpoint.
Studies on fremanezumab in both episodic and chronic cluster headache were terminated following a futility analysis indicating primary outcomes were unlikely to be met.

A small clinical trial found unaltered CGRP plasma levels with low-dose topiramate, suggesting its antimigraine effects may be independent of the CGRP pathway despite preclinical evidence that it decreases CGRP release from trigeminal neurons.
OnabotulinumtoxinA (BoNT-A) inhibits CGRP release from meningeal and extracranial thin myelinated C-fibers by preventing synaptic vesicle adhesion and reducing TRPV1/TRPA1 channel expression.
Propranolol has agonist effects on prejunctional 5-HT1D and 5-HT1F receptors in trigeminal fibers, through which it inhibits CGRP release from fibers innervating the forehead skin and dura mater.
A single point mutation in the seventh transmembrane domain of the 5-HT1 receptor increases the affinity of beta-adrenoceptor antagonists for 5-HT1D/1F receptors 100 to 1000-fold.
Valproate inhibits the NF-kB pathway in the trigeminocervical complex, leading to a reduction in CGRP synthesis, in addition to restoring brain GABA levels.
Non-ictal allodynia, indicating central neuron sensitization independent of peripheral activation, is a useful clinical predictor of lack of response to galcanezumab.
A preclinical study showed that erenumab inhibits CGRP-induced vasodilatory responses especially in the distal portion of the human coronary artery, without affecting other vasodilators.
A clinical study of erenumab in patients with stable angina showed no significant changes in exercise treadmill test results, supporting cardiovascular safety in this population.
Compared to most triptans, ditans (e.g., lasmiditan) have a lower odds ratio for pain freedom and pain relief at 2 hours, though they lack cardiovascular side effects.

Constipation has been described as a side effect of erenumab, galcanezumab, and atogepant, possibly due to simultaneous blockade of CGRP and AMY1 receptors, which may be more relevant at the gastrointestinal level.

Studies examining serum CGRP levels after erenumab treatment report controversial results, with some showing reduced CGRP levels and others no difference, calling into question the use of CGRP as a treatment-response biomarker.
The telephone interview showed substantially higher agreement with the clinical gold-standard diagnosis than the self-report questionnaire for first-order headache diagnoses.

Second-order headache diagnoses (e.g., chronic migraine) were poorly captured by the questionnaire, while the telephone interview showed a non-significant trend toward good agreement with the gold standard.
Neither the questionnaire nor the telephone interview showed agreement with the gold standard for third-order headache diagnoses (medication overuse headache, TTH).
The questionnaire showed only moderate-to-fair agreement with clinical diagnosis for migraine, tension-type headache, and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia.
The telephone interview showed substantial-to-almost-perfect agreement with the gold-standard clinic diagnosis across all first-order headache diagnoses.
There were no significant differences among the three headache specialists performing the telephone interview in determining the first-order headache diagnosis.
Agreement between the outpatient clinic diagnosis and the questionnaire was independently influenced by male sex, headache frequency, headache intensity, and presence of depressive disorders.

Agreement between the outpatient clinic diagnosis and the telephone interview was independently influenced only by headache frequency and psychiatric comorbidity, unlike the questionnaire which was affected by more factors.

The telephone interview achieved high sensitivity and specificity for detecting primary headache disorders, including rare primary headache syndromes that are virtually impossible to detect with the questionnaire.
The questionnaire showed only moderate positive and negative predictive value for migraine, but high negative predictive value for tension-type headache and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia.
Nearly a quarter of patients had more than one headache disorder, and 5% had a third-order (e.g., medication overuse) headache disorder.
In the study cohort, migraine was the most common first-order headache diagnosis, followed by secondary headaches, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, tension-type headache, and rare primary headaches.

Adolescents with chronic headache or chronic abdominal pain showed higher mean heart rate during mental imagery of pain-associated sensations compared with neutral imagery, an effect not seen in healthy controls.
The chronic headache group specifically showed higher heart rate reactivity during pain-associated imagery compared with neutral imagery, distinguishing it from the chronic abdominal pain group.
Startle response magnitude did not differ between pain-associated and neutral mental imagery in any of the three groups (chronic headache, chronic abdominal pain, or controls).
Skin conductance level did not differ between pain-associated and neutral mental imagery in any of the three groups.

Self-reported fear, fear of pain, and desire to avoid were higher during pain-associated compared with neutral imagery overall, and this increase was significantly more pronounced in the chronic pain groups than in the control group.
Sumatriptan reduced PACAP-38 induced activation and sensitization of trigeminocervical neurons and the associated periorbital allodynia in rats.
PACAP-38 administration activated and enhanced the responses of dural-responsive pre-ganglionic pontine-superior salivatory parasympathetic neurons.

Antagonists of PACAP-38-responsive VPAC and PAC receptors attenuated cranial-autonomic and trigeminal-neuronal responses evoked by activation of the cranial parasympathetic projection, an effect dependent on post-ganglionic parasympathetic neurotransmission.
Migraine and tension-type headache were ranked as the sixth leading cause of years lived with disability globally in 2016.
A US study of 25 paediatric emergency departments found a 166% increase in headache-related visits from 2003 to 2013, far outpacing the 57.6% increase in total PED visits over the same period.
In 2013, headaches represented 22.6 per 1,000 PED visits, consistent with other studies' estimates of 0.7% to 2% of all PED visits.
The mean age of children presenting to the PED with headache ranged between 9 and 12 years across studies.
Primary headaches represent between 10% and 75% of all headache visits in the PED, depending on the study.
Infectious non-neurological causes such as upper respiratory tract infections account for between 26.6% and 59.9% of headache visits to the PED.
Serious or life-threatening neurological illnesses causing headache are rare, estimated between 1% and 6% of all PED visits for headache.
Between 8.8% and 36% of children with headache underwent CT or MRI brain imaging as part of their PED work-up.
The frequency of neuroimaging for paediatric headache decreased by approximately 3.7% per year between 2007 and 2014, falling from 36% to 14%.
Rossi et al. reported the lowest neuroimaging rate (8.8%), of whom only 12.5% had pathological findings, suggesting neuroimaging for paediatric headache remains overused in the PED.
An increased risk of developing a brain malignancy or leukaemia in the years following a head CT scan has been identified in the paediatric population.
A recent study of sudden non-traumatic headaches in children under age 6 found a low prevalence of urgent intracranial conditions, reducing the value of young age as a red flag.

Occipital headaches, headaches waking a child from sleep or occurring soon after waking, headaches increasing in frequency/duration/severity, and headaches with vomiting are most associated with serious neurological illness.

Life-threatening secondary headaches are usually accompanied by focal neurological abnormalities such as papilloedema, blurred vision, ataxia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve paralysis, despite their low overall prevalence.
Exercise headaches are frequently misdiagnosed as migraine, but differ in that migraine is aggravated by, rather than provoked by, exertion.

Infantile colic, regurgitation, abdominal migraine, cyclic vomiting syndrome and other disorders of gut-brain interaction are more common in the personal history of children who develop migraine and are recognized predictors of later migraine.
Migraine has a genetic heritability component, and most children who suffer from migraine have a family history of migraine.
Making a positive diagnosis of migraine in the PED and referring the patient to a headache outpatient clinic has been shown to decrease further PED visits for migraine crises.
Cluster headache yearly prevalence in a tertiary outpatient paediatric neurology clinic was estimated at around 0.03%.

Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are typically diagnosed in school-aged children (6-13 years), with mean age at diagnosis 9-13 years and symptom onset typically at 8-10 years, though patients often suffer 12-24 months before diagnosis.
A male predominance and a family history of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias or other primary headache disorders has been described in some but not all reviews of paediatric TACs.

A case report describes an 11-year-old patient with paroxysmal hemicrania who was treated with indomethacin after only 5 days of attacks and was able to stop treatment after just 14 days, much shorter than the typical 1-2 year course.
Verapamil is the prophylactic treatment of choice for cluster headache in children, with corticosteroids, lithium, topiramate, gabapentin, indomethacin, and sodium valproate as alternative options.
High-flow oxygen inhalation via non-rebreathe facial mask or sumatriptan nasal spray are the most common and effective treatments for acute cluster headache attacks.
Primary stabbing headache prevalence among children with chronic headaches is estimated between 1.5% and 3.5% in cohort studies of up to 83 patients.
A family history of chronic headaches was found in up to 58% of children with primary stabbing headache across different cohorts.

In up to one third of paediatric primary stabbing headache patients, stabs last more than a few minutes, exceeding the ICHD-3b duration criterion, suggesting the diagnostic criteria may need modification for children.

Primary stabbing headache is usually treated with indomethacin or anti-epileptic therapies, but no proof of efficacy for either treatment has been established to date, and untreated patients often see spontaneous resolution within months to years.
Thunderclap headaches accounted for 0.8% of all headache visits with a 10/10 pain score, and 42% of these were diagnosed as primary thunderclap headache, a much higher proportion than in adults.
The yearly prevalence of cluster headache in a tertiary pediatric neurology outpatient clinic was estimated at approximately 0.03%.
Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are primarily diagnosed between ages 6-13 (mean 9-13 years), with symptom onset typically at 8-10 years and a diagnostic delay of 12-24 months.
The youngest reported case of paroxysmal hemicrania was diagnosed at age 2 after more than 6 months of attacks.
Some but not all pediatric studies report a male predominance and a family history of TACs or other primary headache disorders in children with trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.

Some pediatric patients with trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia present with migrainous features such as nausea, vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia, suggesting overlap between these headache entities.
Potential triggers of paroxysmal hemicrania in children include heat waves, stress, tobacco smoke and exercise.
Indomethacin is the defining and successful prophylactic treatment for paroxysmal hemicrania, typically required for 1-2 years before it can be stopped.

A case report described an 11-year-old Japanese patient with paroxysmal hemicrania who was successfully treated with indomethacin after only 5 days of attacks and able to stop treatment after 14 days, suggesting early treatment may shorten therapy duration.
Gastrointestinal and behavioral side effects of indomethacin are common and can lead to treatment discontinuation.
Verapamil is the prophylactic treatment of choice for cluster headache, with corticosteroids, lithium, topiramate, gabapentin, indomethacin and sodium valproate as alternatives.
The most effective treatments for acute cluster headache attacks are high-flow oxygen inhalation (7 L/min for over 15 minutes via non-rebreathe mask) or sumatriptan nasal spray.
Primary stabbing headache prevalence among pediatric chronic headache sufferers is estimated between 1.5% and 3.5% in cohort studies of up to 83 patients.
Mean age at diagnosis of primary stabbing headache is around 9 years, with patients experiencing stabs for a mean of 6 to 11 months prior to diagnosis.
Unlike in adults, a clear female predominance has not been established for primary stabbing headache in the pediatric population.
A family history of chronic headache disorders is found in up to 58% of pediatric patients with primary stabbing headache.
In up to one third of pediatric patients, stabbing headache episodes last more than a few minutes, exceeding ICHD-3b criteria and suggesting these criteria may need modification for children.
Soriani et al. found that stabbing headache attacks occurred more than once a week in 52% of patients, once a week in 21%, and once a month in the remainder.
Primary stabbing headache is usually treated with indomethacin or anti-epileptic therapies, but no proof of efficacy for either treatment has been established.
Patients with primary stabbing headache who receive no treatment usually experience spontaneous resolution of symptoms within a few months to years.

In one pediatric cohort, thunderclap headaches accounted for 0.8% of all headache visits with a 10/10 pain score, and 42% were diagnosed as primary thunderclap headache, a higher proportion than reported in adults.
A review found vascular etiologies, most frequently arteriovenous malformations, responsible for 43% of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage cases in children.

Cervical artery dissection presents with acute headache associated with neck pain/tenderness and ipsilateral supraorbital, auricular, or mandibular pain, with symptom location determined by the site of vascular wall laceration, and is often accompanied by focal neurological abnormalities.
In cerebral sinus venous thrombosis, the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses are the most frequently involved sites.
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome triggers identifiable in both children and adults include trauma, exercise, water to the face, hypertension, and medication or substance use.
Given its reversible nature, most patients with reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome experience full recovery of symptoms.

Electroencephalogram can be useful in the diagnostic workup of sudden onset headache for specific cases such as atypical epileptic seizures presenting with peri-ictal headache or atypical migraine auras.
Lumbar puncture is recommended after neuroimaging when intracranial infection, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension is suspected.

Meta-analysis showed that manual therapy or aerobic exercise combined with medication reduced the number of headache days per month in chronic migraine.

Patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection had a 22% relative increase in adjusted risk of developing any of eleven studied immune-mediated inflammatory diseases compared with matched unexposed patients.

Psoriasis incidence was 23% higher in the SARS-CoV-2 exposed cohort than the unexposed cohort and was the second most commonly diagnosed IMID.
Sjögren's syndrome was one of the eleven IMIDs assessed as a secondary outcome but was not among the conditions found to have a significantly increased incidence following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

An Inception-module CNN using rs-fMRI-derived regional functional connectivity strength distinguished migraine patients from healthy controls with 99.25% accuracy and an AUC of 0.99.
A BiLSTM model trained on ICA/dictionary-learning-derived ROI time series classified migraine patients versus healthy controls with 96.94% accuracy and AUC 0.98.
Combining rs-FC strength and dynamic FC pattern features with SVM-based recursive feature elimination gave the best classification of migraine patients versus controls at a 24s time window.
Linear-SVM and RBF-SVM classifiers trained on fine fMRI features achieved 93.97% accuracy distinguishing migraine patients from healthy controls.
Graph theory-derived machine learning classifiers (neural network and SVM) differentiated migraine patients from controls with 92.86% and 87% accuracy respectively.

Degree centrality of the left inferior temporal gyrus was significantly decreased in migraine sufferers and served as an SVM-based diagnostic biomarker with high precision, sensitivity, and specificity.
A 3D-CNN diagnostic algorithm achieved 98.40% accuracy distinguishing migraine without aura patients from healthy controls.
