Abnormal fALFF patterns in the trigeminal-cervical complex/RVM, mid-cingulate cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and temporoparietal junction were used as SVM features to distinguish migraine without aura patients from healthy controls.

A machine learning pipeline analyzing functional connectivity of 33 pain-related seed regions classified chronic migraine patients versus controls with higher accuracy in patients with longer illness duration.

High-resolution fMRI showed significantly reduced hypothalamic volumes in both episodic and chronic migraine patients compared to controls, with anterior hypothalamic volume reduction linked to headache frequency.
A classifier distinguishing migraine from confusable secondary headaches performed better when including functional connectivity data than without it.
Resting-state functional connectivity between the left amygdala and left Heschl's gyrus discriminated migraine from tension-type headache with good diagnostic performance.
Multimodal MRI-clinical machine learning classification using hypothalamic and PAG functional networks distinguished migraine, cluster headache, and healthy controls with high accuracy.
Migraine patients show increased amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations and BOLD signal variability in the insular cortex compared to healthy controls.
Migraine patients show increased BOLD signal variability, regional homogeneity, and sub-low frequency oscillation power in the spinal trigeminal nucleus relative to healthy controls.
Migraineurs show increased resting-state functional connectivity between the periaqueductal gray and the median raphe nucleus, ventromedial medulla, hypothalamus, and thalamus compared to controls.

The duration and intensity of migraine pain positively correlate with resting-state functional connectivity of the PAG and substantia nigra and with ALFF values of the posterior thalamic nuclei and brainstem regions.
Fractional ALFF values of the left middle frontal gyrus negatively correlate with migraine pain intensity.
Hypothalamic activation can be detected within 48 hours prior to migraine headache onset and is interpreted as a marker of the prodromal phase.

Episodic tension-type headache sufferers show increased fALFF in the right posterior and anterior insula and decreased fALFF in the posterior cingulate cortex compared to healthy controls, with insula fALFF negatively correlated with attack frequency.

Cluster headache patients show increased functional connectivity between the hypothalamus and multiple cortical regions including anterior cingulate cortex, visual cortex, somatosensory cortex, occipital gyrus, thalamus, and insula compared to healthy controls.
The hypothalamic cluster shows a heightened BOLD signal response to painful trigeminal nerve stimulation in chronic migraine relative to episodic migraine and healthy controls.

New daily persistent headache patients showed abnormal functional connectivity in brain regions involved in emotion and pain perception/regulation, but these abnormalities did not correlate with clinical features.
A sustained pressure pain challenge temporally altered the occurrence of large-scale brain co-activation patterns (CAPs) in fibromyalgia patients.

Lower occurrence of a co-activation pattern encompassing the attentional (salience/ventral and dorsal) networks during sustained pain mediated the relationship between anterior insula neurochemistry and anterior insula-default mode network connectivity.
Increased occurrence of a co-activation pattern encompassing the sensorimotor network during sustained pain mediated hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia patients.
Systemic mastocytosis is associated with the KIT D816V mutation in more than 90% of cases.
Avapritinib, a KIT tyrosine kinase inhibitor, has recently been approved as the first such inhibitor for indolent systemic mastocytosis.
Other tyrosine kinase inhibitors are currently in clinical trials for patients with non-advanced systemic mastocytosis who have persistent and severe symptoms despite optimized anti-mediator therapy.

The authors previously identified hyperadrenergic orthostatic hypotension (hyperOH) as a distinct OH sub-phenotype marked by an exaggerated rise in norepinephrine on standing despite impaired sympathetic vasoconstriction.
Supine plasma norepinephrine levels were markedly higher in hyperOH patients than in OH patients.
Upright plasma norepinephrine rose much higher in hyperOH than in OH patients upon head-up tilt, whereas OH patients showed a blunted orthostatic increase.
The hyperOH cohort had a smaller orthostatic drop in blood pressure than the OH cohort despite similar heart rate increase on standing.
Upright blood pressure was significantly higher in hyperOH patients compared to OH patients.
Pressure recovery time during the Valsalva Maneuver was significantly shorter in hyperOH than in OH, indicating less severe autonomic impairment in hyperOH.
The heart rate to systolic blood pressure change ratio (ΔHR/ΔSBP) was numerically higher in hyperOH but did not reach statistical significance versus OH.
Valsalva ratio was numerically higher in hyperOH than OH but the difference did not reach significance.
Over 7 years, hyperOH patients had a significantly higher cumulative all-cause mortality rate than OH patients.
HyperOH patients had a significantly higher 7-year rate of phenoconversion to multiple system atrophy compared to OH patients.
OH patients had a numerically greater, but non-significant, rate of phenoconversion to Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies compared to hyperOH patients.

Migraine prevalence did not significantly differ between the non-Mennonite control group (91.1%) and the Mennonite group (81.0%).

The premonitory phase of migraine was identified at similar rates in the control group (80.0%) and the Mennonite group (81.0%).
The postdromic phase of migraine was recognized at similar rates in the control group (28.9%) and the Mennonite group (36.2%).
Among postdromic symptoms, fatigue and demotivation were reported as the most prevalent, affecting about a third of participants in both groups.
Retro-orbital headache pain was significantly more frequent in the non-Mennonite control group (55.6%) than in the Mennonite group (32.8%).
There was a non-significant trend toward more frequent shoulder pain in the control group compared with the Mennonite group.
The duration of headache attacks did not differ significantly between the control and Mennonite groups, with about half of each group reporting pain lasting less than 4 hours.
Use of any acute treatment for headache did not differ significantly between the control group (84.1%) and the Mennonite group (78.9%).
Specific migraine treatments such as triptans and ergot derivatives were used infrequently and similarly by both groups.
Anxiety scores measured by GAD-7 did not differ significantly between the control and Mennonite groups.
Depressive thinking distortions measured by the EPD scale did not differ significantly between the control and Mennonite groups.
Headache-related disability measured by MIDAS did not differ significantly between the control and Mennonite groups.
Intensity of dysautonomic symptoms measured by COMPASS-31 did not differ significantly between the control and Mennonite groups of migraine/headache patients.
The non-Mennonite control group showed more severe depressive symptoms on the PHQ-9 than the Mennonite group.
The non-Mennonite control group showed greater sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale than the Mennonite group.

A cited external study (Buse et al.) found that high-frequency migraineurs (8-14 headache days/month) had an 87% increased risk of moderate to severe depression compared with lower-frequency migraineurs (0-7 days/month), among a sample where a quarter of 11,603 migraineurs had moderate to severe depression on PHQ-9.
Fibromyalgia is associated with a protracted average diagnostic delay of 2.3 years.
In a survey of 800 fibromyalgia patients (84% female), a quarter reported symptoms so severe they could no longer work.
Fibromyalgia's etiology remains unclear but may involve a broader metabolic deficiency in the serotoninergic system.
Brain imaging studies show increased neuronal excitation and amplification of pain signals in fibromyalgia, supporting central sensitization as part of its pathophysiology.
Fibromyalgia patients show a relative excess of pain-facilitating neurotransmitters such as glutamate and substance P.
Fibromyalgia patients show relatively reduced levels of pain-inhibiting neurotransmitters such as GABA and norepinephrine.
Women with irritable bowel syndrome have an 8% to 41% prevalence of comorbid fibromyalgia.
Women with chronic pelvic pain have a 4% to 31% prevalence of comorbid fibromyalgia.
A survey found interstitial cystitis patients reported fibromyalgia symptoms far more often than controls (17.7% vs 2.6%).
In a study of 215 fibromyalgia patients, comorbid obesity was linked to greater pain sensitivity, reduced physical strength, less sleep, and more sleep-related restlessness compared to controls.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a common comorbidity that overlaps with both fibromyalgia and obesity.
The incidence of fibromyalgia is higher among patients with rheumatoid arthritis, axial spondylarthritis, and psoriatic arthritis than in the general population.
Patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and migraine have more intense and severe headaches and more depressive symptoms than patients with migraine alone.
Roughly one-fifth to one-third of migraine patients also have fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia and migraine appear to have a bidirectional relationship, with each condition increasing the likelihood of the other.
A novel ozone therapy produced greater than 50% symptomatic relief in 70% of 65 fibromyalgia patients with no reported side effects.
Gabapentinoids provide better pain control than placebo for fibromyalgia but about a third of patients lose this response by around six months.
Amitriptyline is effective against six main fibromyalgia symptom domains: pain, sleep disturbance, fatigue, affective symptoms, functional deficits, and cognitive impairment.
Low-dose amitriptyline (10-75 mg/day) is considered effective for managing fibromyalgia pain.
Duloxetine (60-120 mg/day) is used to manage fibromyalgia pain but carries an FDA black box warning for suicidality and risk of tachycardia and hypertension.
Milnacipran (100-200 mg/day) reduces pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia but its benefits may be modest, with side effects including sleep disturbance and depression.
An indirect meta-analytic comparison found amitriptyline 25 mg had superior results to pregabalin 450 mg and duloxetine for fibromyalgia.

Fibromyalgia patients had higher cerebrospinal fluid concentrations of the endogenous opioid MEAP, more systemic symptoms, and lower pain thresholds than chronic low back pain patients and healthy controls.

Despite limited evidence of long-term benefit and advice against use from pain specialty societies, opioids are frequently prescribed to fibromyalgia patients and are associated with a greater burden of illness.
In a 91-day study, a fixed-dose tramadol-paracetamol combination significantly reduced pain and improved function versus control, with no serious adverse events.
Low-dose naltrexone (2.5-4.5 mg) has analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties confirmed in a study of 31 fibromyalgia patients.
In a small trial, low-dose naltrexone over 10 weeks reduced fibromyalgia pain by 15%, overall symptoms by 18%, and limited pro-inflammatory cytokines.
A systematic review found low-dose naltrexone effective for controlling fibromyalgia symptoms with no severe adverse events reported.
At very low doses (2.5-4.5 mg), naltrexone was confirmed in a study of 31 fibromyalgia patients to have analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties.

In a small study of eight fibromyalgia patients, low-dose naltrexone taken over 10 weeks reduced fibromyalgia pain by 15%, decreased overall symptoms by 18%, and lowered levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
A systematic review of low-dose naltrexone studies in fibromyalgia patients found the regimen effective in controlling symptoms with no severe adverse events reported.
NSAIDs are typically not effective in treating fibromyalgia pain because they act through peripheral rather than central mechanisms.

The endocannabinoid system, via CB1 (central, analgesic/euphoric, anti-inflammatory, blood pressure lowering) and CB2 (peripheral, immunomodulatory/anti-inflammatory) receptors, modulates pain at spinal, supraspinal, and peripheral levels and may be relevant to nociplastic pain in fibromyalgia.

Aerobic exercise and resistance training improve function and reduce pain intensity in fibromyalgia patients, with recommended strength training at 40-80% intensity, 4-20 repetitions, two to three times weekly.

A Mediterranean-diet-based eating plan has been proposed for fibromyalgia patients to facilitate weight loss and complement other treatment approaches, though nutritional guidelines for fibromyalgia remain scarce overall.
Fibromyalgia patients frequently report that the healthcare system does not believe them or take their symptoms seriously, contributing to poor care coordination and dissatisfaction.
Participants with higher nociplastic pain (fibromyalgia survey) scores reported less improvement in pain and overall health since starting medical cannabis use.
Higher nociplastic pain scores were associated with a greater burden of cannabis-related side effects.
Higher nociplastic pain scores were associated with higher concomitant use of medications, including opioids and benzodiazepines.
Higher nociplastic pain scores were associated with substituting cannabis for a greater number of medication classes, including opioids and benzodiazepines.

Among 32 patients evaluated for suspected or doubtful intracranial hypotension, the diagnosis was confirmed in 18 patients.
Endolymphatic hydrops, detected via bilateral distortion product oto-acoustic emissions, was present in 15 of the 18 patients (83%) with confirmed intracranial hypotension.

Endolymphatic hydrops was also found in seven patients whose final diagnoses were differential conditions (chronic migraine, Chiari malformation, rebound intracranial hypertension, and perilymph fistula) rather than intracranial hypotension, indicating limited specificity of the finding.
The authors conclude that oto-acoustic emission testing for endolymphatic hydrops is insufficient by itself to exclude differential diagnoses when intracranial hypotension is suspected.

High cervical spinal cord stimulation targeting the trigeminocervical complex has been used as a neuromodulation strategy for refractory headache diseases including chronic migraine, cluster headache, and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.

IgG4 staining did not show statistically significant diagnostic performance for Sjögren's syndrome.
SSA-Ro antibody positivity showed the best diagnostic performance among serologic/clinical tests compared with focus score as reference.
Focus score was significantly higher in patients with hypergammaglobulinemia compared to those without.
Focus score was significantly higher in patients positive for rheumatoid factor compared to those negative.
Focus score correlated positively with ANA positivity.
Focus score was highest in patients with a homogeneous ANA pattern compared to a nucleolar pattern.

Focus score did not correlate with C-reactive protein levels.

CD20-positive cell density in salivary gland biopsy showed a strong positive correlation with focus score.

In patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome, focus score was significantly higher in those with glandular enlargement.

In the primary Sjögren's syndrome subgroup, patients with fine-granular or centromere ANA patterns had higher focus scores than those with other ANA patterns.

In the primary Sjögren's syndrome subgroup, presence of systemic disease involvement correlated significantly with erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Two rounds of IVIG treatment (20 g each) improved the patient's autoimmune encephalitis symptoms quickly over subsequent days.

Beta- and gamma-band functional connectivity within the pain-related network was reduced in patients with chronic migraine, chronic migraine with comorbid fibromyalgia, and episodic migraine compared with healthy controls.

Across all 181 participants, headache improved in 55% of the 3,232 recorded migraine attacks following exposure to narrow band green light (NbGL).
Responders (≥50% attack improvement) showed headache improvement in 82% of their NbGL-treated attacks, versus only 21% in non-responders.
Super-responders (≥75% improvement) had headache improvement in 90% of NbGL-treated attacks, whereas super non-responders (<25% improvement) improved in only 13%.
A generalized linear mixed-effects model estimated the expected probability of treatment success for a single attack at 57.8%.
Individuals who treated more attacks with NbGL reported slightly lower treatment success probability than those who treated fewer attacks.
Older participants reported fewer successfully NbGL-treated migraine attacks.
Higher baseline monthly headache frequency was associated with reduced NbGL treatment success.
Treatment success showed strong within-person clustering, indicating a stable individual-level response phenotype to NbGL rather than random attack-to-attack variation.
Accounting for within-person clustering, the marginal likelihood of NbGL treatment success across attacks was 64%.
Photophobia improved in 53% of the 3,232 NbGL-treated migraine attacks.
Photophobia improved in 68% of attacks among responders versus 35% among non-responders.
Photophobia improved in 74% of attacks among super-responders versus 27% among super non-responders.
Anxiety improved in 34% of the 3,232 NbGL-treated migraine attacks overall.
Anxiety improved in 46% of attacks among responders versus 18% among non-responders.
Anxiety improved in 52% of attacks among super-responders versus 10% among super non-responders.
Same-night sleep quality was reported as improved in 49% of the 3,232 attacks in which NbGL was used.
Sleep improved in 59% of attacks among responders versus 36% among non-responders.
Sleep improved in 66% of attacks among super-responders versus 34% among super non-responders.
Across all participants, NbGL exposure duration was about 30 minutes longer during attacks in which headache improved compared to attacks in which it did not.
Compared with non-responders, responders and super-responders were younger, more likely to have episodic (rather than chronic) migraine, and reported less consistent photophobia.

A sensitivity analysis found that the probability of NbGL treatment success did not meaningfully change across successive treated attacks, arguing against reverse causation (better responders self-selecting more exposures) as an explanation for the observed benefit, despite strong within-person clustering.

Prior electroretinography and visual evoked potential recordings in migraine patients showed that retinal and cortical electrical signals evoked by NbGL were the smallest of all tested light colors, smaller than those evoked by blue, red, amber, and white light.

The authors propose that NbGL's effects on headache and light sensitivity in migraine are mediated mainly through a retino-thalamo-cortical pathway involving direct monosynaptic retinal projections to trigeminovascular thalamic neurons.
NbGL's proposed effects on sleep are attributed to dense retinal projections to hypothalamic neurons containing orexin, histamine, and melanin-concentrating hormone.
The AMS/AMPP self-report migraine diagnostic module used to screen participants has high sensitivity and specificity for identifying episodic and chronic migraine per ICHD-3 criteria.
A generalized linear mixed-effects model estimated the expected probability of headache improvement with NbGL for a single migraine attack at 57.8%.
Participants who treated a greater number of migraine attacks with NbGL showed a small but statistically significant decline in probability of treatment success.
Older participants had a lower probability of successfully treated attacks with NbGL compared with younger participants.
Participants with higher baseline monthly headache frequency had reduced likelihood of NbGL treatment success.
There was strong within-person clustering of NbGL treatment success, indicating individual patients consistently responded similarly across their own attacks.
After accounting for within-individual clustering, the marginal likelihood of NbGL treatment success across all recorded attacks was 64%.

A sensitivity analysis found strong within-individual clustering of success (ICC=0.67) but no meaningful increase in success probability across successive attacks, arguing against reverse causation as the explanation for the overall treatment effect.
Compared with non-responders, NbGL responders were on average 5 years younger, more likely to have episodic (rather than chronic) migraine, and reported less consistent photophobia.
Super-responders were on average 7 years younger than super non-responders, less likely to have chronic migraine, and reported less consistent photophobia.
Across all participants, migraine attacks in which headache improved were associated with about 30 minutes longer NbGL exposure than attacks in which headache did not improve.
Among non-responders, duration of NbGL exposure did not differ significantly between attacks with and without headache improvement.
Among super-responders, duration of NbGL exposure was numerically longer in attacks with headache improvement, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
In blind migraine patients who could still detect light, headache is selectively exacerbated by blue light, as reported by Noseda et al.
A novel retino-thalamo-cortical pathway links brain areas that process vision to circuits mediating migraine pain and sensory/cognitive processing.

Narrow bands of blue or red light that activate short- or long-wavelength cones exacerbate migraine headache, whereas narrow band green light (520±10 nm), which activates medium wavelength cones, ameliorates headache.
Exposure to narrow bands of blue, amber, and red light during migraine can trigger or exacerbate stress, irritability, worry, and anxiety, whereas NbGL promotes calm and relaxation.
Daily exposure to NbGL phototherapy was previously shown to reduce monthly headache days, as well as headache intensity and duration, in both chronic and episodic migraine patients.
Animal studies show that exposure to NbGL attenuates responses of thalamic trigeminovascular neurons.
NbGL produces long-lasting antinociceptive effects in animal studies, potentially through anti-inflammatory responses or modulation of the endogenous opioid system.

The AMS/AMPP migraine diagnostic self-report module used for screening has a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 82% for episodic migraine diagnosis, and sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 80% for chronic migraine diagnosis.
Of 3,875 potentially eligible Allay Lamp purchasers, 698 (18%) agreed to participate in the survey/diary study, and only 181 (26% of those enrolled) provided complete diary data used for analysis.

Among non-responders, improvement rates in photophobia (35%) and sleep (39%) exceeded the headache improvement rate (21%), suggesting NbGL may act via pathways partially independent of headache perception.

Anxiety improvement rates among both responders (46%) and non-responders (18%) were lower than corresponding headache improvement rates (82% and 21%), suggesting anxiety improvement may be secondary to headache improvement rather than a direct NbGL effect.

Using electro-retinography and visual evoked potential recordings, prior work showed that electrical signals sent from the eye to the brain, and generated in the cortex, are smaller in response to NbGL than to blue, red, amber, or white light.

Direct monosynaptic retinal projections target trigeminovascular thalamic neurons and hypothalamic neurons involved in regulating sleep, mood, appetite, pain modulation, and sympathetic/parasympathetic tone.
NbGL effects on sleep are proposed to be mediated through dense retinal projections to hypothalamic neurons containing orexin, histamine, and melanin-concentrating hormone.

Retinal projections to hypothalamic neurons that regulate sympathetic and parasympathetic function are proposed to contribute to migraine patients' perception that NbGL reduces anxiety-related physiological symptoms (e.g., increased heart rate, throat tightness, light-headedness).
The study intervention was classified as imposing less than minimal risk and did not meet criteria requiring FDA approval; the estimated cost of NbGL therapy is approximately $10 per year.

Limitations of the study include the absence of a contemporaneous control group, a modest participation rate among eligible purchasers, potential self-selection bias favoring those who did well with treatment, and potential expectation-driven inflation of efficacy since participants purchased the lamp themselves.
Intravenous infusion of PACAP-38 induced migraine-like headache in 95% of participants with persistent post-traumatic headache compared with 10% after placebo.
No carryover effects were detected between the PACAP-38 and placebo experimental days in the crossover design.
The majority of participants developed migraine-like headache exclusively after PACAP-38 infusion, with none doing so exclusively after placebo.
During the 60-minute in-hospital observation period, more participants reported migraine-like headache after PACAP-38 than after placebo.
The baseline-corrected area-under-the-curve for median headache intensity was higher after PACAP-38 than after placebo over the 12-hour observation period.
Median peak headache intensity was higher after PACAP-38 than after placebo.
Median time to peak headache intensity occurred later after PACAP-38 infusion than after placebo, with wide individual variation.
Palpitations were far more frequently reported after PACAP-38 infusion than after placebo.
Flushing occurred in all participants after PACAP-38 infusion but in none after placebo.
Warm sensations occurred in all participants after PACAP-38 infusion but rarely after placebo.
The percentage change in baseline-corrected AUC for mean arterial blood pressure did not differ between PACAP-38 and placebo during the 60-minute in-hospital period.
The percentage change in baseline-corrected AUC for mean heart rate was higher after PACAP-38 than after placebo.

In a prior randomized trial cited by the authors, PACAP-38 induced migraine attacks in 58% of people with migraine compared with none after placebo, with a lower median peak headache intensity than seen in the present PTH cohort.

The authors propose that PACAP-38 binding to its receptor on vascular smooth muscle cells activates cAMP/protein kinase A signalling, opening KATP and BKCa potassium channels and causing meningeal arterial vasodilation that may sensitize meningeal nociceptors.
PACAP-38 is proposed to trigger mast cell degranulation via the MRGX2 receptor, releasing histamine and tryptase that may activate meningeal nociceptors.
Pretreatment with the antihistamine clemastine has been reported to reduce migraine attacks induced by PACAP-38 infusion.
A recent phase II trial reported effectiveness of a monoclonal antibody against PACAP signalling for migraine prevention.
A monoclonal antibody against the PAC1 receptor failed to outperform placebo for migraine prevention in a phase II trial, casting doubt on PAC1 receptor antagonism as a therapeutic strategy.

All three participants who were headache-free at the start of infusion still developed migraine-like headache after PACAP-38 within the 12-hour observation period, supporting robustness of the hypersensitivity finding.
The large majority of persistent PTH participants reported a migraine-like headache phenotype at baseline, and a minority had a family history of migraine.
Generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥6) was present in 38.46% (35/91) of the Nigerian school-aged children studied.
Although GJH was found in 60% of females and 40% of males, this sex difference in prevalence was not statistically significant.
Joint mobility (Beighton score) showed no significant correlation with kinaesthesia, measured either as correct wedge identification or penalty scores.
Greater joint mobility was significantly associated with worse performance on side jump, long jump, and overhand throw fitness items.
Greater joint mobility was associated with a longer ladder run completion time, while ladder step time showed no significant association.
Greater joint mobility was significantly associated with worse ball bounce, ball throw, and dynamic balance performance.
Joint mobility showed no significant correlation with static balance or total jump and hop performance.
Better kinaesthesia was significantly associated with better side jump and long jump performance and faster ladder run time.
Kinaesthesia showed no significant correlation with ladder step time or overhand throw distance.
Better kinaesthesia was significantly associated with better ball bounce, ball throw, and dynamic balance performance.
Kinaesthesia showed no significant correlation with static balance or total jump and hop count.
Lower plasma behenoyl dihydrosphingomyelin was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment for cardiometabolic risk factors.
Lower plasma sphingomyelin was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Lower plasma sphingosine was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Lower plasma sphingadienine was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Higher plasma dihomo-linoleoylcarnitine was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Lower plasma 1-myristoyl-2-arachidonoyl-GPC was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Lower plasma creatine was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Higher plasma glutamine was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Higher plasma glutamine degradant levels were associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
Lower plasma cysteine-S-sulfate was associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.

Lower plasma levels of a glucuronide of piperine metabolite (a black pepper-derived xenobiotic, C17H21NO3) were associated with a more pronounced systolic orthostatic blood pressure decrease after full adjustment.
None of the 818 examined plasma metabolites reached Bonferroni-corrected significance for association with manifest orthostatic hypotension.

Plasma sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), previously linked to hypertension and cardiovascular inflammation markers, was not significantly associated with orthostatic systolic blood pressure responses in this cohort.

In the minimally adjusted model (age, gender, systolic blood pressure), 22 metabolites — six amino acids, five cofactors/vitamins/carbohydrates, nine lipids, and two xenobiotics — were significantly associated with orthostatic systolic blood pressure responses, of which eleven remained significant after full adjustment for cardiometabolic risk factors.

Eleven metabolites that were significant in the minimally adjusted model (including aspartate, bilirubin isoforms, asparagine, carotene diol, phenylacetate, 2-naphthol sulfate, metabolonic lactone sulfate, glycoursodeoxycholic acid sulfate, and 1-stearoyl-2-oleoyl-GPE) lost statistical significance after additional adjustment for BMI, diabetes, smoking and antihypertensive treatment.
The Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 estimated 793.8 million incident cases, 2.60 billion prevalent cases, and 46.6 million years lived with disability due to primary headache disorders worldwide.
Headache disorders rank 3rd globally in YLD rates after low back pain and depressive disorders, but rank 1st among persons aged 15-49, accounting for 8% of total YLDs in that age group.
When fatal and non-fatal outcomes are combined (DALYs), headache disorders rank 15th overall, 2nd among ages 10-24 (5% of total DALYs), and 5th among ages 25-49 (3.7% of total DALYs).
Migraine has a global prevalence of approximately 14%, with substantial impact and symptoms peaking during patients' most productive years.
Tension-type headache is the second most prevalent condition overall, and migraine is the second most disabling condition worldwide.
Headache disorders are long-lasting conditions that usually peak in early adulthood, particularly among women, exacerbating gender inequalities.
Medication overuse headache (MOH) affects 1% of the global population and is classified as a secondary headache disorder in ICHD-3.
In a 12-month longitudinal study, 7.6% of patients with episodic migraine progressed to chronic migraine, while nearly 75% of those with chronic migraine remitted back to episodic migraine.
Medication overuse is present in 30% to more than 50% of patients with chronic migraine.
In a US population study, only 16.8% of the 40.4% of migraine patients eligible for preventive medication actually used it, indicating significant underutilization.
In a European population setting, less than 15% of the 33.8% of migraine patients eligible for preventive treatment actually received it from their general practitioners.
A US population study found that 36.3% of individuals with migraine used opioids for symptomatic treatment, despite poor efficacy and high risk of progression to medication overuse headache.
Developing nations in South-East Asia and Africa have only 0.04 to 0.1 neurologists per 100,000 citizens, compared to 6 per 100,000 in Europe.
Headaches represent 1.5% of all cases seen by general practitioners.
Undergraduate medical education on headache disorders is extremely limited, typically not exceeding 4-6 hours during medical study.
A single-center clinical survey found that community pharmacist-focused educational activities on headache did not achieve the expected effect.
In low- and middle-income countries, approximately 50% of people with migraine rely on self-treatment with over-the-counter drugs such as NSAIDs only.
Approximately 80% of people with headache disorders live in low- and middle-income countries.
Headache remains a leading complaint in neurology clinics, ranging from 7.7% to 31.9% of visits in African countries and from 4% to 29.3% in Asian and South-Asian countries.

Migraine chronification, defined as an increase in headache frequency above 15 days per month, is associated with more severe disability and is driven by comorbidities, genetic predisposition, psychological and lifestyle factors, and medication overuse.

About 20% of the surveyed orofacial pain patient group were diagnosed with primary migraine or tension-type headache, a much higher proportion than previously reported for facial-involvement presentations of these primary headaches.
Trigeminal neuralgia was the most represented diagnosis in the sample, accounting for around 40% of cases.
Persistent idiopathic facial pain (PIFP), which accounts for a significant proportion of cases at specialized centers, was almost completely absent in this patient-association sample.
Acute pain crises were rated at a median of 8/10 on the Visual Analogue Scale, and were not typically characterized by sudden onset and end.
Persisting interictal background pain was rated at a median of 7/10 on the VAS, and was less well-defined than the predominantly burning or throbbing acute pain.
Pain was strictly unilateral in 85% of cases.
About 65% of subjects reported pain irradiation beyond the face, such as to the back, neck, or ears.
Autonomic cranial signs during pain attacks were reported by 45-65% of patients, except facial sweating which occurred in fewer than 20%.
Cutaneous triggers of pain were reported by 61% of patients.
About 40% of patients identified a specific triggering cause for their pain, including trauma, herpes infection, surgical/radiotherapy treatment, or especially dental treatments.
About 70% of subjects consulted at least one additional doctor beyond the first, and more than 30% consulted at least two others, reflecting a fragmented diagnostic pathway.
About 50% of patients directly underwent a brain or maxillofacial MRI as part of their diagnostic work-up.
Almost all patients (>95%) received pharmacological treatment, but about 40% remained unsatisfied with drug therapy.
Patient-rated satisfaction with drug and non-drug therapy had a median of 5/10, while satisfaction regarding side effects had a median of 8/10.

In the isolated trigeminal neuralgia group (group A), about 77% of patients reported discomfort from drug side effects, and more than half were unsatisfied with their first diagnosis and prescribed therapy.

Treatment results were considered insufficient in more than 60% of patients overall and across the different diagnostic groups, indicating inadequate treatment of many facial-involving primary headaches.

Post-hoc reclassification by researchers reduced idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia diagnoses, with more than 40% reassigned as symptomatic trigeminal neuralgia, mainly following dental disorders or dental surgical interventions.
Upon post-hoc reclassification, tension-type headache diagnoses were reduced by almost 50%, while migraine and cluster headache diagnoses remained relatively stable in sample size.

The authors note prior literature indicating primary headaches can involve the lower half of the skull (orofacial region) in about 10-20% of cases, providing context for the unexpectedly high rate of migraine/tension headache diagnoses in this orofacial pain sample.

The authors cite a proposal (Ziegler and May) that the orbitomeatal line used to define orofacial pain versus headache should be revised, since it currently excludes many trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias and migraines with lower-face involvement (e.g., trochlear migraine) from the orofacial pain classification.

The authors conclude that primary headaches such as migraine and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias can present with orofacial localization in adulthood, as has already been observed in pediatric populations, and this localization should not exclude these diagnoses.
KIT D816V is the most prevalent transforming mutation in advanced systemic mastocytosis and drives cytokine-independent autonomous growth of neoplastic mast cell progenitors.
Additional mutations in SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1, or DNMT3A frequently co-occur with KIT mutations in advanced SM, especially SM-AHN, and may drive disease evolution, progression, and drug resistance.
Midostaurin, a KIT D816V-targeting TKI approved for advanced SM, suppresses disease-related symptoms and expansion of neoplastic mast cells in a considerable number of patients.
Avapritinib is described as a superior KIT D816V-targeting drug that induces hematologic remission in a substantial subset of patients with advanced SM.
Cladribine (2CdA) is effective in some patients with advanced SM but has lower response rates compared to midostaurin or avapritinib.
KIT D816V is absent in roughly 80% of well-differentiated advanced SM, 20-30% of MCL cases, and about 90% of true (primary) mast cell sarcoma cases.
In a retrospective multi-center study of HSCT in advanced SM, survival and relapse-free survival outcomes were better for patients with ASM or SM-AHN than for those with MCL.
Myeloablative conditioning prior to HSCT was associated with more favorable outcomes than dose-reduced (non-myeloablative) conditioning in advanced SM.
Most neoplastic mast cells and neoplastic stem cells, including AHN-related NSC, display CD33 in the majority of SM patients, making it a candidate target for antibody-based therapy.
A case report describes disease debulking and sustained remission after gemtuzumab ozogamicin treatment in a patient with drug-resistant SM-AHN.
Combined treatment with gemtuzumab ozogamicin and poly-chemotherapy substantially decreased the numbers of neoplastic stem cells in other patients with advanced SM.

Neoplastic stem cells in advanced SM reside in a small CD34+/CD38- fraction of the malignant clone and can initiate and propagate the disease in vivo in NSGhSCF mice, unlike more mature CD34+/CD38+ progenitors or bulk mast cells.
CD34+/CD38- neoplastic stem cells in most patients with advanced SM express the stem cell markers CD13, CD123, and CD133, which are also found on neoplastic mast cells and often on AHN cells.

CD30 and CD327 are detectable on neoplastic mast cells but not (or only in trace amounts) on the CD34+/CD38- neoplastic stem cell fraction in advanced SM, making them less attractive targets for eliminating disease-propagating cells.
A newly presented tri-specific killer engager (CD16xIL15xCD33) induces NK cell activation and cytotoxicity against neoplastic mast cells, though its clinical utility in advanced SM remains untested.
Post-HSCT avapritinib use in RUNX1-RUNX1T1-positive, KIT-mutated AML patients with minimal residual disease who failed immunotherapy was frequently accompanied by cytopenia.
The estimated prevalence of adult systemic mastocytosis is approximately 1 per 10,000 in the Western world, and this figure has increased with improved diagnosis.
Across the 16 included studies, osteochondral injuries occurred in the majority of patients following patellar dislocation.
One study found male sex was a significant risk factor for osteochondral injury after patellar dislocation.
Two studies found no significant gender difference between patients with and without osteochondral injury.
Male sex was an independent predictor of femoral osteochondral injury but not patellar osteochondral injury in one cohort.
Male sex was an independent risk factor for osteochondral injury of the lateral femoral condyle.
Male sex was an independent risk factor for osteochondral injury in a recent large retrospective cohort.
Skeletally mature patients were more likely to develop osteochondral injuries than skeletally immature patients.
Skeletal maturation was an independent risk factor for patellar osteochondral injury.
Physeal closure was an independent predictor of femoral osteochondral injury.
Most studies found no significant association between patient age and osteochondral injury, with one exception showing a small but significant effect.
BMI of 25 or greater was an independent predictor of femoral osteochondral injury in one cohort.
BMI was significantly associated with osteochondral injury by univariate logistic regression in one cohort.
Patients with osteochondral injury had a higher patellotrochlear index than those without, while Caton-Deschamps and Insall-Salvati indices were not associated with injury.
Evidence on trochlear dysplasia as a risk factor for OCI was inconsistent: two studies found trochlear dysplasia (via sulcus angle) increased OCI risk, while three others found no association.

In contrast to studies implicating trochlear dysplasia, one study found that a normal (non-dysplastic) femoral trochlea was itself an independent risk factor for both patellar and lateral femoral condyle osteochondral injuries.
Trochlear facet and condyle asymmetry ratios were closer to normal anatomy in patients with osteochondral injury than in those without.
Most studies found TT-TG distance was not associated with osteochondral injury risk, although one study found normal TT-TG distance was an independent risk factor for patellar OCIs.
Patients with ligamentous laxity, although not differing in overall OCI rate, rarely had severe (grade 3-4) osteochondral injuries of the patella or femur compared to patients without laxity.
Articular hypermobility decreased the risk of osteochondral injury by approximately 2.5-fold compared to patients without hypermobility following acute patellar dislocation.
A Beighton score of 4 or higher, indicating generalized joint hypermobility, showed a protective effect against osteochondral injury of the patellofemoral joint.
Two studies found no correlation between ligamentous laxity and the presence of osteochondral injury, contrasting with studies showing a protective effect.
Chronicity of patellar instability greater than five years was associated with trochlear lesions on univariate analysis, but this did not hold in multivariate regression.
Complete medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) tears predispose to a higher grade of patellar osteochondral injury than partial MPFL injuries across two studies.
Increased femoral anteversion angle was an independent risk factor for patellar dislocation combined with osteochondral injury.
One study found a shallower trochlear depth in patients with osteochondral injuries compared to those without.
Zhao et al. found no statistically significant difference in trochlear depth between patients with and without osteochondral injuries.
Three of four studies examining sulcus angle found no statistically significant difference between patients with and without osteochondral injuries.
All three studies assessing lateral trochlear inclination angle found no correlation with osteochondral injuries.
Zheng et al. found that a normal (non-elevated) TT-TG distance was an independent risk factor for patellar osteochondral injuries.
Fones et al. found no association between distal or proximal TT-TG distance and osteochondral injuries.
Redler et al. and Jiang et al. concluded that TT-TG distance was unrelated to osteochondral injuries.
Uimonen et al. found no difference in TT-TG distance between patients with and without osteochondral injuries.

Redler et al. found that although overall OCI percentage did not differ by laxity status, patients with ligamentous laxity rarely had severe (grade 3/4) patellar or femoral osteochondral injuries compared to those without laxity.
Stanitski et al. found that articular hypermobility decreased the risk of osteochondral injuries by approximately 2.5-fold after acute patellar dislocation.
Holliday et al. found that a Beighton score of 4 or greater (indicating articular hypermobility) had a protective effect against osteochondral injury.
Kolaczko et al. and Franzone et al. found no correlation between ligamentous laxity and the presence of osteochondral injuries.

Franzone et al. found that chronicity of patellar instability greater than five years was associated with trochlear lesions on univariate analysis, but this association did not hold on multivariate regression.
Fones et al. found that duration of instability symptoms after the initial dislocation was not significantly associated with the presence of osteochondral injuries.
Holliday et al. found no significant association between the number of prior dislocations and the presence of osteochondral injuries.
Zhang et al. (2013) found a significant difference between partial and complete medial patellofemoral ligament injuries in the incidence of patellar osteochondral injuries.
A subsequent study by Zhang et al. found that complete medial patellofemoral ligament tears predispose to a higher grade of patellar osteochondral injury than partial tears.
Jiang et al. found that increased femoral anteversion angle was an independent risk factor for patellar dislocation combined with osteochondral injury.
Jungesblut et al. found that a traumatic mechanism of dislocation was associated with a higher likelihood of patellar and femoral osteochondral injuries.
Kolaczko et al. found that the presence of a joint effusion was significantly associated with occult osteochondral injuries.

A patient developed severe ipsilateral migraine without aura beginning 30 minutes after ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block performed for insomnia, with episodes recurring 2-3 times daily for 2 weeks before resolving.
This case of migraine without aura after SGB differed from two previously reported cases, which involved migraines with aura persisting for several months rather than weeks.

Intravenous infusion of the K_ATP channel opener levcromakalim induced migraine-like headache in a majority of participants with persistent post-traumatic headache, significantly more often than placebo.
Baseline-corrected headache intensity scores over the 12-hour observation period were significantly higher after levcromakalim infusion than after placebo.

The authors suggest that K_ATP channel blockers could represent a promising future therapeutic avenue for persistent post-traumatic headache, based on the demonstrated causal role of channel opening in triggering migraine-like headache.
Pooled analysis of 7 studies found that rapid ingestion of a 350-500 mL water bolus significantly raised systolic blood pressure in patients with orthostatic hypotension.
Water bolus ingestion significantly increased diastolic blood pressure in patients with orthostatic hypotension.
Water bolus ingestion significantly decreased heart rate in patients with orthostatic hypotension.
In three rigorous RCTs of healthy participants, water bolus ingestion produced a small but significant increase in systolic blood pressure compared with control.
In three rigorous RCTs of healthy participants, water bolus ingestion produced a small but significant increase in diastolic blood pressure compared with control.
Water bolus ingestion had no significant effect on heart rate in healthy participants.
Water bolus ingestion had no significant effect on systolic blood pressure in patients with POTS in the seated or supine position.
Water bolus ingestion had no significant effect on diastolic blood pressure in patients with POTS in the seated or supine position.
Water bolus ingestion had no significant effect on heart rate in patients with POTS in the seated or supine position.
Subgroup analysis in patients with multiple system atrophy showed a significant increase in systolic blood pressure after water bolus ingestion.
Subgroup analysis in patients with multiple system atrophy showed a significant increase in diastolic blood pressure after water bolus ingestion.
Subgroup analysis in patients with pure autonomic failure showed a significant increase in systolic blood pressure after water bolus ingestion.
Subgroup analysis in patients with pure autonomic failure showed a significant increase in diastolic blood pressure after water bolus ingestion.
Heart rate did not change significantly after water bolus ingestion in the multiple system atrophy subgroup.
Heart rate decreased significantly after water bolus ingestion in the pure autonomic failure subgroup.

The osmopressor response is proposed to be mediated by rapid-onset hypo-osmolality of the portal vein sensed via the osmo-sensitive TRPV4 channel, which triggers efferent sympathetic activation and raises blood pressure.

Prior literature cited in the background indicates that rapid drinking of 300-500 mL of plain water in patients with orthostatic hypotension raises systolic blood pressure by approximately 35 mm Hg and buffers postprandial hypotension.
The pressor effect of water bolus ingestion begins 10-15 minutes after ingestion, peaks around 25-40 minutes, and largely resolves within 90 minutes.
A case report described a patient with POTS whose standing heart rate had doubled, which resolved within 10 minutes after rapid ingestion of 236.6 mL of water.
In an individual study of 9 patients with POTS while standing, water bolus ingestion decreased heart rate from a mean of 123 to 108 bpm.
In the Z'Graggen et al study, heart rate showed nonsignificant change while supine but decreased significantly by 11.6 bpm during head-up tilt following water ingestion.
In the Rodriguez et al study, heart rate during head-up tilt decreased from a mean of 111 to 92.9 bpm after water ingestion in patients with POTS.

The osmopressor response is thought to be mediated by rapid-onset hypo-osmolality of the portal vein sensed by the osmo-sensitive transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 channel, triggering efferent sympathetic activity and increasing systolic blood pressure.
In a study of 22 healthy adults, water consumption before head-up tilt reduced the incidence of hypotension or bradycardia during testing compared with no water pre-treatment.
A case report described a POTS patient whose standing heart rate had doubled but resolved within 10 minutes after rapid consumption of 236.6 mL of water.

In the Shannon et al study, water ingestion decreased heart rate in 9 standing POTS patients from a mean of 123 to 108 bpm, contrasting with the null findings for supine/seated POTS in the pooled meta-analysis.
Z'Graggen et al found a significant decrease in heart rate during head-up tilt following water ingestion in POTS patients, despite nonsignificant changes while supine.
Rodriguez et al reported a decrease in heart rate during head-up tilt before and after water ingestion in POTS patients.
The larger Jordan et al study, excluded from the pooled meta-analysis due to incomplete data, found a significant decrease in heart rate in response to water bolus ingestion.

Post hoc sensitivity analysis removing Deguchi et al (confounded by concurrent vasoactive medication use) and Lipp et al (nasogastric administration) from the OH group did not substantially reduce between-study heterogeneity or change the significance of pooled BP effect estimates.

Risk of bias assessment found all included cohort studies had moderate to high risk of bias, while RCTs (except Parsons et al) had unclear selection bias risk and high performance bias risk due to unspecified randomization and lack of blinding.

The authors recommend that individuals with orthostatic hypotension drink water in the morning before rising, since the peak pressor effect of water ingestion coincides with the delayed onset of other pressor medications taken upon waking.
An open-label pilot trial reports pain relief in patients with refractory fibromyalgia following vestibulocortical stimulation.

Serum DHEA levels are reduced in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren's syndrome relative to non-affected individuals.
Androgens and DHEA are reduced in nearly half of SLE patients, mainly those with active disease.
DHEA supplementation showed a modest but generally favorable effect on SLE disease activity, with reduction or stabilization across several trials.
In a small study of 13 SLE patients (Marder et al.), DHEA treatment did not demonstrate improvement in disease activity as measured by SLEDAI.
DHEA supplementation was associated with a possible reduction in prednisone dose requirements in SLE patients.
DHEA supplementation increased bone mineral density in SLE patients compared with placebo, including patients on low-dose glucocorticoids.
DHEA treatment reduced the frequency of lupus flares compared with placebo.
DHEA supplementation improved fatigue and general well-being in SLE patients across several studies.
Low-dose DHEA (20-30 mg/day) improved sexual performance in SLE patients in the Nordmark et al. study.
DHEA supplementation in SLE was associated with reductions in HDL cholesterol in at least three studies, suggesting a potentially unfavorable effect on lipid profile.
DHEA treatment was generally well tolerated, with mild androgenic side effects including acne, hirsutism, and altered menses being more frequent than with placebo.
In Sjögren's syndrome, DHEA supplementation showed some improvement in dryness, fatigue, and quality of life, but without significant differences compared to placebo in most studies.

In rheumatoid arthritis, supraphysiological-dose DHEA (200 mg/day) led to an ACR20 response in 18% of patients, while low-dose DHEA (50 mg/day) did not differ from placebo, overall results were not reassuring.
The single fibromyalgia study evaluating DHEA supplementation failed to demonstrate any clinical benefit.
In vitro studies showed DHEA inhibits IL-6 production and up-regulates IL-2, and in animal lupus models DHEA delayed dsDNA autoantibody production and improved survival.
DHEA has anti-inflammatory properties, inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokine production by blocking NF-kappa B activation and increasing the Th1/Th2 cytokine ratio.
In humans, DHEA treatment did not significantly change anti-dsDNA antibody levels despite reported effects on disease activity.

Global migraine prevalence averages 12%, with substantial variation across and within countries.

In deterministic base-case modeling, Topiramate dominated placebo, being both cheaper and generating more QALYs.
BTA was more cost-effective than placebo at the £30,000/QALY threshold, with an ICER of £25,238 per QALY gained.

Fremanezumab (monthly and quarterly), Eptinezumab (100mg and 300mg), and Galcanezumab all had ICERs versus placebo that would not be considered cost-effective under the £20-30k per QALY NICE threshold.
When all medications were compared together, BTA versus Topiramate had an ICER of £68,000 per QALY gained, while Eptinezumab 300mg versus BTA was not within plausible cost-effectiveness thresholds.
Eptinezumab 300mg versus BTA produced an ICER of £2,160,037 per QALY gained in the deterministic all-medication comparison, far exceeding acceptable thresholds.
The cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier indicated Topiramate was the most cost-effective medication across all willingness-to-pay thresholds per QALY.
Under a lifetime time horizon scenario analysis, BTA versus Topiramate produced a much lower, more favorable ICER of £6,077 per QALY gained.

When Monthly Migraine Days (MMDs) rather than Monthly Headache Days (MHDs) were used as the outcome measure, Fremanezumab monthly generated more QALYs than Eptinezumab 300mg, differing from the base-case ranking.

A prior 2013 study by Batty et al. found BTA increased costs by £1,367 and improved QALYs by 0.1 versus placebo (ICER £15,028), with headache days reduced by about 38 per year at a cost of £18 per headache day avoided.
A 2018 study found Erenumab (at an annual price of US$6,900) was dominant (cheaper and more effective) compared to no preventive treatment from a societal perspective.
In the same 2018 study, although the ICER for Erenumab versus BTA (US$65,720) was considered cost-effective in that country's context, it was not within current UK cost-effectiveness thresholds.
The authors' own 2022 systematic review concluded BTA is cost-effective compared to placebo, with an ICER ranging between £15,028 and £16,598.
The same prior systematic review found Erenumab versus BTA ICERs ranged from £59,712 to £182,128, exceeding commonly accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds.

Under widely accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds, all CGRP monoclonal antibodies (Erenumab, Galcanezumab, Fremanezumab) were deemed cost-effective specifically for chronic migraine patients who had already failed BTA treatment.

Adverse events were excluded from the economic model because prior systematic review evidence indicated serious adverse events were not related to the medication itself and were assumed not to influence healthcare resource use.

Eptinezumab 300mg was the most effective and highest ranked treatment for reducing HIT-6 scores.

Using GRADE, the certainty of evidence for Topiramate's effect versus placebo was lower than for the other drugs, all of which were rated high certainty.

A woman with primary Sjögren's syndrome who developed severe COVID-19 pneumonia showed persistent ground glass opacities and interlobular interstitial thickening on HRCT that almost completely resolved by 26 months, ultimately supporting a diagnosis of long-COVID lung disease rather than Sjögren's-related interstitial lung disease.

At three months after acute COVID-19 pneumonia, the patient's pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive deficit (FVC 78%) and reduced diffusion capacity (DLCO 56%), accompanied by asthenia and exertional dyspnoea.

Eleven months after acute onset, the patient's clinical symptoms and PFTs (FVC 81%, DLCO 56%) remained essentially unchanged from the 3-month assessment, indicating a stable but persistent mild functional impairment.

A meta-analysis of 15 observational studies found that residual CT abnormalities at 1-year follow-up were more common in patients with severe/critical COVID-19 (37.7%) than in those with mild/moderate disease (20.7%).
Across both severity groups, ground glass opacity was the most prevalent residual CT finding at 1 year (21.2%), followed by fibrotic-like changes (20.6%).

In a prospective multicentre study, among COVID-19 patients with DLCO impairment at 12 months, 77% had HRCT abnormalities, with 61% showing ground glass opacity and 49% showing reticular abnormalities.
