Patients with non-sports-related concussion had significantly higher autonomic symptom subtype scores than those with sports-related concussion.
Patients with non-sports-related concussion had significantly higher balance symptom subtype scores than those with sports-related concussion.
Patients with non-sports-related concussion had significantly higher low energy/fatigue/sleep symptom subtype scores than those with sports-related concussion.
Patients with non-sports-related concussion had significantly higher emotional changes symptom subtype scores than those with sports-related concussion.
The total postconcussive symptom score was significantly lower in the sports-related concussion group compared to the non-sports-related concussion group.
Migraine comorbidity was one of three comorbidities that significantly contributed to differences in concussion subtype scores between sports-related and non-sports-related groups.
Vertigo comorbidity was one of three comorbidities that significantly contributed to differences in concussion subtype scores between sports-related and non-sports-related groups.
Anxiety comorbidity was one of three comorbidities that significantly contributed to differences in concussion subtype scores between sports-related and non-sports-related groups.

Other comorbidities, including depression, neuropsychiatric disorders, seizures, syncope, and sleep disorder, did not significantly contribute to differences in concussion subtype scores between the sports-related and non-sports-related groups.

Vulvodynia patients reported genital/sexual pain in the last 6 months at the highest rate (97.93%), followed by the comorbidity group (74.29%) and fibromyalgia (55.91%), significantly differing across groups.
Women with chronic headache reported genital/sexual pain slightly more often than healthy controls.
The comorbidity group reported significantly longer duration of genito-pelvic pain (in months since onset) than the chronic headache and healthy control groups.
The proportion of women meeting the FSFI clinical cutoff for sexual dysfunction was highest in vulvodynia, followed by comorbidity, fibromyalgia, chronic headache, and healthy controls.

Fibromyalgia, vulvodynia, and comorbidity groups showed significantly lower overall sexual functioning scores than healthy controls and chronic headache, with the sexual pain domain contributing most to group variance.

Vulvodynia reported the highest genito-pelvic pain scores on the adapted SF-MPQ, followed by comorbidity and fibromyalgia, with chronic headache and healthy controls not significantly different from each other.
Vulvodynia and comorbidity groups reported significantly lower sexual satisfaction (contentment) than the other groups.
Across all clinical pain groups except controls, genital pain was the main significant predictor of central sensitization (CSI) scores, with higher genital pain associated with higher CSI.
In the chronic headache group, higher sexual satisfaction was associated with lower central sensitization (CSI) scores.
In the fibromyalgia group, higher sexual satisfaction was associated with lower central sensitization (CSI) scores.
Only in the vulvodynia and comorbidity groups was genital pain a significant predictor of lower physical quality of life.
In chronic headache and comorbidity groups, higher sexual satisfaction significantly predicted better mental quality of life.

In the vulvodynia group, both genital pain and sexual satisfaction were significant predictors of mental quality of life, with higher pain associated with lower QoL and higher satisfaction associated with higher QoL.
In the fibromyalgia and healthy control groups, no sexual variable (functioning, genital pain, satisfaction) significantly predicted physical or mental quality of life.

Vulvodynia and comorbidity groups more frequently reported pain localized externally (vaginal introitus, external genitalia, clitoris), while chronic headache, fibromyalgia, and healthy controls more often reported internally localized pain (initial and deep vagina).
Long COVID cardiovascular symptoms commonly include chest pain, orthostatic intolerance, tachycardia, syncope, and uncontrolled hypertension.
Endothelial dysfunction, frequently attributed to impaired nitric oxide mechanisms, is proposed as the common underlying mechanism linking Long COVID's cardiovascular symptoms.
Increased inflammation and oxidative stress commonly seen in Long COVID may impair nitric oxide function, leading to decreased vascular reactivity.

Endothelial dysfunction is reported as a major mechanism contributing to cardiovascular disease in people living with HIV, a population with an estimated 26 million individuals affected in Africa in 2022.
People living with HIV are reported to be more likely to develop Long COVID following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Concomitant SARS-CoV-2 infection in people living with HIV may accelerate cardiovascular disease.
TMD patients with comorbid migraine reported longer pain duration, higher pain scores, and greater pain interference than TMD-only patients.
TMD patients with comorbid fibromyalgia had higher pain intensity than TMD-only patients.
Both TMD patients comorbid with migraine and those comorbid with fibromyalgia showed higher anxiety, depression, and health impairment than TMD-only patients.

Patients with all three pain conditions (TMD, migraine, and fibromyalgia) experienced the longest pain duration, highest pain intensity, greatest psychological distress, and most impaired quality of life.
A greater number of comorbid pain conditions was positively associated with worse pain outcomes, psychological distress, and pain's impact on quality of life.
A greater number of comorbid pain conditions was negatively associated with overall self-reported health states.
TMD patients with comorbid migraine showed greater health impairment than patients with TMD only.
TMD patients with comorbid fibromyalgia showed greater health impairment than patients with TMD only.

Patients with triple comorbidity of TMD, migraine and fibromyalgia had the longest pain duration, highest pain intensity, greatest psychological distress, and most impaired quality of life among all groups.
The number of comorbid pain conditions was positively associated with pain outcome measures in TMD patients.
The number of comorbid pain conditions was positively associated with psychological distress measures (anxiety and depression) in TMD patients.
The number of comorbid pain conditions was positively associated with pain's impact on quality of life in TMD patients.
The number of comorbid pain conditions was negatively associated with overall health state ratings in TMD patients.

The supine-to-stand test detected a higher rate of orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson's disease patients than the sit-to-stand test, though the authors argue the sit-to-stand test with adjusted blood pressure thresholds remains a practical screening alternative.

Serotonin stimulates chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the left ventricle, triggering the Bezold-Jarisch reflex whose vagal afferent C-fiber signaling produces parasympathetic efferent bradycardia.
Three lines of evidence implicate cardiac serotonin 5HT3 receptors in mediating the Bezold-Jarisch reflex underlying vasovagal syncope.
Genetic and physiologic evidence links the serotonin 5HT1A receptor, 5HT3 receptor, and serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT) to vasovagal syncope pathophysiology.
Acute pharmacological blockade of SERT provoked vasovagal syncope in humans undergoing head-up tilt table testing.
Inhibition of the serotonin reuptake transporter reduces the hypotension and bradycardia that occur during spinal anaesthesia.
Three randomized clinical trials of serotonin reuptake transporter inhibitors consistently found that these agents significantly reduce the likelihood of vasovagal syncope recurrence.

A 12-week self-guided smartphone-delivered digital acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) programme produced a significantly higher rate of patient-reported improvement in fibromyalgia symptoms than an active control app offering symptom tracking and education.
No safety events related to the digital ACT device were reported during the trial.

Neurovascular coupling, measured as area-under-the-curve during the first 30 seconds of a visual search task (AUC30) in the posterior cerebral artery, was substantially reduced during days 1-3 post-concussion compared to baseline, primarily within mean and systolic velocity.
Heart rate was elevated during both quiet sitting and standing throughout the entire 14-day post-injury testing period.

Time-domain HRV metrics (SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50) were reduced under both seated and standing conditions immediately after injury and gradually trended back toward baseline across the 14-day testing period.

Frequency-domain HRV showed elevated relative low-frequency power and LF/HF ratio alongside reduced high-frequency power across the 14-day post-concussion period, indicating heightened sympathetic activation and reduced vagal tone.

Gain and normalized gain metrics of dynamic cerebral autoregulation were elevated in the posterior cerebral artery at both 0.05 Hz and 0.10 Hz across the 14 days post-injury, indicating reduced buffering of blood pressure oscillations.
Phase metrics of dynamic cerebral autoregulation were reduced within the middle cerebral artery at both 0.05 Hz and 0.10 Hz across the 14 days post-injury, consistent with impaired autoregulation.

Clinical symptoms (SCAT5 scores and overall condition) declined toward baseline by day 7, but autonomic and cerebrovascular impairments persisted through day 14, demonstrating a disconnect between clinical and physiological recovery after concussion.
A history of migraines/headaches is cited as a known risk factor for prolonged concussion recovery, and this case had such a history contributing to its elevated risk profile.

A cited population-based study found that individuals with bipolar disorder have the highest risk of persistent post-concussion symptoms among comorbid conditions, relevant to this case who had type II bipolar disorder.
Mild ADHD is cited as a known risk factor associated with prolonged concussion recovery and was present as a comorbidity in this case.
A cited study (Cook et al.) reported that mean symptom severity score after concussion increased progressively with greater numbers of prior concussions.

The case was chronically medicated with valproic acid and escitalopram for bipolar disorder II; these drugs' GABAergic and serotonergic effects could theoretically blunt the neurovascular coupling response, a noted limitation of the study.

Despite chronic psychiatric medication use, the case's AUC30 neurovascular coupling values corresponded to the 75th-80th percentile relative to previously published normative data, suggesting the medications did not substantially blunt the observed NVC response.
6-month-old Marfan syndrome (MFS) mice show decreased cerebral microvascular density in the dentate gyrus, CA1, and CA3 hippocampal regions, similar to 12-month-old aged control mice.

6-month-old MFS mice show increased blood-brain barrier permeability (via IgG extravasation staining) in the DG, CA1, and CA3 hippocampal regions, comparable to that seen in 12-month-old control mice.
6-month-old MFS mice show a higher number of hippocampal microglia compared to age-matched controls, resembling the microglial pattern of 12-month-old control mice.
The authors' prior work found that peak blood flow velocity in the posterior cerebral artery of 6-month-old MFS mice was reduced, similar to levels in 12-month-old control mice.
A missense mutation in fibrillin-1 (FBN1) in the Marfan syndrome mouse model leads to systemic increases in the bioavailability and signaling of TGF-beta.
In the established Marfan syndrome mouse model, premature aging of the aortic wall and progression of aortic root aneurysm are observed by 6 months of age.
Case studies of Marfan syndrome patients have documented neurovascular manifestations including intracranial aneurysms, stroke, arterial tortuosity, headaches, migraines, pain, and chronic fatigue.
The mean incidence of pediatric autoimmune encephalitis in Latvia between 2014 and 2022 was 0.56 per 100,000 children.
Most patients in this cohort (66.6%) had seronegative autoimmune encephalitis, without detectable specific autoantibodies.
Among seropositive patients, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was the most common subtype, with two patients having other antibody types.
The most prevalent clinical features in pediatric autoimmune encephalitis patients were personality change, cognitive impairment, autonomic dysfunction, and movement disorders.
Most patients (58.8%) with pediatric autoimmune encephalitis received only first-line immunotherapy treatment.
More than half of the pediatric autoimmune encephalitis cohort (55.6%) had long-term sequelae.
The Trendelenburg position acutely raises intracranial pressure, so a patient's headache improving in this position suggests low CSF volume while worsening suggests elevated CSF pressure.

In a 34-year-old man with new daily persistent headache and a post-lumbar-puncture headache, repeated home self-Trendelenburg testing tracked his transition from a low-CSF-volume state back to his neutral baseline headache, avoiding an unnecessary epidural blood patch.

A 34-year-old woman with a persistent positional headache after an epidural blood patch worsened in self-Trendelenburg, leading to a diagnosis of rebound intracranial hypertension rather than a persistent CSF leak, and her headache abated after low-dose acetazolamide.

A 58-year-old woman's daily persistent headaches worsening in Trendelenburg were traced to spinal epidural venous congestion from left renal vein compression (nutcracker physiology); her headaches ceased after lumbar vein coil embolization, and self-Trendelenburg later helped identify that her acetazolamide dose had become excessive, causing a low CSF volume state.

A woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and episodic long-duration migraine had two distinct headache etiologies—CSF pressure-dependent nutcracker physiology and CSF hypotension from a T12-L1 CSF-venous fistula—that home self-Trendelenburg response helped her and her physician differentiate to guide treatment, greatly improving her quality of life.

A 43-year-old man with a long-standing daily persistent headache developed a new superimposed CSF leak, identified because his headache improved in self-Trendelenburg (using an inversion table); he underwent a CT-guided epidural fibrin glue and blood patch procedure at T3-4, T7-8, and L1-2 with significant improvement, after which he no longer needed self-tipping.

A woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and chronic migraine developed sleep-associated headaches from nutcracker physiology with spinal epidural venous congestion, confirmed by worsening with self-Trendelenburg; bedtime acetazolamide then lumbar coil embolization completely abolished the sleep-associated headaches off medication.

A man in his early sixties with 18 months of exertional and Valsalva-triggered headaches improved immediately with self-Trendelenburg, prompting investigation that identified a left thoracic (T8) CSF-venous fistula on dynamic CT myelography; embolization made him completely headache free with exertion on long-term follow-up.
The author reports no complications from mild Trendelenburg positioning used in the office for durations longer than recommended for home use over more than 10 years.

At-home self-Trendelenburg testing can give the treating headache physician diagnostic information about underlying etiology and guide treatment strategy remotely without requiring immediate in-person evaluation.
The patient developed right-sided harlequin syndrome, marked by loss of facial flushing and sweating on the right side during exercise while the left side responded normally.

Pupillometry with apraclonidine testing revealed denervation supersensitivity consistent with a subtle right-sided Horner's syndrome, shown by greater pupil dilation on the affected side after apraclonidine application.
Indomethacin 75 mg/day induced complete remission of the headache, confirming a diagnosis of probable hemicrania continua.
Despite increasing indomethacin to 150 mg/day, exertional headache and harlequin syndrome persisted at seven months follow-up, while hemicrania continua remained in remission.
The patient tested positive for anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies and had a positive minor salivary gland biopsy, leading to a diagnosis of Sjögren's syndrome.
Suspected small fiber neuropathy could not be confirmed, as skin biopsy and sudometry testing were negative.
Gabapentin (900 mg/day, later increased to 1.8 g/day) and pregabalin (225 mg/day) failed to relieve the patient's neuropathic pain.
Anti-inflammatory treatment with prednisone 20 mg/day and methotrexate 15 mg weekly, combined with high-dose gabapentin (1.8 g/day), did not alleviate the patient's pain symptoms.
A single treatment combining greater occipital nerve infiltration and onabotulinumtoxin A produced a positive response for the patient's occipital neuralgia/migraine-like headaches.
Discontinuation of pharmacologic treatment and adoption of lifestyle changes, including resuming sports and meditation, resulted in the patient feeling much better.

CGRP-induced dilation of the internal carotid artery is proposed as a possible mechanistic link causing distension-related dysfunction of perivascular sympathetic vasomotor and sudomotor fibers, connecting trigeminal autonomic headache pathophysiology to harlequin syndrome.

Primary exertional headache co-occurred in 4 of 11 previously published harlequin syndrome cases with primary headache disorders, a higher rate than the 1%-12.3% prevalence reported in the general population, which shows female predominance.
Among 11 previously reported cases of harlequin syndrome with a primary headache disorder, two had cluster headache, eight had migraine, and one had post-traumatic headache.
The patient developed diffuse body pain, morning-predominant muscle stiffness, and numbness/tingling in the feet, severely impairing her ability to work and perform daily activities.
The patient developed sicca syndrome (dry eyes) concurrent with the onset of Sjögren's syndrome-related symptoms.
Migraine-like headache was the most common post-traumatic headache sub-phenotype, reported in seven of eight military studies, ranging from 33% to 92% of participants.
Tension-type headache (TTH)-like was the second most common post-traumatic headache sub-phenotype, reported in four studies.
Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) were reported in 13% to 36% of participants in two studies from the same cohort, with blast injury and prior concussion identified as contributing factors.
The reported incidence of post-traumatic headache attributed to mTBI ranged widely, from 16% to 79% at three months and 15% to 58% at one year across civilian and military cohorts.
A large U.S. military study reported PTH incidence at the lower end of the overall range, 16-27% at three months and 20-28% at 12 months.
Among deployed UK military personnel, estimated mTBI prevalence was 4.4%, rising to 9.5% in those in combat roles.
The U.S. military reported mTBI prevalence ranging between 12% and 23%, higher than UK figures.
Schwedt et al. observed structural differences in cortical thickness, without changes in cerebral volume, in PTH patients compared with healthy controls, potentially reflecting diffuse axonal injury.
Intravenous infusion of CGRP induced headache exacerbation with migraine-like features in patients with persistent PTH who had no pre-existing headache history.

One study found lower plasma CGRP levels in 100 participants with persistent PTH compared with sex-matched healthy non-headache controls, contrasting with the elevated CGRP levels typically seen in migraine.
In a military cohort with chronic PTH after mTBI, Topiramate significantly reduced headache frequency by 4.5 days per month compared with tricyclic antidepressants, propranolol, and valproate.

An open-label trial found erenumab reduced mean monthly headache days of moderate-to-severe intensity by 2.8 days from a baseline of 15.7 days by weeks 9 through 12 in patients with persistent PTH, but was not compared to placebo.
Female participants were underrepresented in military PTH studies, averaging 3% (44/1,406) compared with 11.3% representation among UK Regular Forces.
Family history of primary headache was reported in 28% to 32% of the included studies, and six studies included participants with previous concussions affecting 18% to 79% of cohorts.
Across seven military studies reporting monthly headache days, mean values ranged from 9.9 to 26.7 MHD.
Migraine is three to four times more frequent in women than in men, and women report longer migraine attack durations than men.

A study comparing mTBI cohorts with healthy controls found that PTH patients had predominantly migrainous features, with visual or sensory aura, allodynia, and daily or continuous headaches strongly associated with PTH.
In a large study of 3,952 U.S. Army personnel deployed in Iraq, 587 self-reported concussions, of which 72.2% were blast-related.
A two-week low-FODMAP, low-starch, low-sucrose dietary intervention significantly reduced IBS symptom severity scale (IBS-SSS) scores from a mean of 295.5 to 240.
About one-third of IBS patients (32.8%) achieved clinical improvement, defined as at least a 50% decrease in IBS-SSS after the dietary intervention.
A baseline IBS-SSS greater than 400 was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of symptomatic response to the dietary intervention.
IBS patients reporting chronic headache were nearly twice as likely to show symptomatic response to the dietary intervention.
IBS patients reporting chronic fatigue were more likely to show symptomatic response to the dietary intervention.
IBS patients with arthralgia were significantly less likely to respond to the dietary intervention.
Presence of fibromyalgia was associated with a lower likelihood of symptomatic improvement after the dietary intervention.
A composite clinical score combining IBS-SSS, chronic headache, chronic fatigue, arthralgia, and fibromyalgia predicted dietary response with an AUC of 0.72.
A composite score threshold of 3 or higher showed moderate sensitivity and specificity for predicting symptomatic improvement.
In the Norwegian cohort, anxiety/depression was the top-ranked individual predictor of long COVID quality-adjusted life days (QALDs) among clinical and demographic variables in a random forest model.
In Norway, being in the top two quintiles of educational attainment was associated with substantially higher long COVID QALDs, largely independent of clinical mediators.
In Norway, female sex was significantly associated with lower long COVID QALDs, with most of this association not explained by clinical mediators.
In the UK cohort, self-reported full-time employment (versus any other status excluding retirement) was associated with higher long COVID QALDs, largely unmediated by comorbidities.
In the UK cohort, full-time employment versus unemployment was associated with a large and significant increase in long COVID QALDs, mostly unmediated by comorbidities.
In the UK cohort, female sex was associated with markedly lower long COVID QALDs, with the lowest proportion non-mediated observed among all cohort contrasts.
In the Russian cohort, full-time employment versus all other employment categories was significantly associated with higher long COVID QALDs via the direct effect.
In the Russian cohort, female sex was associated with lower long COVID QALDs via the direct effect, while the indirect effect through mediators was inconclusive and possibly opposite in direction.
In the Norwegian cohort, males reported slightly higher unadjusted long COVID QALDs than females.
In the UK cohort, males reported slightly higher unadjusted long COVID QALDs than females.
In the Russian cohort, males reported higher unadjusted long COVID QALDs than females.
In the UK cohort, employment status was the leading predictor of long COVID QALDs, ranking above psychological disorder, age, chronic neurological disorder, and rheumatological disorder.
In the Russian cohort, age was the top-ranked predictor of long COVID QALDs, followed by employment status, hypertension, and chronic neurological disorder.
Asthma was the most commonly reported comorbidity among long COVID participants in the Norwegian cohort.
Hypertension was the most commonly reported comorbidity among long COVID participants in the UK cohort.
Hypertension was the most commonly reported comorbidity among long COVID participants in the Russian cohort.
Among 84,241 Turkish patients with Behçet's syndrome, celiac disease was identified in 175 patients, a frequency of 0.2%.
BS patients with concomitant celiac disease were significantly younger than those without celiac disease.
Female sex was significantly overrepresented among BS patients with concomitant celiac disease.
Inflammatory bowel disease was significantly more common among BS patients with celiac disease than those without.
Uveitis was significantly less frequent in BS patients with celiac disease compared to those without.
No significant difference was found in the frequency of major vascular events (arterial aneurysms, pulmonary thromboembolism, other thrombosis) between BS patients with and without celiac disease.
Depression was significantly more prevalent in BS patients with celiac disease than in those without.
Migraine was significantly more prevalent in BS patients with concomitant celiac disease than in BS patients without celiac disease.
Fibromyalgia was significantly more prevalent in BS patients with celiac disease compared to those without.
Osteoporosis was significantly more prevalent in BS patients with celiac disease compared to those without.

No significant differences were observed in the frequency of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, or malignancy between BS patients with and without celiac disease.
Cyclosporine use was significantly more frequent among BS patients with celiac disease than among those without.
TNFα inhibitor biologic agents were more frequently used in BS patients with celiac disease compared to those without.
Colchicine usage was similar between BS patients with and without celiac disease.
Logistic regression showed that concomitant celiac disease was significantly associated with inflammatory bowel disease in Behçet's syndrome patients.
Logistic regression showed that concomitant celiac disease was significantly associated with autoimmune hepatitis in Behçet's syndrome patients, though with a wide confidence interval.
Logistic regression showed that concomitant celiac disease was significantly associated with fibromyalgia in Behçet's syndrome patients.
Logistic regression showed that concomitant celiac disease was significantly associated with osteoporosis in Behçet's syndrome patients.

Among 104 evaluable biopsy results in the celiac disease group, 74 cases (71.2%) showed histopathologic confirmation of celiac disease (intraepithelial leukocyte infiltration, crypt hyperplasia, or villous atrophy/hypoplasia).
In the only RCT of cardioneuroablation for vasovagal syncope, CNA achieved 92% efficacy in preventing syncope compared with 46% for optimal non-pharmacological treatment.

A meta-analysis of 14 studies including 465 patients found 91.9% freedom from syncope after cardioneuroablation, with no significant difference across GP-mapping techniques but lower success with right-atrial approaches.
A case-control study of 101 patients found that cardioneuroablation was associated with significantly lower risk of syncope recurrence versus conservative therapy.
In an RCT comparing right-atrial vs left-atrial cardioneuroablation approaches, the left-atrial approach produced significantly more vagal denervation confirmed by extracardiac vagal stimulation.
Right-atrial ablation of the PMLGP achieved complete AVN denervation in 40% of patients, which increased to 70% after subsequent left-atrial ablation.
Bi-atrial ablation of the PMLGP restored 1:1 atrioventricular conduction in most patients with persistent atrioventricular block.
Meta-analytic comparison found freedom from syncopal recurrence was lower with right-atrial-only approaches than with left-atrial-only or bi-atrial approaches.
Two RCTs of yoga as a non-invasive alternative therapy showed a significant decrease in the number of syncope and presyncope episodes along with quality-of-life improvement.
Symptomatic sinus tachycardia occurred after cardioneuroablation in up to 27% of patients in a recent study, with 7% requiring long-term beta-blocker and/or ivabradine therapy.
Median radiofrequency ablation time during cardioneuroablation is significantly shorter than during AF ablation procedures.

In a nationwide study of patients receiving their first pacemaker for AVB before age 50, cardioinhibitory reflex was the identified aetiology in only 5% of cases, while the cause remained unknown in half.
Among 31 patients with symptomatic AVB treated with cardioneuroablation, recurrent AVB episodes occurred in only 2 patients over a mean follow-up of about 19 months.

In a cohort of 50 patients believed to have vagally mediated syncope, the estimated 1-year syncope recurrence rate after cardioneuroablation was around 25% regardless of whether patients were selected by tilt test or documented sinus pauses.
High-amplitude fractionated atrial electrograms predicted ablation-induced vagal responses (presumable GP sites) with 72% sensitivity and 91% specificity.
Using spectral-analysis-guided cardioneuroablation, 93% of patients had no new syncope during follow-up.

Three studies with the longest follow-up reported a durable reduction in cardiovagal innervation lasting at least two years after cardioneuroablation, based on HRV variables, despite a statistically non-significant partial recovery between 12 and 18 months.

Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, a state with increased heart rate and decreased HRV similar to the post-cardioneuroablation phenotype, tripled the risk of all-cause death and increased cardiovascular death risk two- to three-fold.
In animal models, ablation of cardiac cholinergic neurons enhanced susceptibility to ventricular arrhythmias, likely via suppression of the cardioprotective effects of vagal innervation.

A blunted heart rate response (<25% increase) to intravenous atropine, or a PR interval that is not or only partially reversible, suggests an intrinsic sinoatrial or atrioventricular node disorder that should exclude patients from cardioneuroablation.

Older patients (>60 years) undergoing cardioneuroablation show less favorable outcomes, including absence of increased sinus rate after ablation, higher syncope recurrence, and no improvement in quality of life.
Among patients undergoing cardioneuroablation for vasovagal syncope where VASIS classification was available, most had a cardioinhibitory (66%) or mixed (31%) form, with vasodepressor form rare (2%).
A pronounced vagal response during ablation was observed in 21-36% of patients when targeting the RSGP with a multifocal approach, versus no vagal response reported with a unifocal approach.
Eighty-seven percent of individuals with multiple system atrophy reported experiencing pain.
Pain in MSA was significantly more prevalent among women than men.
Low-income status was significantly associated with higher prevalence of pain in MSA individuals.
Neck/shoulder, back, and leg pain were the most commonly affected body regions in MSA individuals.
Orthostatic intolerance was significantly associated with neck and shoulder pain in individuals with MSA.
Antecollis, a core motor feature of MSA, was significantly associated with neck and shoulder pain.
Orthostatic intolerance was associated with increased odds of neck and shoulder pain in people with multiple system atrophy.
Antecollis was associated with increased odds of neck and shoulder pain in people with multiple system atrophy.
Among MSA individuals with pain, 76% received treatment, most commonly nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (47%), acetaminophen (39%), and opioids (28%).
Only 53% of respondents reported at least partial satisfaction with their current pain management, indicating suboptimal treatment.
Pain in MSA individuals mostly impacted their work, household activities, and hobbies.
Pain experienced by MSA individuals also impacted the social activities of their informal caregivers.
Headache was reported by 44 of 48 (92%) patients with spontaneous intracranial hypotension due to CSF venous fistula.
Despite the classic orthostatic pattern, 18 of 48 (40%) patients did not report relief of headache when lying flat.
A subset of six of 48 (13%) patients reported worsening of symptoms, rather than relief, when lying flat.
Nineteen of 48 (40%) patients with SIH due to CVF reported at least one migraine symptom.
Six of 48 (13%) patients presented with both at least one migraine symptom and no relief of headache when lying flat, an atypical combination for SIH.
Patients with a 'classic' clinical presentation of SIH due to CVF were significantly more likely to report relief when lying flat compared to those with an 'atypical' presentation.
Frontal head pain was significantly more common in the 'atypical' SIH presentation compared to the 'classic' presentation.
Neck pain was significantly less common in the 'atypical' SIH presentation compared to the 'classic' presentation.
Stabbing or sharp headache quality was significantly more common in the 'atypical' SIH presentation compared to the 'classic' presentation.

Brain MRI findings in SIH due to CVF clustered into three imaging subtypes: one with most classic SIH findings occurring concurrently, one with brain sag but relatively less pachymeningeal/venous engorgement, and one with pachymeningeal/venous engorgement but relatively less brain sag.
The annual prevalence of fibromyalgia among active duty service members was estimated at 0.015% in 2018.
Service members assigned female were about 9 times more likely to receive a fibromyalgia diagnosis than those assigned male.
Fibromyalgia diagnosis was about twice as common among non-Hispanic Black service members compared to White service members.
Co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis was the most common comorbidity, present in 35% of service members around their fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Insomnia was diagnosed as a comorbidity in 24% of service members around fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Migraine was a co-occurring diagnosis in 20% of service members around the time of fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Abdominal and pelvic pain diagnoses co-occurred with fibromyalgia in 19% of service members within the study window.
Approximately 52% of service members received a follow-up visit within 3 months of their fibromyalgia index diagnosis.
About 52% of service members with fibromyalgia received exercise classes or activities as part of pain management care.
About 52% of service members with fibromyalgia received behavioral health care.
About 50% of service members with fibromyalgia received physical therapy.
Chiropractic/osteopathic care was received by 40% of service members with fibromyalgia, among the less commonly used therapies.
Massage therapy was received by 40% of service members with fibromyalgia.
Massage therapy was received by 40% of active duty service members around the time of fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation was received by 33% of service members around the time of fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Self-care education/management was received by 29% of service members around the time of fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Biofeedback and other muscle relaxation therapies were received by 22% of service members around the time of fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Acupuncture or dry needling was the least commonly received therapy, provided to 14% of service members around the time of fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Non-opioid pain medications were the most commonly prescribed treatment, received by 72% of service members around fibromyalgia diagnosis.
44% of active duty service members with fibromyalgia received a muscle relaxant prescription in the 3 months before or after diagnosis.
Nearly one in three (32%) service members with fibromyalgia received an opioid prescription despite guideline recommendations against opioid use in fibromyalgia.
31% of service members with fibromyalgia received an anxiolytic prescription in the 3 months before or after diagnosis.
26% of service members with fibromyalgia received a gabapentinoid prescription in the 3 months before or after diagnosis.
21% of service members with fibromyalgia received a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor prescription in the 3 months before or after diagnosis.
Nausea was identified as the most severe gastrointestinal adverse event signal for rimegepant in the VigiAccess database.
Constipation was the most prevalent gastrointestinal AE signal for atogepant, followed by rimegepant, in the VigiAccess database.
Rimegepant showed higher frequencies of rash and pruritus among skin and subcutaneous tissue disorder AE signals compared with the other gepants.
Alopecia appeared more common with rimegepant than atogepant, and is described as a newly reported AE associated with gepants.
Ubrogepant accounted for a large proportion of detected cardiac and musculoskeletal/connective tissue AE signals in the VigiAccess database.
Atogepant showed a strong cardiac AE signal in FAERS, including cardiac flutter.
Musculoskeletal AEs such as muscle tightness and neck pain showed increased signal numbers for ubrogepant in FAERS.
Raynaud's phenomenon was identified as a rare vascular AE signal, strongest for rimegepant, followed by atogepant, in FAERS.

The change in standing SBP at 1 minute did not differ significantly between atomoxetine and placebo at either 2 or 4 weeks.

One participant reported vivid dreams following a 5 mg psilocybin dose.

5D-ASC altered-states-of-consciousness scores were higher than would be predicted from previous psilocybin dosing literature, despite the low doses used (5-10 mg).
No meaningful improvement or worsening in headache-related impact (HIT-6) was observed over the course of the trial.

Two of the three trial completers had greater than 50% improvement in headache frequency from baseline, a rate historically defined as the threshold for treatment response.
Both patient- and clinician-rated Clinical Global Impression scores indicated overall improvement as the trial progressed.

Thematic analysis of clinical notes identified 'psychological insights' as the most extensively coded theme, reflecting participants' altered, more symbolic relationship with their pain and disorder following psilocybin dosing and psychological support.

The trial was terminated early after enrolling only 4 of a planned 6-12 participants due to recruitment difficulties; 15 of 19 referrals failed pre-screening because of concomitant medications or comorbid disorders.
One participant withdrew from the study prior to the second dosing session due to worsening pain following the first psilocybin dosing session.

An open-label study (n=10) using the same low-to-moderate psilocybin dosing regimen reported a 30% reduction in cluster headache frequency.
An exploratory placebo-crossover trial in migraine found that oral psilocybin (0.143 mg/kg) reduced weekly migraine days by 1.65 days per week.

Indomethacin resolved the headache and autonomic features of hemicrania continua but did not improve the persistent visual aura.
Oral divalproex sodium treatment improved the patient's persistent visual aura that had not responded to indomethacin.

Atomoxetine 40 mg twice daily was associated with suppression of vagally mediated asystole and elimination of sleep syncope in this patient with recurrent vasovagal syncope.

Norepinephrine transporter (NET) inhibition increases intrasynaptic norepinephrine at the sinus node, which recaptures up to 90% of released norepinephrine, a mechanism proposed to prevent the vagally mediated bradycardia/asystole underlying vasovagal syncope.
In the POST 6 trial, atomoxetine prevented terminal profound bradycardia and the conversion of vasovagal presyncope to full syncope during drug-free head-up tilt table testing.

Prior to treatment, the patient's implantable loop recorder documented a 35.6-second asystolic pause preceded by sinus slowing and followed by progressive sinus bradycardia recovery, meeting EHRA criteria for vagally mediated asystole.
Sleep syncope, a loss of consciousness during sleep in a nonintoxicated adult, is an uncommon variant occurring in about 5% of patients with vasovagal syncope.

During 124 days of follow-up on atomoxetine 40 mg twice daily, the patient had no episodes of sleep syncope and only brief sinus pauses (5-6 seconds) rather than prolonged asystole, along with two brief episodes of Mobitz I second-degree AV block.
During atomoxetine treatment, awake presyncopal events were associated with a mean sinus rhythm rate of 52 ± 11 beats/min (range 40-75 bpm), with no auto-transmissions below 40 bpm.

NET inhibition produces a central sympatholytic effect lowering blood pressure alongside a peripheral stimulatory effect raising it, but under stress predominantly causes sinus tachycardia rather than vascular effects, likely owing to narrower synaptic clefts in the sinus node compared to the vasculature.
Atomoxetine's pharmacokinetic half-life (5-21 hours) varies depending on CYP2D6 alleles, which determine the rate of atomoxetine metabolism.
The LRP1 intronic variant rs11172113 was previously reported to be associated with migraine risk with an odds ratio of 1.11.
The same LRP1 variant rs11172113 was previously reported to be associated with fibromuscular dysplasia with an odds ratio of 1.33.
rs11172113 was reported to be associated with spontaneous coronary artery dissection with an odds ratio of 1.62.
rs11172113 was reported to be associated with sporadic thoracic aortic dissection with an odds ratio of 1.21.
rs11172113 showed a suggestive association with cervical artery dissection with an odds ratio of 1.22.

Multitrait Bayesian colocalization of migraine, fibromuscular dysplasia, pulse pressure, and FEV1/FVC association signals supported a single shared causal variant, rs11172113, with a posterior probability of 99.3%.
Colocalization of GWAS and eQTL signals in aorta, tibial, and coronary arteries identified LRP1 as the most likely and only target gene at the rs11172113 locus.
rs11172113 overlaps open chromatin regions specifically in vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, but not in endothelial cells, macrophages, or T lymphocytes.

A 1-kb genomic region centered on rs11172113 showed significantly higher luciferase reporter activity than control in both rat and iPSC-derived SMCs, confirming enhancer activity, but no significant difference was observed between the T and C allele constructs.
Deletion of the 88 bp enhancer region containing rs11172113 in iPSC-derived SMCs led to a significant decrease in LRP1 expression compared with wild-type cells.
NAB2, located 40 kb upstream of rs11172113, also showed significantly decreased expression in enhancer-deletion iPSC-SMCs.

Although rs11172113 is reported as a splicing QTL for the STAT6 exon 1-2 junction in tibial artery, no changes in STAT6 exon junction expression were observed in the iPSC-SMC model, failing to support rs11172113 as the causal variant for this splicing QTL.
In a second, independent iPSC line of male origin, enhancer-deletion clones showed about a 20% reduction in LRP1 mRNA and protein levels, though the protein-level decrease did not reach significance.

siRNA knockdown of MECP2 or SNAI1 in iPSC-derived SMCs significantly increased LRP1 expression, whereas knockdown of RREB1 had no effect, supporting MECP2 and SNAIL as transcriptional repressors of LRP1.
LRP1 knockout iPSC-derived SMCs showed decreased proliferation and migration capacities compared with wild-type SMCs.

LRP1 knockout iPSC-SMCs showed no significant difference from wild-type in collagen gel contraction or intracellular calcium release in response to contractile inducers, contrasting with prior mouse data implicating LRP1 in contractility.

Bulk RNA sequencing identified 213 differentially expressed genes between LRP1 knockout and wild-type iPSC-SMCs, mostly upregulated, with strong enrichment for collagen-containing extracellular matrix genes.
TGFBI, a TGF-β-induced exocrine protein, was among the genes deregulated in LRP1 knockout SMCs.
After TGF-β1 stimulation, LRP1 knockout SMCs showed increased phosphorylated SMAD2/3 with no change in total SMAD2/3, indicating hyperactivation of canonical TGF-β signaling.
LRP1 knockout SMCs secreted increased levels of CYR61, a cysteine-rich angiogenesis inducer and LRP1 ligand involved in vascular integrity, into the extracellular matrix.
LRP1 knockout SMCs showed higher amounts of TIMP3, a matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor normally cleared via LRP1 binding, in the extracellular matrix.
iPSC-SMCs with the rs11172113-associated enhancer deleted (DEL) showed decreased migration capacity compared with wild-type SMCs, mirroring the LRP1 knockout phenotype.
iPSC-SMCs with the rs11172113-associated enhancer deleted (DEL) showed a slightly but significantly increased proliferation capacity compared with wild-type SMCs.
DEL iPSC-SMCs (enhancer-deleted) showed an increased ratio of phosphorylated to total SMAD2/3 after TGF-β1 treatment, similar to LRP1 knockout SMCs, indicating enhanced canonical TGF-β signaling.

RNA sequencing of enhancer-deleted (DEL) iPSC-SMCs found only 5 differentially expressed genes overall, but nominal analysis showed enrichment for ECM organization and extracellular structure organization genes, consistent with LRP1 knockout findings.
Unlike complete LRP1 knockout, enhancer-deleted (DEL) iPSC-SMCs showed no change in secreted amounts of CYR61 and TIMP3 compared with wild-type cells.
TIMP3 was independently prioritized as a candidate gene in a spontaneous coronary artery dissection GWAS, supporting a mechanistic link between LRP1 and TIMP3 in this arterial disease.
At least one cranial autonomic symptom (CAS) was present in nearly two-thirds of migraine patients evaluated in this cross-sectional study.

CAS-positive migraine patients were most frequently in the 21-40 year age group and least frequently older than 60 years.
Most CAS-positive migraine patients experienced a limited symptom burden, with about 70% reporting no more than two cranial autonomic symptoms.
Lacrimation was the most common cranial autonomic symptom reported by migraine patients.
Conjunctival injection was the second most common cranial autonomic symptom in migraine patients.
Aural fullness was the third most common cranial autonomic symptom and was more prevalent than in a comparable Indian study, supporting its inclusion in ICHD-3 criteria.
Eyelid edema was reported in about 30% of CAS-positive migraine patients.
Nasal congestion was reported in about a quarter of CAS-positive migraine patients, comparable to a Taiwanese study.
Sweating on the face and forehead was reported in a quarter of CAS-positive migraine patients.
Facial flushing was reported in about 16% of CAS-positive migraine patients.
Rhinorrhea was reported in about 10% of CAS-positive migraine patients.
Ptosis was one of the least common cranial autonomic symptoms in migraine patients.
Miosis was the least commonly reported cranial autonomic symptom in migraine patients.
Bilateral cranial autonomic symptoms were much more common than unilateral CAS among migraine patients, including many with unilateral headache.
Prior evidence suggests TRESK potassium channels are involved in migraine pathophysiology, though the effects of TRESK activation were previously unclear.
The TRESK activator cloxyquin attenuated nitroglycerin-induced mechanical allodynia in the in-vivo rat migraine model.

Cloxyquin reduced trigeminal ganglion CGRP levels in the in-vivo nitroglycerin-induced migraine model.
Cloxyquin reduced meningeal mast cell degranulation and number in the in-vivo nitroglycerin-induced migraine model.
Cloxyquin diminished capsaicin-induced CGRP release from ex-vivo meningeal, trigeminal ganglion and brainstem preparations.

The selective TRESK channel inhibitor A2764 blocked all the anti-migraine effects of cloxyquin in both in-vivo and ex-vivo preparations, confirming that cloxyquin acts specifically via TRESK channel activation.
Combining cloxyquin with the migraine drug sumatriptan produced a synergistic reduction of capsaicin-induced CGRP release in ex-vivo trigeminovascular preparations.
