Alpha and beta adrenergic receptor autoantibodies have been reported as associated with POTS and orthostatic hypotension.
Cholinergic receptor autoantibodies have been reported as associated with POTS and orthostatic hypotension.
Angiotensin II type I receptor autoantibodies have been reported as associated with POTS and orthostatic hypotension.
Case reports and series suggest that immunotherapy with intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis can benefit patients with severe POTS refractory to standard therapies.

Among functional gastrointestinal disorder patients positive for ganglionic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antibodies, three of four also had dry eyes and dry mouth, whereas antibody-negative patients had no such symptoms.
A separate study confirmed that fibrin drives thromboinflammation and neuropathology following COVID-19 infection, corroborating earlier findings of microclots in long COVID patients.

ME/CFS patients who tested positive for POTS or orthostatic hypotension on tilt table testing had more sleep problems, more post-exertional malaise, and greater physical and health function limitations than those who tested negative.
Mast cell activation syndrome is described as a multisystemic immunologic disorder with an estimated prevalence of 17%.
Six of eight MCAS patients with refractory neuropsychiatric symptoms had comorbid autonomic disorders (most commonly POTS), and four had hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

All eight MCAS patients experienced significant improvement in neuropsychiatric and multisystemic symptoms after mast-cell-directed therapy including antihistamines, mast-cell-stabilizing agents, and a low-histamine diet.
An estimated 17.6% of U.S. adults have experienced Long COVID, a condition marked by new or lingering symptoms after initial COVID-19 infection.
Long COVID is associated with significantly reduced quality of life, and patient-provider relationships are known to influence QoL more generally.
Respondents with at least a bachelor's degree reported higher quality of life than those with less education.
Older respondents with Long COVID were more likely to report lower quality of life.
Trust in healthcare providers was a significant predictor of higher quality of life among Long COVID patients.
Greater trust in healthcare providers was a significant predictor of higher quality of life among Long COVID patients.
Patients who felt their Long COVID symptoms were dismissed by providers reported lower quality of life.
Headaches/migraine was the sixth most commonly self-reported diagnosed condition among Florida medical cannabis users, reported by about a third of respondents.
Headaches/migraine was reported by about one-fifth of respondents as one of their main reasons for using medical cannabis.
Among respondents with headaches/migraine, most perceived improvement in this condition with medical cannabis use.
A small minority of respondents with headaches/migraine perceived that medical cannabis worsened this condition.
Fibromyalgia was self-reported as a diagnosed condition by 13.0% of medical cannabis users surveyed.
Fibromyalgia was cited as a main reason for using medical cannabis by 10.6% of respondents.
The large majority of respondents with fibromyalgia perceived improvement in this condition with medical cannabis use.
A small proportion of respondents with fibromyalgia perceived that medical cannabis worsened this condition.
CGRP levels are elevated during acute cluster headache attacks, implicating it as a pathophysiological driver and therapeutic target.
VIP levels are elevated during acute cluster headache attacks, suggesting parasympathetic involvement in pathophysiology.
PACAP-38 levels are elevated during acute cluster headache attacks, supporting its role as a novel therapeutic target.
PET studies show hypothalamic and cortical activation during cluster headache attacks, supporting a central hypothalamic role in pathogenesis.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy reveals altered hypothalamic metabolite levels in cluster headache patients.
A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found high-flow oxygen to be the most effective acute treatment for cluster headache at 15 and 30 minutes, outperforming sumatriptan, nVNS, octreotide, and zolmitriptan.
Subcutaneous sumatriptan is the only FDA-approved triptan for acute cluster headache, with proven efficacy and tolerability at doses up to 6 mg (max 12 mg/24h).
Intranasal sumatriptan at 20 mg is effective for acute cluster headache but has slower onset than the subcutaneous formulation.
Intranasal and oral zolmitriptan show a modest effect as acute treatment options for cluster headache.
Small retrospective studies suggest intravenous dihydroergotamine (DHE) may be effective for cluster headache in inpatient and outpatient settings, though supporting evidence remains limited.
Corticosteroid treatment appears to decrease CGRP and melatonin metabolite levels in cluster headache patients.

Occipital nerve block with anesthetic and corticosteroid produced side effects in about 40% of patients, with chronic CH patients reporting a median relief duration of 3 months after a series of three injections.
Long-half-life triptans such as frovatriptan and naratriptan may provide additional preventive benefit for cluster headache as add-on therapy, based on limited uncontrolled evidence.
Verapamil doses above 480 mg/day are associated with PR interval prolongation, requiring regular ECG monitoring.
Galcanezumab, a CGRP monoclonal antibody, reduces weekly attack frequency in episodic cluster headache, but all trials in chronic cluster headache have failed.
Fremanezumab trials for cluster headache were aborted early because of futility analysis results.
OnabotulinumtoxinA may decrease frequency and intensity of chronic cluster headache attacks, but shows no significant improvement in episodic cluster headache in one lower-dose study.
Targeted injections into the sphenopalatine ganglion have reduced headache frequency and severity in cluster headache patients across two studies.
A small trial of otic ganglion injection in 10 participants demonstrated safety of the technique but no statistically significant change in headache patterns.
Lithium carbonate efficacy for cluster headache prevention is supported by only a few trials and has a longer latency to efficacy compared to verapamil.
Topiramate acts on GABAergic, glutamatergic (AMPA/kainate), and sodium channel pathways, and increases cerebral GABA concentrations, which may underlie its analgesic mechanism in cluster headache.
A double-blind randomized controlled trial found no significant benefit of valproate for cluster headache prevention, contradicting earlier open-label and retrospective studies suggesting benefit.
Patients with cluster headache have low melatonin levels both during and between bouts.
High-dose melatonin (10 mg) reduces attack frequency in early days of the bout in episodic cluster headache, with excellent tolerability and safety.
Verapamil is regarded as the first-line preventive treatment for cluster headache despite being used off-label without FDA/EMA approval for this indication.
Only 50-80% of cluster headache patients respond to verapamil, and many require very high doses, limiting its use because of side effects.
Verapamil doses above 480 mg/day are associated with cardiac conduction abnormalities, particularly PR interval prolongation, requiring regular ECG monitoring.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies reduced the number of weekly cluster headache attacks in patients with episodic cluster headache.
All clinical trials of CGRP monoclonal antibodies in chronic cluster headache have failed to demonstrate efficacy.
Trials of fremanezumab for cluster headache were terminated early following a futility analysis.
Small-scale studies and case reports indicate that onabotulinumtoxinA (OTA) may decrease the frequency and intensity of chronic cluster headache attacks.
One study found onabotulinumtoxinA showed no significant improvement in episodic cluster headache when fewer units were used.
Targeted injections into the sphenopalatine ganglion reduced headache frequency and severity in two studies.
A small trial of 10 participants showed injection into the otic ganglion was safe but produced no statistically significant change in headache patterns.
Lithium carbonate has limited supporting trial evidence for cluster headache and has a longer latency to efficacy compared with verapamil.

Topiramate is thought to act on cluster headache via blockade of voltage-sensitive sodium channels and AMPA glutamate receptors and enhancement of the GABAergic system, including increasing cerebral GABA concentrations.
Evidence for valproate in cluster headache is conflicting: open-label and retrospective studies suggested benefit, but a double-blind randomized controlled trial found no significant difference.
Patients with cluster headache have low melatonin levels both during and between cluster bouts.
High-dose melatonin (10 mg) reduced the frequency of attacks in the early days of the bout in episodic cluster headache with excellent tolerability and safety.
Non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation (gammaCore) showed efficacy in only 40% of patients during the first month, dropping to less than 30% in subsequent months.
Percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation of the occipital nerve showed efficacy and tolerability in medically intractable chronic cluster headache.
Percutaneous pulsed radiofrequency aimed at the C1 and C2 nerve roots and ganglia resulted in moderate improvements without serious adverse effects.
Sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) neurostimulation produced significant analgesic effect in approximately 70% of chronic cluster headache patients unresponsive to established preventive therapies.
SPG stimulation produced a tenfold improvement in pain relief compared to placebo, with some patients experiencing complete pain cessation within 15 minutes of activation.
Longitudinal follow-up showed that two-thirds of patients maintained continued symptom relief from SPG stimulation after 2 years.
Occipital nerve stimulation reduced the frequency of weekly cluster headache attacks but carries a risk of serious adverse events such as lead migration and battery failure.

CT-guided pulsed radiofrequency therapy targeting the sphenopalatine ganglion, enhanced by post-procedure lidocaine and methylprednisolone, significantly extended remission periods in both episodic and chronic cluster headache.

A systematic review of five small open-label studies found that hypothalamic deep brain stimulation significantly reduced pain in 42% of chronic cluster headache patients, while 58% experienced adverse effects, most commonly trigeminal sensory disturbances.
Children with cluster headache have a lower maximum daily attack frequency than adults (6 versus 8) and may experience longer remission periods, potentially contributing to delayed diagnosis.
In the blinded extension phase of a randomized controlled trial, a repeat psilocybin pulse significantly reduced cluster headache attack frequency by 50%.

Preclinical studies suggest that activation of the 5-HT1F receptor by lasmiditan may offer potential efficacy for cluster headache, particularly in patients with vascular risk factors who cannot use triptans.
A clinical trial evaluating intranasal ketamine spray for chronic cluster headache, acting via NMDA receptor antagonism to modulate central sensitization, has results pending.
An ongoing clinical trial is investigating an infusion of ketamine combined with magnesium sulfate for chronic cluster headache.
Rimegepant, a CGRP receptor antagonist used for migraine, is being investigated in an open-label pilot study for cluster headache.
A clinical trial is investigating long-term exposure to eptinezumab, a CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibody, for chronic cluster headache.
A clinical trial is investigating the efficacy of erenumab, a CGRP receptor monoclonal antibody, for chronic cluster headache.

PACAP-38 has been proposed as a novel therapeutic target for cluster headache, acting as a ligand for VPAC1/2 and PAC1 receptors to modulate cranial-autonomic and trigeminovascular responses via parasympathetic projections.
A phase 3 clinical trial is investigating repeated greater occipital nerve injections with methylprednisolone as a prophylactic treatment for chronic cluster headache.
A randomized, placebo-controlled, triple-blinded trial of a single onabotulinumtoxinA injection into the sphenopalatine ganglion for chronic cluster headache is ongoing.
In a blinded extension phase of a randomized controlled trial, a repeat psilocybin pulse significantly reduced cluster headache attack frequency by 50%.
A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial investigating oral LSD for episodic and chronic cluster headache is ongoing.
The therapeutic mechanism of psychedelics in cluster headache is hypothesized to involve serotonin 5-HT2A receptor agonism, with ongoing research into the role of the beta-arrestin pathway.
Prior to controlled trial data, evidence for psychedelics including psilocybin and LSD in cluster headache management was primarily supported by case series and patient surveys.
In a randomized double-blind trial of 67 IBS-D patients, mirtazapine reduced IBS symptom severity and improved quality of life and anxiety compared to placebo.
A cohort study using a large US health plan dataset found IBS patients had a 60% elevated risk of migraine compared to those without IBS.
In a crossover RCT of chronic tension-type headache patients, mirtazapine significantly reduced the headache area-under-the-curve compared to placebo.
In a placebo-controlled parallel trial of 93 headache patients, low-dose mirtazapine alone reduced headache severity by 20%, showing a dose-response relationship.
Serotonin reuptake transporter transcription is decreased in IBS patients, raising serotonin levels via reduced neuronal uptake and contributing to anxiety.
A case report described successful treatment of comorbid panic disorder, depression, and mixed-type IBS with mirtazapine, with improvement in diarrhea, constipation, and psychiatric symptoms.
In depressed patients aged 65 and older, mirtazapine produced a faster response than paroxetine and a greater reduction in anxiety/somatization and sleep disturbance scores.
A systematic review found that IBS patients have significantly higher anxiety and depression levels than controls.
A meta-analysis found the prevalence of comorbid sleep disorders in IBS patients to be 37.6%.
A 2-week trial of mirtazapine (15 and 30 mg) in 130 depressed patients with insomnia showed symptom improvement at both doses, with an initial 10% somnolence incidence decreasing over the trial.
Mirtazapine showed similar efficacy and safety compared to amitriptyline in treating depressed patients aged 60-85 years.
A 12-week open-label study found mirtazapine achieved a 79.5% response rate in generalized anxiety disorder based on HAM-A and CGI-I criteria.
In depressed adults aged 65 and older, mirtazapine produced a faster treatment response than paroxetine (26 vs 40 days) and greater reductions in anxiety/somatization and sleep disturbance scores.
A systematic review found IBS patients had significantly higher anxiety and depression levels than controls, with standardized mean differences of 0.76 (anxiety) and 0.80 (depression).
A meta-analysis found the prevalence of sleep disorders comorbid with IBS to be 37.6%.
In a 2-week trial of 130 depressed patients with insomnia, mirtazapine at 15 mg and 30 mg doses improved insomnia symptoms, with an initial 10% incidence of somnolence declining over the trial.
In a double-blind study of 19 depressed patients with insomnia, mirtazapine improved total sleep time and sleep latency compared to fluoxetine, but this was not statistically significant.

In a rat model of colonic sensitization, mirtazapine dose-dependently reduced visceral hypersensitivity and marginally improved delayed gastric emptying while slightly delaying small intestinal transit.
In an Iranian double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, mirtazapine produced significantly greater improvement in IBS symptom severity score than placebo.
Mirtazapine reduced the average number of daily bowel movements from 2.30 to 1.83 in IBS-D patients over the course of the trial.
Mirtazapine treatment produced significantly greater improvement in IBS-related quality of life scores than placebo over 8 weeks.
In an open-label study of 19 IBS-D patients titrated from 15 to 30 mg mirtazapine, significant reductions were observed in abdominal pain, urgency, diarrhea, and bloating scores.
In an Iranian RCT of IBS-D patients, mirtazapine produced a significantly greater reduction in IBS symptom severity score than placebo.
Mirtazapine reduced the average number of daily bowel movements from baseline to end of trial in IBS-D patients.
IBS-D patients treated with mirtazapine reported improvements in depression symptoms compared to placebo.
Mirtazapine significantly improved quality of life scores (IBS-QoL) compared to placebo in an IBS-D RCT.
Mirtazapine improved stool consistency and reduced stool frequency, urgency, and abdominal pain in IBS-D patients, increasing symptom-free days.
An open-label study of 19 IBS-D patients treated with mirtazapine 15-30 mg showed significant reductions in abdominal pain, urgency, diarrhea, and bloating scores.
A randomized placebo-controlled trial found that a single dose of mirtazapine before orthopedic surgery significantly lowered the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting.
Mirtazapine significantly reduced nausea and vomiting in patients with refractory gastroparesis at 2 and 4 weeks post-treatment.
Mirtazapine use is associated with average weight gain, greater with long-term than short-term use.
In women with depressive episodes, six weeks of mirtazapine monotherapy significantly increased body weight, body fat mass, and leptin concentration.
An open-label trial in healthy men found mirtazapine increased hunger, appetite for sweets, carbohydrate preference, and insulin/C-peptide release after meals.

In a phase II trial of non-depressed cancer patients with cachexia/anorexia, 24% gained at least 1 kg after 4 weeks of mirtazapine therapy, with correlated reductions in fatigue, nausea, and early satiety.
IBS has been noted to be associated with atopic dermatitis, reflecting a bidirectional gut-skin axis.
In a crossover trial of hemodialysis patients with chronic pruritus, mirtazapine produced significantly greater improvement in pruritus severity than gabapentin.
In a 6-week open-label trial of fibromyalgia patients treated with mirtazapine, 54% of completers reported clinically significant reduction in pain intensity and analgesic use.
A post-marketing surveillance study of psychiatric and neurological outpatients found that mirtazapine significantly reduced pain in patients with chronic pain and concurrent depression.
Approximately 70% of patients taking mirtazapine experienced at least one adverse event, a rate similar to other antidepressants.

A common-factor GWAS combining six chronic overlapping pain conditions identified 663 SNPs across 15 genomic risk loci (24 independent SNPs) significantly associated with a latent nociplastic pain factor.
The latent nociplastic pain factor was found to be significantly SNP-heritable on the liability scale.
Nociplastic pain showed extremely high genetic correlation with multisite chronic pain (MCP), a general chronic pain trait.
Nociplastic pain was only weakly genetically correlated with rheumatoid arthritis, a condition considered predominantly nociceptive/inflammatory rather than nociplastic.
Nociplastic and neuropathic pain were significantly, though incompletely, genetically correlated, indicating both shared and distinct genetic architecture.
A multivariate transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) across the six COPCs found 819 tissue-wide significant gene-tissue associations involving 127 unique genes across 49 GTEx tissues.

Of the 819 tissue-wide significant gene-tissue associations, 450 showed significant heterogeneity (i.e., effects driven by a subset of COPCs rather than the shared nociplastic pain factor), while 369 did not.

Cultured fibroblasts, atrial appendage of the heart, tibial nerve, and thyroid tissue showed a significantly higher proportion of tissue-wide significant TWAS gene-tissue associations with nociplastic pain than expected by chance.
Amygdala, substantia nigra, EBV-transformed lymphocytes, terminal ileum, and vagina showed significantly fewer tissue-wide significant TWAS associations with nociplastic pain than expected by chance.
At nominal significance, whole blood and skeletal muscle showed a higher proportion of significant gene-tissue TWAS associations with nociplastic pain than expected by chance.
The KEGG nitrogen metabolism pathway gene set was significantly enriched among genes associated with nociplastic pain in TWAS, a pathway also previously implicated in ME/CFS.

Genes specifically upregulated in liver tissue (SU_LIVER gene set) were enriched among genes specifically associated with nociplastic pain, suggesting liver-related changes may precede development of nociplastic pain.
44 GWAS Catalog traits, including cognitive function, extremely high intelligence, sleep duration, and headache, were enriched among all tissue-wide significant nociplastic pain-associated genes.

Migraine, migraine without aura, and headache GWAS Catalog trait gene sets were enriched only among non-specific (heterogeneous) nociplastic pain genes, indicating migraine and headache pathology is largely distinct from the shared nociplastic pain factor across other COPCs.
GWAS Catalog traits for amino acid and acylcarnitine levels were enriched among genes specifically associated with nociplastic pain (non-heterogeneous genes).
Among chronic overlapping pain conditions with available ICD-10 codes in UK Biobank, fibromyalgia was the condition most overrepresented among individuals classified as multisite chronic pain cases.

The authors note that increased tibial nerve cross-sectional area has been observed on ultrasound in fibromyalgia patients compared with controls, and tarsal tunnel syndrome (involving the tibial nerve) is more common in fibromyalgia, consistent with the TWAS enrichment of nociplastic pain genes in tibial nerve tissue.

The authors cite prior work indicating that infection may trigger or exacerbate existing painful conditions and that individuals with a pre-existing chronic overlapping pain condition were more likely to develop long COVID.

Enrichment of nociplastic pain gene associations in thyroid tissue may reflect thyroid involvement in COPCs or comorbid/misdiagnosed hypothyroidism among participants, since autoimmune hypothyroidism can be misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia and can cause or worsen pain.

Enrichment of nociplastic pain genes in atrial appendage tissue, combined with prior links between chronic pain and electrocardiogram abnormalities such as atrial fibrillation, suggests atrial fibrillation and associated stroke risk may be commonly associated with nociplastic pain.
Among non-treatment-seeking adults with OUD, 35.0% (49/141) met ACRFMS criteria for fibromyalgia.
In a single-predictor ordinal regression model, fibromyalgia was associated with over three-fold higher odds of endorsing that pain had previously caused a relapse to opioid use.
After adjusting for age, sex, anxiety/depression, and OUD severity, fibromyalgia remained the only significant predictor of increased odds of prior pain-precipitated relapse.
Age, sex, anxiety/depression (RAND-36 Mental Health domain), and OUD severity were not significantly associated with odds of endorsing pain-precipitated relapse.
Fibromyalgia remained significantly associated with increased odds of prior pain-precipitated relapse even after accounting for pain severity as a covariate.
Moderate, severe, and very severe pain (RAND-36 item 21) were each significantly associated with greater odds of endorsing prior pain-precipitated relapse, independent of fibromyalgia.
Total ACRFMS score was positively correlated with self-reported pain severity, and fibromyalgia status was moderately associated with reporting very severe pain.
Bodily pain was highly prevalent in this non-treatment-seeking OUD sample, with over two-thirds reporting at least moderate pain in the past 4 weeks.
Nearly half of participants reported multi-focal pain (pain at four or more body sites), a hallmark feature of the nociplastic pain phenotype; low back, upper back, and neck pain were most common.
Non-pain symptoms associated with the nociplastic/fibromyalgia phenotype (cognitive problems, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep) were common in this OUD sample.
A majority of non-treatment-seeking participants (59.7%) reported that pain had previously caused them to relapse to opioid use.
Participants with and without fibromyalgia did not differ significantly in age of first opioid use, duration of use, frequency of daily use, or daily money spent on opioids.

A model including fibromyalgia plus pain severity fit the data better than a model with pain severity alone, indicating fibromyalgia contributes uniquely to pain-precipitated relapse beyond pain severity.
Headache is reported by roughly 30-70% or more of patients with acromegaly and can be a severe, disabling symptom.
Migraine is the most common headache type in acromegaly, occurring in 30-50% of patients who report headache, followed by tension-type headache and rarely trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.
In a prospective study, cavernous sinus invasion by nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas (per Knosp grading) was linked to headache occurrence in 97 patients.
Mean intrasellar pressure was significantly higher in pituitary adenoma patients with headache than in those without headache.

Intraoperative measurement showed that reduction of intrasellar pressure after transsphenoidal adenomectomy was greater in headache patients, and headache significantly improved in most patients postoperatively.
In a large cohort of children treated with supraphysiologic doses of recombinant human growth hormone for GH deficiency, headache was a reported adverse effect at treatment initiation.
In pituitary adenoma patients, plasma CGRP levels were several times higher in those with headache compared with those without headache.
PACAP plasma levels were similarly several times higher in pituitary adenoma patients with headache than those without headache in the same study.
Chronic migraine is reported to be eight times more common in patients with temporomandibular joint pathology than in the general population.
Arterial hypertension is one of the most frequent complications of acromegaly, occurring on average in about 35% of cases.
Migraine and hypertension share proposed pathogenic mechanisms including endothelial dysfunction, RAAS hyperactivation, and insufficient autonomic nervous regulation.
Pituitary apoplexy causes severe frontal or retro-orbital headache in 80-90% of affected patients, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and ophthalmologic disturbances.

In a prospective study of 84 pituitary tumor patients with headache (33% acromegaly), the most common syndromes were chronic migraine (often in those with prior migraine history) and episodic migraine.
In Schankin et al.'s prospective study, headache occurred in 41% of pituitary adenoma patients, with migraine being the most common subtype among headache sufferers.
In a cross-sectional study of 146 pituitary adenoma patients (19.9% acromegaly), over half reported headache, and most of those had migraine.
Levy et al. found that among patients with unilateral headache related to pituitary adenoma, cavernous sinus invasion was ipsilateral to the headache side in more than half of a subset of patients.
Multicenter randomized placebo-controlled trials found that short-acting subcutaneous octreotide relieved headache in approximately 80% of acromegaly patients.

A small observational study found that combining long-acting octreotide with short-acting octreotide reduced the number of short-acting injections needed, suggesting improved headache control in acromegaly patients without SSA resistance.
A retrospective study found that a subset of acromegaly patients experienced temporary worsening of headache in the early post-radiotherapy period.
Headache is listed as a common side effect at initiation of pegvisomant therapy, and tumor growth observed in some patients during the first year of treatment may worsen headache.

Resistance to first-generation somatostatin analogs in acromegaly is associated with several tumor molecular features including truncated SSTR5 expression, low SSTR2 expression, high baseline GH, high Ki-67, sparsely granulated somatotroph subtype, low E-cadherin, low Raf kinase inhibitor protein, AIP gene mutation, hyperintense T2 MRI signal, young age, and male sex.

Pituitary apoplexy, a hemorrhagic or infarctive event in the pituitary gland, causes severe frontal or retro-orbital headache in 80-90% of affected patients, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and ophthalmologic disturbances.
The prevalence of pituitary apoplexy among pituitary adenoma patients is reported to range from 2% to 12% across different sources.

The Eurolight project found an association between migraine and depressive/anxiety disorders, with medication-overuse headache showing a stronger link to depression and anxiety, while tension-type headache was associated only with anxiety.

In Levy et al.'s prospective study of 84 pituitary tumor patients with headache (33% acromegaly), chronic migraine (46%) and episodic migraine (30%) were the most common headache syndromes, followed by primary stabbing headache (27%) and rarer trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.

In Schankin et al.'s prospective study, headache occurred in 24 of 58 (41%) pituitary adenoma patients, with migraine in 45.8%, tension-type headache in 33.3%, both in 16.7%, and migraine combined with cluster headache in 4.2%.
A cross-sectional study by Dallel et al. of 146 pituitary adenoma patients (19.9% with acromegaly) found headache in 79 (54.1%), of whom 44 (55.7%) reported migraine.
A retrospective review by Wang et al. found that in patients with both hormone-secreting and non-functioning pituitary adenomas, headache laterality corresponded to the side of the tumor.
Yu et al. also noted that in patients with unilateral headache associated with pituitary adenoma, cavernous sinus invasion was ipsilateral to the headache.
In the Levy et al. study, correlation between cavernous sinus invasion and ipsilateral headache was found in 10 of 18 patients.
Several older prospective studies found that many pituitary adenoma patients experienced reduced headache intensity and attack frequency after surgical treatment.
A case report by Rocha et al. described complete resolution of SUNCT syndrome following surgical removal of a non-functioning pituitary adenoma.
In contrast to studies showing benefit, Andersson et al. reported incomplete headache relief and even worsening of headache following pituitary surgery in some patients.
Favorable prognostic factors for headache relief after transsphenoidal adenomectomy are considered to be younger patient age and a hormone-secreting microadenoma.

No clear correlation was found between headache in acromegaly and serum IGF-1 and growth hormone levels or pituitary adenoma size; headache could resolve without biochemical control or persist despite IGF-1/GH suppression with somatostatin analogs.

The analgesic properties of first-generation somatostatin analogs may be explained by their high affinity for SSTR2, a receptor widely expressed in the trigeminal spinal nucleus and periaqueductal gray matter that plays a role in nociception.
Multicenter randomized placebo-controlled trials found that short-acting subcutaneous octreotide relieved headache in approximately 80% of acromegaly patients.
Chronic migraine occurs about eight times more often in patients with temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pathology than in the general population.

The Eurolight project found an association between migraine and comorbid depression/anxiety disorders, with a stronger link seen for medication-overuse headache and both depression and anxiety, while tension-type headache was associated only with anxiety.
Sleep quality is frequently impaired in patients with pituitary disease, especially acromegaly, likely due to obstructive sleep apnea, bruxism, and insomnia.
Mutation in the AIP gene has been associated in the literature with resistance to first-generation somatostatin analogue therapy in acromegaly.
Headache is reported as a frequent adverse effect at initiation of pegvisomant therapy according to the drug's approved product information.
Some patients on pegvisomant show tumor growth during the first year of treatment, which may contribute to worsening headache, warranting periodic MRI monitoring.
In a retrospective study, 8 of 83 acromegaly patients (9.6%) treated with radiotherapy experienced temporary worsening of headache in the early post-radiation period.
Headache remission with dopamine agonist treatment is achieved more often in prolactinoma than in acromegaly, likely due to a greater degree of tumor shrinkage in prolactinoma.
Arterial hypertension is one of the most common complications of acromegaly, occurring on average in 35% of cases.
Compared with the general population, acromegaly patients more often show elevated diastolic blood pressure and a non-dipper pattern of nocturnal blood pressure variation.
Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in acromegaly leads to sodium and water retention, causing peripheral edema, weight gain, and carpal tunnel syndrome.
Finocchi et al. describe pathogenic mechanisms shared between migraine and hypertension, including endothelial dysfunction, RAAS hyperactivation, and insufficient autonomic nervous system regulation.
In a cohort of 57,968 children receiving supraphysiological doses of recombinant human growth hormone, headache was reported at a rate of 793.5 per 100,000 patient-years at the start of therapy.
Pituitary apoplexy prevalence among pituitary adenoma patients is estimated at 2-12% across different reports.

In 80-90% of pituitary apoplexy cases, patients experience severe frontal or retro-orbital headache, which can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and ophthalmologic disturbances including cranial nerve palsies and bitemporal hemianopsia.
SSTR1 and SSTR4 receptors, belonging to the SRIF2 group, are proposed to mediate anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects and are expressed in human vascular endothelium.

The analgesic properties of first-generation somatostatin analogues may be explained by high affinity for SSTR2, which is widely expressed in the trigeminal spinal nucleus and periaqueductal gray matter and plays a role in nociception.
Somatostatin receptors may heterodimerize with opioid receptors, which could lead to headache worsening and tachyphylaxis with frequent use of somatostatin analogues.

Pasireotide, a second-generation somatostatin analogue with high affinity for SSTR1, SSTR2, SSTR3, and SSTR5, may provide good analgesic effect in patients resistant to first-generation somatostatin analogues.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab) have shown good efficacy in the prevention of chronic migraine, the headache type most frequently reported in acromegaly patients.
Verapamil and lithium preparations have shown the best efficacy for cluster headache prophylaxis, while subcutaneous/intranasal triptans and 100% oxygen inhalation are used for acute attacks.
In multicenter randomized placebo-controlled trials, subcutaneous short-acting octreotide relieved headache in approximately 80% of acromegaly patients.

A small observational study (n=18) found that combining long-acting with short-acting octreotide reduced the number of short-acting injections needed, indicating better headache control in patients without resistance to first-generation somatostatin analogues.

Matharu et al. conducted a placebo-controlled study demonstrating octreotide's efficacy for cluster headache in patients without acromegaly, suggesting it may help patients unresponsive to or intolerant of triptans.
Wang et al. reported in a retrospective review that in patients with both hormone-producing and non-functioning pituitary adenomas, headache side corresponded to the side of the tumor.
In Levy et al.'s study, a correlation between cavernous sinus invasion and ipsilateral headache was found in 10 of 18 patients.
Favorable prognostic factors for headache relief after transnasal transsphenoidal adenomectomy are considered to be young age and hormone-producing microadenoma.
In contrast to studies reporting improvement, Andersson et al. found incomplete surgical effect and even worsening of headache after adenomectomy in some patients.
A case report by Rocha et al. demonstrated resolution of SUNCT syndrome following surgical removal of a non-functioning pituitary adenoma.
Among 100 consecutive patients with brain MRI scans reported as normal, 26% complained of headache.
25% of patients with normal MRI brain scans reported focal neurological symptoms.
15% of patients with normal MRI brain scans complained of dizziness.
13% of patients with normal MRI brain scans had seizure or collapse episodes.
Nearly half (46%) of patients with normal MRI brain scans had no final diagnosis established.
18% of patients with normal MRI brain scans were diagnosed with migraine.
7% of patients with normal MRI brain scans were diagnosed with functional neurological disorder.
6% of patients with normal MRI brain scans were diagnosed with epilepsy.

The authors argue that clinical overlap between patients with 'normal' brain MRIs and patients with known venous sinus disease suggests that current understanding of normal craniocervical venous anatomy is derived circularly and may misclassify subtle venous outflow compromise as normal.
Mastocytosis was found to be more prevalent among non-Hispanic white patients in this cohort.
Compared with the general population, mastocytosis patients had similar rates of atopy and allergies overall.
Mastocytosis patients showed a slight increase in reported asthma prevalence compared with the general population.
Anaphylaxis occurred in 28% of the mastocytosis cohort overall, with the great majority occurring in patients with systemic disease.
Hymenoptera (insect) venom was identified as the most common trigger of anaphylaxis in this mastocytosis cohort.
Anaphylaxis was rare among patients with cutaneous mastocytosis, in contrast to systemic disease where it was much more common.
The study found an increased prevalence of contrast-induced anaphylaxis in mastocytosis patients compared with previous literature.
