Post-prandial distress syndrome was the only DGBI significantly associated with meeting depression criteria on the PHQ-2, while post-prandial distress syndrome, rumination syndrome and proctalgia fugax were associated with meeting anxiety criteria on the GAD-2.
Women meeting anxiety criteria had significantly higher total sleep problems, somnolence, and waking with shortness of breath or headache scores.
Women meeting depression criteria had significantly worse total sleep problems, sleep disturbance, somnolence and waking with shortness of breath or headache scores.

Partial least squares analysis identified the SF36 bodily pain domain as a stronger predictor of pain-related outcomes than the widespread pain index, leading to its use in subsequent regression models of mental health.

In a logistic regression controlling for DGBI count, FBDSI, diet quality, sleep problems, comorbidities and BMI, only pain (SF36-BP) was significantly predictive of meeting PHQ-2 depression criteria, with the overall model explaining 33.4%-47.2% of variance.

Higher diet quality (Healthy Eating Index) was associated with a small but significant reduction in the likelihood of meeting anxiety criteria, in a model where SF36-BP remained the strongest predictor and overall explained 23.3%-31.4% of variance.
The overall DGBI prevalence in this fibromyalgia cohort (93%) was slightly lower than the 98% reported previously by Almansa's group using older Rome II criteria.
Only 18% of controls (comparator women without fibromyalgia) met criteria for at least one DGBI, notably lower than the 39% reported for controls in Almansa's earlier study.

Cited literature reports that experiencing a migraine attack predicted a flare of fibromyalgia pain within 12 hours, and that prophylactic migraine medication significantly reduced the number of fibromyalgia flares.
Cited literature reports that around 16.7% of people with fibromyalgia attempt suicide, a rate that rises to over 58% when migraine is comorbid.
Women with tension-type headache (TTH) were significantly less likely to meet criteria for Rome IV oesophageal, gastroduodenal, or anorectal disorders than those without TTH.
Significant associations were found between OI genetic variants and dental anomalies including dentinogenesis imperfecta, enamel hypoplasia, taurodontism, and hypodontia.
Truncated COL1A1/COL1A2 variants were linked to atypical intercanine width in OI patients.
Midface hypoplasia was correlated with reduced overjet and overbite in OI patients.
Bisphosphonate treatment, especially when initiated before age two, was associated with enamel hypoplasia in OI patients.
Better oral hygiene habits, including higher brushing frequency and use of additional dental products, were linked to lower DMFT scores in OI patients.
In the OI group, Angle Class III malocclusion was significantly associated with reduced brushing frequency.
A deep palatal vault was associated with increased DMFT in the OI group.
A correlation was observed between maximum mouth opening and joint hypermobility in OI patients.
A correlation was observed between maximum mouth opening and joint hypermobility in OI patients, linking systemic connective tissue laxity to orofacial mobility.
Non-collagen gene variants in OI were associated with novel dental observations not previously described, expanding the understood role of non-collagenous genes in OI oral pathology.
All 20 patients who completed the socioeconomic questionnaire reported that chronic post-dural puncture headache severely impaired their social, family, sex, and work life.
All patients reported social isolation, being unable to attend social events because of cPDPH.
One female patient's marriage ended in divorce as a direct consequence of her chronic post-dural puncture headache.
Patients with cPDPH spent a median of 31 days in acute hospital care due to their condition.
Patients with cPDPH consulted a median of 5 different doctors or institutions seeking care for their condition.
Working patients with cPDPH were on sick leave for a median of 381 days, with one patient reaching 4,015 days (about 11 years).
Two patients permanently lost their jobs and three patients had not returned to work by the end of follow-up because of cPDPH-related disability.
Two partners of patients quit their jobs to provide caregiving for the patient and/or their children.
Four of the 30 cPDPH patients were diagnosed with subdural hematoma on imaging, and one required trepanation, illustrating a potentially life-threatening complication that can mimic cPDPH.
Clinical characteristics of cPDPH did not significantly differ between patients whose condition followed diagnostic lumbar puncture versus peridural anesthesia.
The reported overall incidence of post-dural puncture headache in the literature is up to 36%, and it is more likely to occur in younger patients.
Prior literature cited in the discussion indicates that patients with post-dural puncture headache benefit from early intervention with an epidural blood patch.
Prior literature cited by the authors suggests that in females, peridural anesthesia should specifically be recognized as a possible cause of chronic post-dural puncture headache.

The authors suggest that the social isolation and psychological burden of cPDPH may, over time, contribute to comorbid anxiety, depression, or sleep disorders that blend with the orthostatic symptoms.
Episodic migraine without aura was one of the most common pain conditions studied using transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) in the reviewed literature.
Fibromyalgia was identified as one of the pain conditions commonly studied using taVNS in the reviewed clinical trial literature.
Irritable bowel syndrome was identified as one of the pain conditions commonly studied using taVNS in the reviewed clinical trial literature.
The reviewed evidence suggests taVNS use for pain management is also associated with reductions in co-occurring symptoms such as depression.
Cochrane reviews found no eligible fibromyalgia trials at all for carbamazepine, clonazepam, lamotrigine, oxycodone, phenytoin, topiramate or valproate.
Only two small trials of cannabinoids in fibromyalgia were available, insufficient for a reliable conclusion.
Only one trial of gabapentin in fibromyalgia was available, insufficient for a reliable conclusion.
Only one trial of lacosamide in fibromyalgia was available, insufficient for a reliable conclusion.
Data on mean pain for MAOIs came from only two trials with unclear risk of bias, insufficient to draw conclusions.
Two trials of quetiapine 50-300 mg daily showed no difference from placebo for at least 50% pain intensity reduction.
For ≥30% pain relief, more participants improved on quetiapine than placebo, though the confidence interval bordered no effect.
NSAID trials found no benefit over placebo for either ≥50% or ≥30% pain intensity reduction in fibromyalgia.
Clinical heterogeneity across combination-analgesic trials prevented any useful meta-analysis of their effect on fibromyalgia pain.
SSRIs showed a modest apparent benefit for ≥30% pain intensity reduction, but the evidence was susceptible to publication bias.
SSRIs were the only medication class (besides mirtazapine for sleep) to show a substantial effect size for a non-pain outcome, specifically depression.
Amitriptyline 25 mg or 50 mg daily produced a substantial pain relief effect equivalent to ≥50% pain intensity reduction, but the trials were subject to high risk of bias.
Mirtazapine 15-45 mg/day showed no statistical difference from placebo for ≥50% pain intensity reduction.
Mirtazapine showed a statistically significant difference from placebo for ≥30% pain intensity reduction.
Mirtazapine produced a small improvement in patient-reported sleep problems but no improvement in fatigue, negative mood, or health-related quality of life.
Duloxetine produced substantial pain relief lasting at least 12 weeks in about 1 in 10 people with moderate or severe fibromyalgia pain.
Milnacipran produced substantial pain relief lasting at least 12 weeks in about 1 in 10 people with moderate or severe fibromyalgia pain.
Pregabalin produced substantial pain relief lasting at least 12 weeks in about 1 in 10 people with moderate or severe fibromyalgia pain.
In enriched enrolment randomized withdrawal trials lasting 13-26 weeks, pregabalin was significantly more likely than placebo to maintain therapeutic pain relief of at least 30%.
Withdrawal due to adverse events occurred in 6-9% of participants on duloxetine, milnacipran or pregabalin, with rare serious adverse events not statistically different from placebo.
Somnolence, dizziness and weight gain were common adverse events with pregabalin, while nausea was common with SNRIs (duloxetine and milnacipran).
SSRIs were the only medication class shown to have a substantial effect (SMD >0.2) on depression among non-pain outcomes assessed.
Mirtazapine (15-45 mg/day) produced a small improvement in participant-reported sleep problems but not in fatigue, negative mood, or health-related quality of life.

Duloxetine (60 mg and 120 mg daily) significantly improved SF-36 physical subscore, bodily pain subscore, Patient Global Impression of Improvement, British Pain Inventory severity, and night pain within 12 weeks, with the SF-36 mental subscore improving only at the 120 mg dose.
SNRIs (duloxetine and milnacipran), overall and individually, improved fatigue, depression, anxiety and health-related quality of life.
There was an overall improvement in tender point threshold with duloxetine but not with milnacipran.
There was no overall improvement in patient-reported sleep problems with SNRIs combined, although duloxetine analysed independently showed an improvement in sleep.
Three large trials comparing mirogabalin, placebo and pregabalin 300 mg found that mirogabalin had comparable efficacy to pregabalin for Patient Global Impression of Change.

The FDA licensed duloxetine (2008), milnacipran (2009) and pregabalin (2007) for treating fibromyalgia in the US, whereas the European Medicines Agency refused marketing authorization for this indication because the benefits did not outweigh the risks.
The overview concluded that current evidence does not support guideline recommendations for amitriptyline at doses below 50 mg daily, cyclobenzaprine, or tramadol for fibromyalgia.
A network meta-analysis comparing medications trialed for VVS found midodrine to be an effective treatment for preventing VVS recurrence.
A midodrine-specific meta-analysis demonstrated efficacy in reducing VVS recurrence and positive head-up tilt tests.
Network meta-analysis found fluoxetine could decrease VVS spells, particularly in patients with concomitant anxiety.
Patients with vasovagal syncope suffer from anxiety and other psychological disorders more frequently than the general population.
Atomoxetine has shown significant results in diminishing positive head-up tilt tests among patients with VVS.
Atomoxetine reduced the composite endpoint of presyncope and syncope, but no significant difference was found for syncope alone.
The POST II randomized controlled trial initially failed to demonstrate efficacy of fludrocortisone at the starting dose but ultimately showed a significant reduction in recurrent VVS.
Atomoxetine treatment has been associated with an increase in blood pressure, similar to other vasoactive VVS medications.
The vasoactive nature of midodrine leads to a relative contraindication in hypertensive patients and pregnant women, who have higher risk of hypertension-related complications.
In the SPAIN trial, DDD-CLS pacing decreased the risk of VVS recurrence by an 89% relative risk reduction.

The BIOSync CLS double-blinded RCT found that patients with recurrent VVS, positive HUTTs, and asystolic pauses ≥3 seconds randomized to DDD-CLS pacing had a significant decrease in VVS recurrence compared with inactive pacing.
Early open-label unblinded trials of cardiac pacing showed a decrease in syncope recurrences in HUTT-positive VVS patients.
Later trials in the 2000s demonstrated no significant benefit of cardiac pacing for patients with VVS.
Elastic compression stockings can benefit patients with VVS by increasing venous blood return and reducing venous pooling.
Elastic compression stocking efficacy has been demonstrated among patients with orthostatic hypotension, supporting their potential use as a mechanical treatment for VVS.
A meta-analysis of 14 studies on cardioneuroablation in VVS patients found a high freedom rate from syncope of 91.9%.
Traumatic syncope episodes are reported in as many as 33.5% of patients with vasovagal syncope.
In a cohort of hospitalized patients with a history of vasovagal syncope, one-third reported disruption in daily activities such as driving and working.
Fludrocortisone treatment increased 24-hour systolic blood pressure in patients with hypotension-related symptoms.
Fludrocortisone reduced the daily frequency of SBP drops below 90 mmHg.
Fludrocortisone reduced the daily frequency of SBP drops below 100 mmHg.
Midodrine produced a non-significant increase in 24-hour systolic blood pressure.
Midodrine reduced the daily frequency of SBP drops below 90 mmHg.
Midodrine reduced the daily frequency of SBP drops below 100 mmHg.
In the seven patients taking both fludrocortisone and midodrine, 24-h systolic blood pressure increased from a mean of 110.1 mmHg to 114.0 mmHg after combined treatment.
In patients on combined fludrocortisone and midodrine, the number of daily SBP drops below 90 mmHg decreased by 69% but this was not statistically significant.
In patients on combined fludrocortisone and midodrine, the number of daily SBP drops below 100 mmHg decreased by 44%.
Fludrocortisone appeared to be more effective than midodrine in raising 24-h SBP and reducing SBP drops on ambulatory blood pressure monitoring.
A single 60 mg dose of pyridostigmine modestly increased upright blood pressure on average, but individual responses ranged widely from a large decrease to a large increase.
Pressor response to pyridostigmine did not differ between patients with multiple system atrophy and those with pure autonomic failure.
Higher supine blood pressure was associated with a smaller (more negative) upright pressor response to pyridostigmine.
Longer pressure recovery time on the Valsalva maneuver, indicating more severe autonomic impairment, was associated with a poorer pressor response to pyridostigmine.

In patients with multiple system atrophy, a greater increase in upright heart rate relative to the fall in systolic blood pressure (a surrogate of residual autonomic function) was positively correlated with the systolic pressor response to pyridostigmine.

In patients with multiple system atrophy, higher upright plasma norepinephrine, a surrogate of residual autonomic function, was positively correlated with the systolic pressor response to pyridostigmine.
In patients with severe autonomic failure and supine hypertension, pyridostigmine failed to produce the preferential upright pressor effect that would have been most beneficial for them.
The combined ABPM plus SCAFA (2STEPS) protocol identified a likely haemodynamic mechanism of syncope in 89% of patients with autonomic syncope.
The hypotensive phenotype, defined by drug-related/unrelated persistent hypotension or hypotensive SBP drops on ABPM, accounted for the majority (68%) of syncope mechanisms identified.
The bradycardic phenotype, defined by asystole/bradycardia detected on carotid sinus massage or tilt testing, was identified as the mechanism of syncope in 6% of the cohort.
A mixed phenotype, combining both hypotensive and bradycardic patterns detected across two or three tests, was found in 15% of patients.
The proportion of patients with an asystolic reflex detected by CSM/HUT was similar in younger (≤40 years) and older (>40 years) patients.
The SCAFA battery (carotid sinus massage, passive standing, and head-up tilt) had a mean total procedure duration of 25 minutes.
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring alone provided a diagnosis in 16% of patients whose syncope mechanism would otherwise have remained unexplained.
ABPM revealed a hypotensive susceptibility in patients who also had an asystolic response on CSM or HUT, enabling diagnosis of a mixed phenotype that would otherwise have been missed.
ABPM detected isolated daytime SBP drops in more than half of the cohort, a target for therapy aimed at preventing syncopal recurrences.
Increasing age was independently associated with a higher likelihood of a positive carotid sinus massage response.
Male sex was independently associated with a substantially higher likelihood of a positive carotid sinus massage response.
Presence of prodromes before syncope was independently associated with a higher likelihood of a positive ABPM finding.
Lower office systolic blood pressure at baseline was independently associated with a higher likelihood of a positive ABPM finding.
No baseline clinical variable was found to independently predict a positive head-up tilt test response.

Positivity rate of carotid sinus massage varied widely between centres, being much higher in some centres than others even after adjustment for clinical variables, indicating strong inter-operator variability.
Most positive head-up tilt tests occurred during the active nitroglycerine-provoked phase rather than the passive phase.

For patients with a dominant bradycardic phenotype of extrinsic cause, cardiac pacing, cardioneuroablation, and adenosine-receptor antagonist drugs such as theophylline are described as proven effective therapies.

For patients with drug-unrelated persistent or intermittent hypotension, BP-elevating agents such as fludrocortisone and midodrine, along with elastic compression garments, are recommended to prevent syncope recurrence.
Active kinetic oscillation stimulation significantly reduced monthly headache days with moderate to severe intensity compared with sham during the 4-week performance assessment period.
The reduction in moderate-to-severe headache days with active treatment persisted into the 4-week follow-up period after stimulation ended.
Active treatment significantly reduced monthly migraine days compared with sham during the performance assessment period.
The reduction in monthly migraine days with active treatment persisted through the follow-up period.
Participants receiving active treatment used abortive migraine medication on fewer days than the sham group, reaching statistical significance during the follow-up period.
Nearly twice as many patients in the active treatment group achieved a ≥30% reduction in moderate-to-severe headache days compared with sham during the performance assessment period.
During the follow-up period the difference in 30% responder rates between active and sham groups was smaller and no longer statistically significant.
Overall treatment-emergent adverse events occurred at a similar rate between active and sham groups, indicating good tolerability of the device.
Dizziness as an adverse event occurred more frequently in the active treatment group than in the sham group.
The number of device-related treatment-emergent adverse events was higher in the active group than the sham group, though the proportion of participants affected was similar.
Prior evidence cited by the authors indicates that PACAP, a parasympathetic neuropeptide, is increased during spontaneous migraine attacks.
Prior evidence cited by the authors indicates that VIP, a parasympathetic neuropeptide, is increased during spontaneous migraine attacks.
Cited prior literature reports that intravenous administration of PACAP or VIP can trigger migraine-like attacks.

The authors cite a monoclonal antibody targeting the PACAP ligand as recently shown effective for preventive migraine treatment, supporting the rationale for targeting parasympathetic neuropeptide pathways.
More than half of patients with cluster headache had comorbid migraine and/or fibromyalgia.
The prevalence of comorbid fibromyalgia among patients with cluster headache in this study (40.6%) was substantially higher than the 6.7% and 3% reported in two prior studies.
Female sex predominated among patients with cluster headache comorbid with migraine and/or fibromyalgia, whereas male sex predominated among noncomorbid cluster headache patients.
The number of comorbid medical diseases was highest in patients with cluster headache and comorbid fibromyalgia and lowest in patients with noncomorbid cluster headache.

Osteoarticular conditions, mainly osteoarthritis, were the most frequently associated medical diseases and were mostly observed in patients with cluster headache and fibromyalgia, with or without migraine.

Chronic fatigue syndrome, multiple chemical sensitivity, and food intolerance were especially frequent comorbidities in patients with cluster headache and comorbid fibromyalgia, with or without migraine.
Nearly three-quarters of the overall sample had clinically relevant depression, with the highest rate in patients with cluster headache comorbid with both migraine and fibromyalgia.
Suicidal ideation was present in every subgroup and was most severe among patients with cluster headache comorbid with fibromyalgia.
Insomnia severity scores were significantly higher (worse sleep) across subgroups, with all patients in the cluster headache plus migraine plus fibromyalgia group scoring above the insomnia cutoff.

Health-related quality of life scores were significantly lower across subgroups, with the lowest scores in patients with cluster headache comorbid with both migraine and fibromyalgia, compared to Spanish population norms.
Emergency room use was higher than 40% across all subgroups and was highest among patients with all three comorbid conditions (cluster headache, migraine, and fibromyalgia).
Overall, nearly half of the sample required surgical intervention and more than one-fifth required hospitalization in the past six months.
University education level was lowest among patients with cluster headache associated with both migraine and fibromyalgia.
Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome is associated with a perturbed endocannabinoid system, implicating CB1 signaling in this CVS-related endophenotype.
CVS is comorbid with dysautonomia and anxiety, contributing to a heterogeneous clinical picture beyond a simple emetic disorder.
Migraine is described as one of the recognized endophenotypes of cyclic vomiting syndrome, historically linking CVS to migraine biology.
Behavioral management via meditation appears efficacious for CVS with few untoward effects, possibly by restoring parasympathetic autonomic balance.
Vagal neuromodulation appears efficacious for CVS with few untoward effects, potentially via restoring parasympathetic autonomic balance.
The neurokinin-1 (NK1) pathway is listed as a confirmed pathophysiologic pathway involved in cyclic vomiting syndrome.
The HPA axis is listed as a confirmed contributing pathway in CVS pathophysiology.
The HPA axis is listed as one of the confirmed pathophysiologic pathways implicated in cyclic vomiting syndrome.
The PPM1D gene is cited as a confirmed pathway/mechanism implicated in cyclic vomiting syndrome.
A biological calendar or circannual rhythm pattern is cited as a confirmed contributing pathway in cyclic vomiting syndrome.
Estrogen is identified as a confirmed hormonal pathway implicated in cyclic vomiting syndrome.
The PPM1D gene is cited as a confirmed contributing pathway in the pathophysiology of cyclic vomiting syndrome.
A cyclic 'biological calendar' or rhythmic pattern is cited as a confirmed contributing pathway to cyclic vomiting syndrome pathophysiology.
Estrogen is cited as a confirmed hormonal pathway contributing to cyclic vomiting syndrome pathophysiology.
TRPV-1 is proposed as a possible, unconfirmed pathway contributing to cyclic vomiting syndrome pathophysiology.
CGRP is proposed as a possible, unconfirmed pathway contributing to cyclic vomiting syndrome, echoing its established role in migraine.
Estrogen is identified as a confirmed pathway involved in the pathophysiology of cyclic vomiting syndrome.
A biological calendar (periodicity) mechanism is described as a confirmed pathway contributing to cyclic vomiting syndrome's episodic pattern.
Mitochondrial dysfunction is proposed as a possible (unconfirmed) contributing pathway in cyclic vomiting syndrome.
Impaired cation transport is suggested as a possible (unconfirmed) mechanistic pathway underlying cyclic vomiting syndrome.
In a systematic review of 26 patient-level case descriptions of autoimmune encephalitis treated with electroconvulsive therapy, a favorable clinical response occurred in 76.9% of cases.
Noteworthy adverse effects of ECT were reported in only 3 of the 26 autoimmune encephalitis cases reviewed.
Catatonic and psychotic syndromes, sometimes co-occurring with dysautonomia, are common presenting features of autoimmune encephalitis, particularly the anti-NMDAR subtype.
Autoantibodies against different neuronal epitopes are linked to specific clinical manifestations and are used within diagnostic criteria for autoimmune encephalitis.
Patients with orofacial migraine were significantly more likely to be woken from sleep by pain than patients with neurovascular orofacial pain.
Accompanying migraine symptoms such as photophobia, phonophobia, nausea and vomiting were significantly more common in OFM than NVOP.
OFM pain occurred concomitantly with headache in about two-thirds of cases, compared to only about a third of NVOP cases, a significant difference.
Pain mimicking a toothache was far more common in NVOP than in OFM patients.
Cranial autonomic symptoms were significantly more frequent in OFM than in NVOP, occurring roughly three times as often.
In multivariate logistic regression, presence of cranial autonomic symptoms increased the odds of an OFM (versus NVOP) diagnosis by 5.6-fold.
In multivariate logistic regression, orofacial pain mimicking toothache markedly increased the odds of an NVOP (versus OFM) diagnosis.
Both NVOP and OFM cohorts showed a similar male-to-female ratio of about 1:5, a much higher female proportion than typically reported in migraine.
The mean age of NVOP/OFM patients (~40 years) was consistently higher than that reported for typical migraine.

A field test of a prior cohort found that Type 1 (headache with concurrent facial pain) was the most common presentation in both facial migraine and TAC patients, while Type 2 (facial pain replacing prior headache) occurred only in facial migraine and Type 3 (de novo facial pain resembling headache) was rare in both.
A population-based study identified only one patient with isolated facial migraine, though the authors suggested this low rate may reflect biased sampling.

The authors propose that NVOP pathophysiology may involve antidromic trigeminal nerve activation causing neurogenic inflammation in the dental pulp, analogous to mechanisms proposed for migraine and cluster headache.
NVOP, despite presenting as tooth pain, is reported to respond well to antimigraine medications, supporting its migraine-related pathophysiology.
About one third of NVOP patients had bilateral pain, with no significant difference compared to OFM.
Pain intensity was similar between OFM and NVOP patients, despite the hypothesis that cranial autonomic symptom frequency relates to pain intensity.

The authors hypothesize that the predominantly lower facial third location of NVOP versus the middle-and-lower facial thirds involvement in OFM may explain the higher frequency of cranial autonomic symptoms in OFM.
In a German cohort of 156 patients with fibromyalgia syndrome, 25.6% met the DSM-5 SSD B2 criterion (persistently high health anxiety, defined by Whiteley Index score ≥8).
Among FMS patients, current anxiety or depressive disorder was present in 95.0% of those meeting SSD criteria versus 71.6% of those not meeting SSD criteria.

FMS patients meeting SSD criteria scored significantly higher on self-reported disability and pain catastrophizing than those without SSD, though sick leave, disability pension applications, and healthcare visit frequency did not differ.
Blinded record review found that a need for psychotherapy, per German FMS guidelines, would have been recommended for 80.0% of SSD-positive FMS patients versus 66.7% of SSD-negative patients.
In a Swedish clinical trial cohort of 140 self-referred individuals with self-reported physician-diagnosed FMS, 35% met the SSD B2 criterion, which was associated with higher symptom burden.

In an ecological momentary assessment study of 28 German FMS outpatients over 14 days, somatic illness beliefs were reported by 71%, health anxiety by 57%, and devoted time/energy to health concerns by 64% of participants at least once daily, with 82% meeting at least one SSD B criterion overall.
In a nationally representative German population survey, 4.5% met SSD criteria, FMS prevalence was 3.4%, and among FMS cases 28.1% also met SSD criteria.

In 132 Swedish patients diagnosed with SSD or illness anxiety disorder, therapist-guided or unguided internet-delivered CBT, or unguided bibliotherapy, reduced health anxiety more than waiting-list control.

In a randomised controlled trial of 120 Chinese patients with SSD, integrative group psychotherapy combining CBT, psychodynamic techniques, and mindful body/emotional awareness reduced somatic symptom burden more than nonspecific supportive group psychotherapy or treatment as usual at 4, 8, and 12 weeks.

In a randomised controlled trial of 240 FMS patients, emotional awareness and expression therapy addressing psychosocial adversities and emotional conflicts was more effective than a basic educational intervention and comparable to CBT for overall symptoms, widespread pain, physical functioning, cognitive dysfunction, anxiety, depression, positive affect, and life satisfaction at 6 months.
The authors speculate that ongoing discussion of an autoimmune basis or small fiber neuropathy underlying FMS may heighten patients' disproportionate health-related worry and anxiety.

High-likelihood-ratio PAF patients showed reduced neuromelanin-MRI contrast in the locus coeruleus compared with healthy controls and low-LR PAF patients, with values similar to Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies.

High-likelihood-ratio PAF patients showed reduced neuromelanin-MRI contrast in the substantia nigra compared with healthy controls and low-LR PAF patients, with values similar to Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies.
Neuromelanin-MRI contrast in the substantia nigra correlated with presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity in the striatum as measured by FDOPA-PET.
In a longitudinal subset of six PAF patients, those who went on to develop a central synucleinopathy showed reduced neuromelanin-MRI and FDOPA-PET values over time.

The authors propose that NM-MRI and FDOPA-PET may serve as biomarkers for early brain involvement and for predicting progression from pure autonomic failure to central synucleinopathies, potentially aiding selection of patients for early intervention.
Low-LR PAF patients did not show significantly reduced NM-MRI contrast in the locus coeruleus or substantia nigra compared with healthy controls, unlike high-LR patients.

The authors propose that NM-MRI and FDOPA-PET may serve as biomarkers for early brain involvement and for predicting progression from PAF to central synucleinopathies, potentially guiding early intervention.
In a small longitudinal subset of PAF patients, those who went on to develop a central synucleinopathy showed reduced FDOPA-PET dopamine synthesis values over time.
Patients with autoimmune connective tissue diseases (SS, RA, SLE) had significantly higher CSI-A scores, CSI-B scores, and CS positivity than healthy controls.
Among ACTD subgroups, Sjögren's syndrome patients had the highest rate of clinical central sensitization positivity compared to RA and SLE patients.
Post hoc analysis showed Sjögren's syndrome patients had a significantly higher CSI-A score than RA or SLE patients, whose scores were similar to each other.
The prevalence of coexisting fibromyalgia was highest among Sjögren's syndrome patients compared to RA and SLE.
In RA patients, disease activity (DAS-28 CRP) showed a low positive correlation with CSI-A central sensitization scores.
Unlike RA, disease activity indices (ESSDAI in SS, SLEDAI-2K in SLE) did not correlate with central sensitization scores.
In SLE patients, lower vitamin D3 levels were moderately to highly correlated with higher central sensitization (CSI-A and CSI-B) scores.
In Sjögren's syndrome patients, folic acid levels were moderately correlated with CSI-B (central sensitization-related syndromes) scores.
In Sjögren's syndrome patients, TSH levels were moderately correlated with CSI-B scores, suggesting a link between thyroid function and central sensitization symptoms even within normal TSH range.
In RA patients, hemoglobin levels showed a low negative correlation with CSI-B scores.
ACTD patients with clinically significant central sensitization (CSI-A≥40) were more frequently female than those below the cutoff.
COPD or asthma comorbidity was significantly more frequent in ACTD patients with CSI-A≥40 than those below the cutoff.
Coexisting fibromyalgia was more common in ACTD patients with CSI-A≥40 than those below the cutoff.
ACTD patients with CSI-A≥40 reported significantly higher visual analog scale pain scores than those below the cutoff.
Exocrine gland involvement was significantly more common in ACTD patients with CSI-A≥40 than those below the cutoff, particularly relevant given its prevalence in Sjögren's syndrome.
ACTD patients with CSI-A≥40 were on a higher corticosteroid dose than those below the cutoff, consistent with a prior report linking persistent glucocorticoid use to fibromyalgia.
There were significant differences in CRP levels among the ACTD and healthy control groups.

Herbal medicines containing Cinnamomi Cortex (Gyejigayonggolmoryeo-tang and Shihogayonggolmoryeo-tang) reduced pain intensity and attack frequency in a patient with chronic migraine unresponsive to sumatriptan.
The patient's migraine was unresponsive to three years of sumatriptan treatment prior to switching to herbal medicine.
Oreongsan, another herbal medicine containing Cinnamomi Cortex, was used during pain attacks and was associated with near-complete resolution and eventual sustained remission of migraine symptoms.
All 21 Qatari ATS patients carried a homozygous pathogenic SLC2A10 variant c.243C>G (p.Ser81Arg), classified likely pathogenic per ACMG criteria.
Four of the 21 ATS patients experienced migraine headaches as a neurological manifestation.
Migraine headaches and epilepsy were reported to be more prevalent in this Qatari ATS cohort compared to previous literature reports.
Aortic tortuosity was present in all patients, with tortuosity of other arteries also seen in nearly all patients.
Pulmonary artery stenosis was less common in this Qatari p.Ser81Arg cohort than reported in prior mixed-variant ATS literature.
Respiratory manifestations were more prevalent in this cohort than reported in prior mixed-variant ATS literature, possibly reflecting variant-specific effects.
Hypermobile joints were observed in a substantial minority of ATS patients, overlapping with hypermobility-spectrum connective tissue phenotypes.
No mortality attributable to ATS occurred in this cohort, and all patients were hemodynamically stable, suggesting a milder phenotype than the historically described infantile-fatal course.

A cited functional study found that knocking down SLC2A10 caused a widespread increase in immune and inflammatory signaling and immune cell (particularly macrophage) infiltration, hypothesized to be regulated via the COX-2 pathway.
Atopic features were present in five patients and were hypothesized to be linked to increased immune signaling from SLC2A10 loss-of-function.
The majority of patients (15/21) were born from consanguineous marriages, consistent with the autosomal recessive inheritance of ATS.
Family history was significant, with seven patients having affected relatives (mainly siblings), and one family used IVF that resulted in dizygotic twins both affected by ATS.
Ocular anomalies including bilateral nasolacrimal duct obstruction, allergic conjunctivitis, and latent nystagmus were observed and had not been previously described in association with ATS.
Novel urogenital findings including parapelvic cysts, kidney malrotation, vesicoureteral reflux, and nephrolithiasis were identified, expanding the known ATS phenotype.
Skeletal abnormalities uncommon in the ATS spectrum, including bilateral temporomandibular joint cysts and bilateral syndactyly of the toes, were newly noted in this cohort.
No genotype-phenotype correlation was established in this cohort, consistent with prior ATS studies.
No difference in sex predilection for ATS was observed in this cohort, consistent with prior reports.
Cardiovascular surgical interventions (balloon dilatation and catheterization) were required in only a small proportion of patients and were successful, with no reported mortality.
Nearly half of the cohort required surgery for non-cardiovascular manifestations, mostly hernia repair.
OD complications were significantly more common among IBD patients than non-IBD patients referred to the vertigo clinic.
Multivariate logistic regression adjusting for age and sex showed IBD remained significantly associated with OD complications.
Psychogenic vertigo complications tended to be more common in IBD patients than non-IBD patients, but this difference was not statistically significant.
The prevalence of migraine complications did not differ significantly between IBD and non-IBD groups.
Psychological and dizziness questionnaire scores tended to be higher in the IBD group than the non-IBD group but the difference was not statistically significant.
Caloric testing and VEMP abnormalities showed no significant difference in vestibular dysfunction between IBD and non-IBD groups.
Force-plate postural sway measurements were significantly more normal (less sway) in the IBD group than the non-IBD group, likely reflecting the younger age of IBD patients.
In multivariate analysis, sex significantly affected postural sway total length under both eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions, with women showing more normal (lower) values than men.

Age significantly affected Romberg rate (velocity, with rubber) and total length under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions, with younger age associated with more normal values (except for Romberg rate).
In multivariate analysis, the presence of IBD significantly affected Romberg rate (velocity, with rubber) and total length (eyes closed), with more normal values observed in IBD cases.
Among IBD cases, females had more migraine complications than males, suggesting a sex difference in migraine prevalence within this population.
OD complications were equally prevalent among male and female IBD patients.
All three IBD cases treated with ustekinumab (an IL-12/IL-23-targeting monoclonal antibody) had comorbid OD complications, possibly reflecting greater disease severity.
Mesalazine was prescribed in 8 IBD cases and was not associated with OD complications.
There was no significant association between OD complications and elevated liver enzymes (AST or ALT) among IBD patients.
No significant association was found between anemia and OD complications in IBD patients, possibly because anemic patients were receiving iron supplementation.
OD complications were not significantly associated with zinc testing results, though zinc testing was performed in all OD cases but not consistently in non-OD cases, limiting the comparison.
CRP, a marker of systemic inflammation, along with nutritional, liver-function, dehydration, and anemia markers, did not differ significantly between IBD patients with and without OD complications.

In the fascia exercise (treatment) group, the number and duration of migraine attacks and daytime/night-time VAS pain scores were significantly reduced after the six-week intervention compared to baseline.

The conventional physiotherapy (control) group also showed significant within-group decreases in medication use, attack frequency, attack duration, and daytime/night-time VAS pain scores after treatment.

Despite within-group improvements in both arms, there was no statistically significant difference between the fascia exercise group and the conventional physiotherapy group in the magnitude of change in medication use, attack frequency/duration, or VAS pain scores.

Both the fascia exercise group and the conventional physiotherapy group showed significant improvements after treatment in migraine-related disability (MIDAS), sleep quality (PSQI), and the anxiety component of the HADS.

The fascia exercise group showed a significantly greater reduction in depression scores compared to the conventional physiotherapy group, suggesting a psychological benefit specific to fascia exercises.

Neither the fascia exercise group nor the conventional physiotherapy group showed significant changes in 24-hr-MQoLQ (migraine quality of life) scores, and there were no significant between-group differences.
Within the conventional physiotherapy (control) group, mean RR interval (an HRV parameter) improved significantly after treatment, while no such change was seen in the fascia exercise group.

Aside from mean RR in the control group, no other HRV parameters changed significantly within or between groups, suggesting the six-week fascia exercise intervention did not produce an immediate measurable effect on autonomic regulation.
Patient satisfaction with treatment was significantly higher in the fascia exercise group than in the conventional physiotherapy group after the intervention.
Headache frequency decreased progressively from 26 episodes pre-treatment to 13, 12, 11, and 10 episodes at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months respectively after onabotulinumtoxinA treatment.
A third of patients discontinued overusing acute headache medication after receiving onabotulinumtoxinA treatment.
In univariate logistic regression, having fibromyalgia was associated with a reduced likelihood of achieving a 50% or greater response to onabotulinumtoxinA in chronic migraine patients.
Having secondary education was associated with an increased likelihood of achieving a 50% or greater response to onabotulinumtoxinA in univariate analysis.
After adjustment for other variables, fibromyalgia remained significantly associated with reduced likelihood of achieving a 50% or greater response to onabotulinumtoxinA.

People living with coexisting endometriosis, fibromyalgia and/or hormonal migraine describe overlapping and blurry symptoms that become entangled in ambiguous, open-ended ways, complicating self-management and treatment.

The single-disease model underlying healthcare systems fails to address the needs of patients living with multiple chronic conditions, creating discrepancies between lived illness experience and biomedical/healthcare structures.
The patient's ataxia severity, measured by SARA, improved from a score of 13 at baseline to 11 at 4 weeks and 10.5 at 12 months of taVNS treatment.
UMSARS disease severity scores decreased from 28 at baseline to 24 at 4 weeks and 23 at 12 months of taVNS treatment, rather than the expected annual increase.
Sleep quality, assessed by PSQI, improved markedly from 19 at baseline to 13 at 4 weeks and 6 at 12 months of taVNS treatment.
Anxiety symptoms, measured by HAMA, improved from 13 at baseline to 3 at 4 weeks and remained stable at 12 months of taVNS treatment.
Depressive symptoms, measured by HAMD, improved from 7 at baseline to 4 at 4 weeks and remained stable at 12 months of taVNS treatment.
No adverse effects were observed in the patient during the 12-month course of taVNS treatment, supporting the safety of this intervention.

Stimulation of the auricular branch of the vagus nerve is proposed to project via the nucleus tractus solitarius to the reticular formation, forebrain, mesencephalon, limbic system, and cerebellum, thereby modulating neural activity relevant to ataxia and non-motor symptoms.

Prior literature indicates that MSA patients typically show an average increase of about 4 UMSARS points per year as the disease progresses, which contrasts with the decrease observed in this taVNS-treated patient.
Cranial MRI of the patient showed the hot cross bun sign and cerebellar atrophy, consistent with MSA-cerebellar subtype.
People experiencing physical pain were significantly more likely to have suicide-related outcomes than people without pain.
Physical pain was associated with increased lifetime death wish, with the strongest odds ratio among the suicide-related outcomes examined.
Physical pain was associated with increased current suicidal ideation.
Physical pain was associated with increased lifetime suicide attempts.
Among adolescents, self-harm was notably higher among those experiencing physical pain compared to those without pain.
Among adults, physical pain was associated with a higher risk of lifetime suicide attempts and suicide death.
In older adults, suicidal ideation and suicide attempts were more strongly linked to physical pain than in other age groups.
Females with physical pain had higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to males with physical pain.
Fibromyalgia was linked to an increased risk of suicide-related outcomes.
Migraine was among the specific painful conditions associated with increased suicide risk in the meta-analysis.

Persons diagnosed with headache had more than double the hazard of attempted suicide compared with matched persons without a headache diagnosis, after adjusting for demographic and comorbidity factors and accounting for competing risk of death.
Persons diagnosed with headache had a 40% higher hazard of completed suicide compared with matched persons without a headache diagnosis.
The 15-year absolute risk of attempted suicide was higher among persons diagnosed with headache than among matched comparison cohort members, yielding a risk difference of 0.45 percentage points.
The 15-year absolute risk of completed suicide was higher among persons diagnosed with headache than among matched comparison cohort members, yielding a risk difference of 0.06 percentage points.

The association between headache diagnosis and suicide risk was consistent across headache subtypes (migraine, tension-type headache, posttraumatic headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia) but was strongest for trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia and posttraumatic headache.
Among headache subtypes, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia showed a stronger association with attempted and completed suicide compared to the overall headache cohort.
Posttraumatic headache diagnosis was associated with a stronger risk of attempted and completed suicide relative to other headache types.
The elevated risk of suicidal behavior was consistently observed across all examined headache diagnoses, including migraine and tension-type headache, not just the most severe subtypes.
Women with chronic migraine had significantly higher adjusted odds of having dyspareunia or any type of pelvic pain compared to women without migraine.
Interstitial cystitis had the highest odds ratio among pelvic pain conditions assessed in women with chronic migraine relative to women without migraine.
Vaginismus prevalence/odds were significantly increased in women with chronic migraine compared to women without migraine.
Pelvic pain (ICD-10 R10.2) was significantly more common in women with chronic migraine than in women without migraine.
Dyspareunia (ICD-10 N94.1) was significantly more common in women with chronic migraine than in women without migraine.
Vulvodynia was significantly more common in women with chronic migraine than in women without migraine.
Among women with chronic migraine, comorbid vulvodynia was associated with the highest odds of also having dyspareunia.
Among women with chronic migraine, comorbid vaginismus was strongly associated with also having dyspareunia.
Among women with chronic migraine, comorbid interstitial cystitis independently increased odds of also having dyspareunia.
Among women with chronic migraine, comorbid pelvic pain independently increased odds of also having dyspareunia.
Among women with chronic migraine, comorbid endometriosis independently increased odds of also having dyspareunia.
Comorbid fibromyalgia independently increased the odds of dyspareunia in patients with chronic migraine.
Comorbid IBS independently increased the odds of dyspareunia in patients with chronic migraine.
Comorbid anxiety independently increased the odds of dyspareunia in patients with chronic migraine.
Comorbid PTSD independently increased the odds of dyspareunia in patients with chronic migraine.
Comorbid depression independently increased the odds of dyspareunia in patients with chronic migraine.
Older age (>50 years) was independently associated with increased odds of dyspareunia in patients with chronic migraine.

A history of giving birth showed an increased unadjusted odds ratio for dyspareunia in women with chronic migraine, but this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for confounders.
The prevalence of dyspareunia or pelvic pain was more than twice as high in women with chronic migraine compared to women without migraine.
Over a third of patients with longstanding orthostatic headache and suspected spontaneous intracranial hypotension had comorbid Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder.
A quarter of the orthostatic headache cohort had comorbid postural tachycardia syndrome, which was optimally treated before ICP monitoring when present.
Most patients with orthostatic headache and suspected SIH had a coexisting primary headache diagnosis, most commonly chronic or episodic migraine.
Anxiety and depression were common comorbidities in this orthostatic headache cohort.
24-hour ICP monitoring identified pathologically low ICP in a small proportion of patients with imaging-negative suspected SIH and treatment-refractory orthostatic headache.
24-hour ICP monitoring unexpectedly identified pathologically high ICP in a subset of patients presenting with orthostatic headache and clinical suspicion of SIH.
Audiovestibular disturbances (aural fullness and/or muffled hearing) were significantly more common in patients with abnormal (high or low) ICP results than in those with normal/borderline ICP.
Mean ICP pulse amplitude, a marker of brain compliance, did not significantly differ between patients with low, high, or normal/borderline ICP.
Among patients with confirmed high ICP, ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion produced mixed outcomes, with some achieving resolution or partial benefit and others deriving no benefit.
The one patient with high ICP managed medically with acetazolamide derived no benefit and could not tolerate doses above 750 mg/day due to side effects.

Non-targeted lumbar epidural blood patches, administered a median of 3 times per patient, were largely ineffective or only partially/temporarily effective in this imaging-negative orthostatic headache cohort.
Intravenous caffeine infusion, received by sixteen patients, was ineffective or only partially/temporarily effective for orthostatic headache in this cohort.
Invasive 24-hour intracranial pressure monitoring with an intraparenchymal probe was performed without any procedural complications in the study cohort.
Patients undergoing ICP monitoring had had orthostatic headache for a long duration on average, reflecting the chronic and diagnostically challenging nature of their presentation.

Patients with orthostatic headache and suspected SIH frequently reported migrainous associated symptoms including motion sensitivity, phonophobia, nausea/vomiting, and photophobia, alongside audiovestibular and cognitive symptoms.
Headache during the previous 3 months was reported by 62% of 104 patients with pituitary adenoma.
Among pituitary adenoma patients with headache, migraine and tension-type headache were the most prevalent phenotypes.
Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias were observed exclusively among patients with prolactinoma.
Headache occurred at similar rates in both sexes, being present in 64% of female and 58% of male pituitary adenoma patients.
Patients with pituitary adenoma who experienced headache were significantly younger than those without headache.
Tumor characteristics were not found to be determinant of whether patients experienced headache.
Among patients with acromegaly, those who reported headache had higher growth hormone levels than those without headache.
Headache was more frequent in patients with prolactinoma than in those with non-functioning pituitary adenoma.
After disease remission or control following treatment, headache resolved in 83% of NFPA patients, 50% of somatotropinoma patients, and 33% of prolactinoma patients.
Overall, surgical and medical treatments completely resolved headache in about half of the treated pituitary adenoma patients.
In patients with new daily persistent headache (NDPH), 34.5% experienced a ≥30% improvement in monthly moderate-to-severe headache days at 24 weeks after two cycles of OnabotulinumtoxinA.
In chronic migraine with daily headache (daily-CM), 43.2% of patients experienced a ≥30% improvement in monthly moderate-to-severe headache days at 24 weeks after OnabotulinumtoxinA treatment.
In chronic migraine without daily headache (non-daily-CM), 51.2% of patients experienced a ≥30% improvement in monthly moderate-to-severe headache days at 24 weeks after OnabotulinumtoxinA treatment.
Response rates to OnabotulinumtoxinA did not significantly differ between NDPH, daily-CM, and non-daily-CM groups.
In NDPH, only 6.9% of patients experienced an improvement in monthly headache days (as opposed to moderate-to-severe headache days) with OnabotulinumtoxinA.
In NDPH, 27.6% of patients experienced an improvement in headache severity with OnabotulinumtoxinA.
Among NDPH patients treated with OnabotulinumtoxinA, 25.9% achieved a ≥6 point improvement in HIT-6 score at 24 weeks.
59% of NDPH patients reported subjective improvement after OnabotulinumtoxinA treatment.
Adverse event rates with OnabotulinumtoxinA were similar across NDPH, daily-CM and non-daily-CM groups, with no serious adverse events reported.
The authors argue against the common misconception that anemia causes orthostatic hypotension, stating anemia is not itself an etiologic driver of the condition.

Orthostatic hypotension is described as arising from some combination of autonomic dysfunction, neuroendocrine failure, or hypovolemia, which may be worsened by underlying arrhythmic or structural heart disease.

Anemia and orthostatic hypotension can co-occur when they share a common antecedent, such as blood loss causing both hypovolemia and anemia, or systemic conditions like vitamin B12 deficiency, amyloidosis, or chronic liver disease causing both autonomic neuropathy and anemia.
The 2018 European Society of Cardiology guideline lists erythropoietin among additional therapies for orthostatic hypotension, but notes its efficacy is less established.

The review found that central, peripheral, and autonomic nervous system manifestations occur in patients with primary Sjögren's disease but are not systematically evaluated as part of the disease's autoimmune presentation.
The expert panel reached ten recommendations, with 100% agreement, on the investigation and management of neurological involvement in Sjögren's disease using the Delphi method.

Patients with fibromyalgia showed increased resting-state functional connectivity between the default mode network and interoceptive self-related brain regions such as the insula compared to healthy controls.

FM patients also showed increased resting-state functional connectivity between the default mode network and exteroceptive self-related regions including premotor and visual/auditory cortices compared to healthy controls.
FM patients showed reduced resting-state functional connectivity among pain matrix regions, including the periaqueductal gray matter and somatosensory areas, relative to healthy controls.
Within the FM group, increased resting-state functional connectivity within the default mode network was positively associated with self-reported pain intensity.
Heightened resting-state functional connectivity between the default mode network and interoceptive self areas (e.g., insula) was positively associated with pain intensity in FM patients.
The acute-phase ACPE-Gi score showed a moderate positive correlation with the 3-month modified Rankin Scale score, indicating higher initial severity scores predict worse functional outcome.
Mean 3-month mRS scores differed significantly across mild, moderate, and severe acute-phase ACPE-Gi score categories.
Logistic regression showed each one-point increase in ACPE-Gi score increased the odds of poor 3-month outcome (mRS>2), with a 50% probability of poor outcome at a score of 11.36.
There was no statistically significant difference in mean 3-month mRS scores among patients grouped by antibody type (seronegative, intracellular antigen, surface antigen, other).
Patients with worse 3-month prognosis (mRS≥3) had significantly higher mean acute-phase ACPE-Gi scores than those with better prognosis.

Patients with autonomic dysfunction (8/25, 32%) had a significantly higher risk of poor functional outcome (mRS>2) at 3 months compared with those without autonomic symptoms; three patients died from paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity.
Altered mental status (consciousness alteration) at presentation significantly predicted higher 3-month mRS scores.
Although 88% of patients had brain MRI abnormalities (limbic encephalitis pattern most common at 44%), MRI abnormality presence was not significantly associated with 3-month mRS.
A relapsing clinical course (2 patients) was not a significant predictor of loss of physical independence at 3 months.
A rapidly progressive course (<15 days to bedridden, seen in 48% of patients) was not significantly associated with 3-month mRS.
There was no significant difference in 3-month prognosis based on the acute-phase therapeutic strategy used (methylprednisolone alone vs. combined with IVIG or rituximab).
Short-term memory impairment was the most common clinical feature in the cohort, present in 68% of patients.
An underlying tumor was identified in 4 of 25 patients (16%), with most detected antibodies belonging to the lower cancer-risk category.
The antibody-based cancer risk category was not directly associated with worse 3-month prognosis in this cohort.
At 3-month follow-up, 44% of patients had a poor outcome (mRS>2), and 16% of the total cohort had died.
The PREMICE sham-controlled trial found within-group reductions in monthly migraine days with eTNS but the verum vs sham between-group difference did not reach statistical significance.
In the PREMICE trial, the 50% responder rate for migraine days was significantly greater with verum eTNS than sham.
A Japanese population study of eTNS for migraine prevention found a significant decrease in migraine days at 12 weeks with high compliance.
An open-label 2023 study found limited efficacy of eTNS for chronic migraine, with only a minority achieving meaningful headache reduction.
The ACME trial found eTNS produced significantly greater acute pain reduction than sham at 60 minutes.
The real-world TEAM trial showed significant benefit of eTNS during acute migraine attacks for 2-hour pain freedom and improvement of the most bothersome symptom.
In an emergency department RCT, the HeadaTerm TENS device produced significantly greater acute migraine pain reduction than sham.
sTMS was superior to sham for pain freedom at 2 hours in a migraine-with-aura RCT.
In the ESPOUSE study, preventive sTMS use resulted in a significantly greater reduction in headache days than a statistically derived placebo estimate.
An open-label study of high-frequency and chronic migraine patients found a significant reduction in monthly headache days with sTMS at 3 months.
In the PRESTO trial, nVNS achieved significantly higher acute pain freedom than sham at 30 and 60 minutes but not at the 120-minute primary endpoint.
The PREMIUM trial's primary preventive endpoint for nVNS was not met, though post hoc analysis suggested benefit in high-frequency users and those with aura.

The underpowered PREMIUM II trial (terminated early due to COVID-19) did not show a significant primary reduction in monthly migraine days with nVNS, though the 50% responder rate favored active treatment.
A preliminary study in adolescents found nVNS produced a positive acute response without need for rescue medication in nearly half of treated attacks.
nVNS (ACT1/ACT2 trials) was superior to sham for acute treatment of episodic cluster headache but not for chronic cluster headache.
The PREVA study found nVNS added to standard of care significantly improved response rate for chronic cluster headache prevention versus standard of care alone.
A case series found two patients with SUNA did not have a significant response to nVNS treatment.
A pilot RCT found that stronger REN stimulation intensities produced a greater 2-hour improvement rate for acute migraine than sham.
A large double-blind sham-controlled RCT found REN produced significantly greater acute migraine pain reduction and pain freedom than sham.
A prospective RCT found REN was effective for prevention of both episodic and chronic migraine, significantly reducing monthly migraine days versus sham.
An open-label adolescent safety study of REN reported a low adverse event rate and meaningful rates of pain freedom and functional improvement at 2 hours.
A retrospective survey-based study found no significant difference in pregnancy or newborn outcomes between pregnant women using REN for migraine and those not using it.
An RCT found eCOT-NS produced significantly greater acute reductions in migraine pain severity than sham at 1, 2, and 24 hours, though sustained relief at 24 hours was not demonstrated.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found potential for tDCS targeting the primary motor cortex and visual cortex to reduce monthly migraine days.
Case series evidence supports use of non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation for indomethacin-sensitive headaches such as hemicrania continua and paroxysmal hemicrania.
A case report described relief of primary cough headache with non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation.
A small case series found that two patients with SUNA did not have a significant response to non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation.

A 2017 pilot RCT of remote electrical neuromodulation found a 46-48% reduction in migraine pain with the strongest stimulation intensities compared to 26% improvement with sham in 71 patients with episodic migraine.
A double-blind sham-controlled RCT of 252 participants found REN produced pain reduction in 66.7% of the active group versus 38.8% of sham, and pain freedom in 37.4% versus 18.4%.
A 2023 RCT of 179 participants found REN used as a preventive treatment every other day significantly reduced monthly migraine days compared to sham in both episodic and chronic migraine subgroups.
An open-label study of acute REN use found pain relief at 24 hours in 45% of participants in at least half of their attacks, informing the 48-hour interval used in subsequent preventive trials.

A prospective open-label safety study in adolescents aged 12-17 found REN was well tolerated with one adverse event (2%) of arm pain, and reported 35% pain freedom and 69% functional improvement at 2 hours.
A real-world study of 83 high-frequency adolescent REN users showed a considerable month-to-month reduction in the mean number of REN treatment days.

A survey-based retrospective study of 140 pregnant women found no significant difference in gestational age, newborn weight, miscarriage rate, preterm birth rate, birth defect rate, stillbirth rate, or developmental milestones between REN users and non-users during pregnancy.
In a randomized sham-controlled trial of 27 eCOT-NS participants versus 28 sham participants with migraine, eCOT-NS produced significantly greater pain reduction at 1, 2, and 24 hours post-treatment.
A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found anodal tDCS of the primary motor cortex and visual cortex, and cathodal inhibition of the visual cortex, showed potential to reduce monthly migraine days.
A separate systematic review of 12 tDCS studies (mostly anodal stimulation) for migraine found only one study was graded as high quality with low risk of bias.
The ongoing TACTIC trial is planned to investigate combined tDCS and anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment for migraine.

A double-blind RCT of kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) for acute migraine found a 3.3-point greater reduction in pain scores compared to placebo, significant as early as 5 minutes into treatment.
A randomized sham-controlled multicenter trial of weekly KOS for chronic migraine prevention found significantly reduced monthly headache days with moderate-severe intensity versus sham.

A resting-state fMRI study comparing migraine patients and controls during KOS treatment provided initial evidence that KOS alters intrinsic functional brain activity, potentially via the trigeminal parasympathetic reflex.
In a cohort of cluster headache patients, KOS produced ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms such as lacrimation but did not reduce cluster headache attacks themselves.
Whole-brain BOLD-fMRI suggests that external trigeminal nerve stimulation (eTNS) has antinociceptive effects on the anterior cingulate cortex when used preventively for migraine.

An fMRI study elucidated the functional connectivity underlying the modulatory effect of noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation on the trigeminal autonomic reflex, involving a network including the hypothalamus, left pontine nucleus, parahippocampal gyrus, and spinal trigeminal nuclei.

In a randomized crossover sham-controlled study, vagal nerve stimulation modulated the nociceptive withdrawal reflex in healthy subjects, suggesting it acts partly through central descending pain-control pathways.
Cost-effectiveness analyses found reduced healthcare utilization and overall costs with nVNS plus standard of care compared to standard of care alone for acute migraine management.
Deep brain stimulation has demonstrated efficacy for cluster headache, but its clinical use is limited by risk of complications.
An RCT of surgically implanted sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation showed favorable results for chronic cluster headache, though the device is not currently available.
Real-world studies confirmed nVNS efficacy and improved quality of life in cluster headache patients who did not respond to or were intolerant of multiple prior preventive and/or acute treatments.
nVNS treatment of chronic cluster headache was associated with lower cost and higher quality-adjusted life year benefits.
A retrospective single-center case series demonstrated relief of vertigo, headache, and nystagmus with nVNS used for acute treatment of vestibular migraine.
An open-label study supports use of nVNS as mini-prophylaxis for menstrual migraine.
Case series evidence supports nVNS use for indomethacin-sensitive headaches, including hemicrania continua and paroxysmal hemicrania.
A case report describes nVNS use for primary cough headache.
Two patients with short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic symptoms (SUNA) did not have a significant response to nVNS treatment.
A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found tDCS targeting the primary motor cortex and visual cortex (activation) or visual cortex inhibition had potential to reduce the number of migraine days per month.
A separate systematic review of 12 tDCS studies for migraine found that only 1 of the 12 studies was graded as high quality with low risk of bias.
The ongoing TACTIC trial (NCT05161871) is investigating combined transcranial direct current stimulation and anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment for migraine.

A double-blind placebo-controlled RCT of kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) for acute migraine met its primary endpoint, with a 3.3-point greater reduction in VAS pain score at 15 minutes versus placebo.

A randomized double-blind sham-controlled multicenter trial of weekly KOS for chronic migraine prevention met its primary endpoint, reducing monthly headache days with moderate-to-severe intensity by 3.5 days versus 1.2 days with sham.

A resting-state fMRI study of 10 migraine patients and 10 controls found all migraine patients responded to KOS within 10-20 minutes, providing initial evidence that KOS alters intrinsic functional brain activity via the trigeminal parasympathetic reflex.
In cluster headache patients, KOS produced ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms quantified by lacrimation but did not trigger cluster headache attacks.

In a single-center RCT of auricular transcutaneous vagal nerve stimulation for chronic migraine, the 1 Hz stimulation group had a significantly larger decrease in headache days per 28 days compared to baseline than the 25 Hz group.
Invasive vagal nerve stimulation has demonstrated efficacy in the treatment of refractory epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression.
nVNS has been shown to improve symptoms and gastric emptying in patients with gastroparesis.
Whole-brain BOLD-fMRI suggested that eTNS exerts antinociceptive effects on the anterior cingulate cortex when used preventively for migraine.
sTMS is theorized, based on animal studies, to modulate cortical spreading depression, brain excitability, GABAergic neurotransmission, and thalamocortical activity.

Proposed mechanisms for nVNS efficacy in headache include modulation of the autonomic nervous system, inhibition of cortical spreading depression, and alteration of trigeminovascular nociceptive neurotransmission.

An fMRI study of the trigeminal autonomic reflex found the modulatory effect of nVNS involves a network including the hypothalamus, left pontine nucleus, parahippocampal gyrus, and spinal trigeminal nuclei.
In a randomized crossover sham-controlled study, nVNS modulated the nociceptive withdrawal reflex in healthy subjects, suggesting effects via central descending pain pathways.
Deep brain stimulation shows efficacy data for cluster headache but its clinical use is limited by risk of complications.
An RCT of surgically implanted sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation showed favorable results for chronic cluster headache, though the device is not currently available.
Real-world studies confirmed nVNS efficacy and improvement in quality of life in cluster headache patients who did not respond to or tolerate other preventive/acute treatments.
Treatment of chronic cluster headache with nVNS was associated with lower cost and higher benefit in quality-adjusted life years.
A retrospective single-center case series demonstrated nVNS relief of vertigo, headache, and nystagmus in vestibular migraine, potentially via trigeminal-vestibular-vagal brainstem connections.
An open-label study supports the use of nVNS as mini-prophylaxis for menstrual migraine.
Case series evidence supports nVNS use for indomethacin-sensitive headaches, including hemicrania continua and paroxysmal hemicrania.
A case report described use of nVNS for primary cough headache.
A case series found that two patients with SUNA (short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic symptoms) did not have a significant response to nVNS treatment.

REN stimulation of upper arm peripheral nerves is thought to induce conditioned pain modulation in the brainstem, causing serotonergic and noradrenergic modulation resulting in pain inhibition and reduced associated symptoms.
eCOT-NS is proposed to function through trigeminal and cortical neurotransmission to the trigeminocervical complex.

A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found that tDCS targeting the primary motor cortex and visual cortex (activation), as well as visual cortex inhibition, had potential to reduce the number of monthly migraine days.

The ongoing TACTIC trial (NCT05161871) will investigate combined tDCS and CGRP-targeting monoclonal antibody treatment for migraine.

Physiological studies show the left vagus nerve has modulatory effects on headache and somatic pain, providing rationale for auricular transcutaneous VNS in chronic migraine.

6-month-old MFS mice showed decreased Glut1 staining (reduced microvascular density) in the dentate gyrus compared to age-matched controls, but did not differ from 12-month-old aged controls.
Glut1 staining was decreased in the CA1 hippocampal region both in 6-month MFS mice and in 12-month aged control mice compared to 6-month controls, with no difference between MFS and aged controls.
Glut1 staining was decreased in the CA3 hippocampal region both in 6-month MFS mice and 12-month aged controls compared to 6-month controls, with no difference between MFS and aged controls.
IgG staining, a marker of blood-brain barrier permeability, was increased in the dentate gyrus of 6-month MFS mice compared to age-matched controls, resembling levels in 12-month aged controls.
In the CA1 hippocampal region, IgG staining (BBB permeability) did not differ significantly between 6-month MFS, 6-month control, and 12-month control mice.
IgG staining was increased in the CA3 hippocampal region of 6-month MFS mice compared to controls, with no difference from 12-month aged controls.
In the dentate gyrus, MFS mice showed increased microglia soma number and decreased microglial branch length and endpoints per soma compared to controls, indicating reactive microglial morphology.

12-month aged control mice showed similarly increased microglia soma number and decreased endpoints (but unchanged branch length) in the dentate gyrus compared to 6-month controls, mirroring the MFS phenotype.
In the CA1 region, MFS mice showed increased microglia soma number and decreased branch length and endpoints per soma compared to controls.

12-month aged control mice showed a similar increase in CA1 microglia soma number and decreased endpoints (without a branch-length difference) compared to 6-month controls, resembling the MFS phenotype and supporting premature aging.
In the CA3 region, MFS mice showed increased microglia soma count and decreased branch length and endpoints per microglia compared to controls.
12-month aged control mice showed similarly increased CA3 microglial soma count with decreased branch length and endpoints compared to 6-month controls, matching the MFS phenotype.

In prior work by the same group, peak blood flow velocity in the posterior cerebral artery of 6-month-old male MFS mice was reduced to a level similar to that of 12-month-old control mice, suggesting premature vascular aging.
Mutant fibrillin-1 fails to sequester latent TGF-β, leading to uncontrolled TGF-β release that activates matrix metalloproteinases and drives elastin degradation in the extracellular matrix.
Prior studies in MFS patients and mouse models have shown increased expression and activity of MMP-2 and MMP-9 in peripheral tissues such as blood and aortic wall.

A 67-year-old woman with secondary Sjögren's syndrome developed longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis presenting with progressive back pain, sensory loss, paraparesis and fecal incontinence.

MRI demonstrated a T2 hyperintense signal extending from T4 to the conus medullaris with meningeal thickening and abnormal post-contrast enhancement, indicating multifocal meningeal, medullary, and radicular involvement.
Lumbar puncture showed CSF pleocytosis with mononuclear cell predominance, marked hypoglycorrhachia (19% of glycemia), and elevated protein levels, consistent with lymphocytic meningitis.
Anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies were negative in the patient, supporting differentiation of her myelopathy from neuromyelitis optica.
Antinuclear antibodies were positive at a titer of 1:160 with a fine granular pattern in peripheral blood, but ANA was negative in the CSF.
Meningeal biopsy revealed a non-specific, sparse mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate, excluding lymphoma or granulomatous disease.
Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for three days) followed by five cycles of cyclophosphamide resulted in resolution of the transverse myelitis and improved walking ability.

A cited study found peripheral nervous system involvement was more prevalent in secondary Sjögren's syndrome than primary Sjögren's syndrome (31% vs 19%, p<0.05), while CNS involvement rates were similar between subtypes (13% vs 15%).

Pathological studies show CNS involvement in Sjögren's syndrome is associated with vasculitic changes including perivascular mononuclear infiltration, microinfarcts, microhemorrhages, and endothelial damage.
Autoimmune demyelination has also been implicated as a contributing mechanism in CNS manifestations of Sjögren's syndrome.
Recurrence of transverse myelitis has been associated with the presence of anti-Ro/SSA antibodies.
Transverse myelitis is more frequently associated with secondary Sjögren's syndrome, particularly cases secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis.

Neurological involvement affects up to 20% of Sjögren's syndrome patients, with peripheral nervous system manifestations occurring in approximately 10-20% of primary SS patients, while CNS involvement is often underreported.
Sicca symptoms typically appear about five years before the onset of CNS involvement in Sjögren's syndrome.

Out-of-pocket costs for the high-cost CGRP-targeting migraine medications (atogepant, eptinezumab, erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, rimegepant, ubrogepant) increased by 187% between 2018 and 2021.
Aggregate out-of-pocket costs for NTM migraine medications increased by 1,993% from 2018 to 2021.
Aggregate total costs for NTM migraine medications increased by 1,752% from 2018 to 2021.
In 2021, average total cost per patient for guideline-supported generic migraine medications was approximately $2,500 lower than for NTM medications.

Modeled substitution of generic guideline-supported medications for NTM medications among migraine patients prescribed NTM drugs in 2021 would have saved an estimated $135 million in aggregate costs that year.

Among migraine medications, erenumab, galcanezumab, rimegepant, and ubrogepant had the highest aggregate costs in 2021, each exceeding $5 million, with trends suggesting further increases beyond 2021.
The migraine patient sample in this claims database was 84% female, consistent with known migraine epidemiology, while other neurologic conditions studied had more even sex distributions.
Droxidopa had the highest out-of-pocket costs among orthostatic hypotension medications but showed a downward cost trend toward the end of the study period.
Older generic medications for orthostatic hypotension, fludrocortisone and midodrine, had out-of-pocket costs that remained below $100 annually throughout the entire 2012-2021 study period.

Aggregate cost burden for orthostatic hypotension medications was $4.3 million in 2021, driven mostly by droxidopa, whose costs declined toward the end of the study period, plausibly related to the introduction of 12 generic formulations in 2021.

The authors note that newer CGRP-targeting migraine prophylactic medications may be cost-effective compared with placebo but are likely cost-ineffective relative to some generic alternatives given similar efficacy and substantially higher price.
