Fatigue classification using accelerometer features alone performed similarly to using baseline participant characteristics alone.

The affinity-matured, pH-sensitive anti-PAR2 antibody MEDI0618 showed a 7-fold reduction in systemic clearance in rats compared with the non-pH-dependent parent antibody P67, attributed to engineered histidine substitutions enabling FcRn-mediated recycling rather than lysosomal degradation.
MEDI0618 fully and potently inhibited matriptase-induced calcium signalling in PAR2-expressing 1321N1 cells with an IC50 of 100 pM, without agonist activity.
MEDI0618 was approximately 15-fold more potent at inhibiting human PAR2 than the previously identified anti-PAR2 antibody PAR650097.

MEDI0618 showed no inhibitory activity at the related receptor PAR1, with no significant effect on thrombin-mediated calcium transients versus isotype control, in contrast to PAR1-selective inhibitors (vorapaxar and anti-PAR1 antibodies) which fully blocked the response.

MEDI0618 fully and potently inhibited matriptase-induced calcium transients in primary human dural fibroblasts and human dural microvascular endothelial cells, with IC50 values of 108 pM and 435 pM, respectively.
In the mouse brain endothelial cell line bEnd.3, MEDI0618 inhibited matriptase-evoked PAR2 calcium responses with an IC50 of 168 pM, mirroring findings in human dural endothelial cells.

The PAR2 agonist LIGRLO activated a calcium transient in approximately 20% of acutely dissociated mouse trigeminal ganglion neurons, confirming functional expression of PAR2 in trigeminal sensory neurons.

Supradural or systemic administration of the mast cell degranulator compound 48/80 induced periorbital and hindpaw cutaneous allodynia in mice, and this migraine-like pain behaviour was fully prevented by pretreatment with MEDI0618 (50 mg/kg s.c.) but not by isotype control protein.

Systemic compound 48/80 decreased spontaneous rearing (vertical episodes) in female mice, interpreted as spontaneous migraine-like headache behaviour, and MEDI0618 fully prevented this decrease compared to isotype control.

In mice sensitized by prior restraint stress, MEDI0618 dose-dependently reduced periorbital and hindpaw cutaneous allodynia reinstated by inhalational umbellulone (a TRPA1 agonist), with maximal effect at 50 mg/kg.
Systemic nitroglycerin and supradural inflammatory mediators both induced periorbital and hindpaw cutaneous allodynia in mice, and pretreatment with MEDI0618 fully prevented allodynia in both models.
The small molecule CGRP-receptor antagonist olcegepant fully blocked cutaneous allodynia induced by supradural CGRP, confirming adequate CGRP-receptor occupancy in this model.

Olcegepant, despite fully blocking CGRP-induced allodynia, failed to alter periorbital and hindpaw cutaneous allodynia induced by supradural inflammatory mediators, indicating a CGRP-receptor-independent component to this pain model.

MEDI0618 fully prevented CGRP-receptor-independent periorbital and hindpaw cutaneous allodynia induced by supradural inflammatory mediators, even in mice pretreated with olcegepant, demonstrating efficacy against a CGRP-receptor-independent migraine mechanism.

In contrast to its efficacy across all migraine models tested, MEDI0618 given repeatedly after mild traumatic brain injury failed to prevent transient acute post-traumatic headache-like allodynia or its reinstatement by bright light stress or umbellulone challenge.
MEDI0618 has been reported to be safe and well tolerated in healthy volunteer phase I clinical trials, supporting its progression to clinical development for migraine prevention.
Mast cell degranulation products have been reported in the plasma of human patients following a migraine attack, supporting a role for mast cell activation in clinical migraine.

Administration of the mast cell degranulator compound 48/80 has been reported to trigger hemicranial migraine-like headache in humans, supporting translational relevance of the mouse compound 48/80 model.

Spasticity accompanied by mental status changes and dysautonomia raises suspicion for PERM (progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus) syndrome, a rare autoimmune subset of stiff person syndrome.
The patient's serum anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibody titer was elevated at 150 IU/mL on two separate occasions, supporting the diagnosis of PERM/stiff-person spectrum disorder.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, consistent with an inflammatory/autoimmune central nervous system process.
Electroencephalography showed diffuse slowing with background rhythms up to 7 Hz, consistent with diffuse encephalopathy.

Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone combined with rituximab over four weeks led to gradual improvement in encephalopathy and reduced episodes of muscular rigidity, with return to baseline function.

PERM is thought to result from autoantibody formation against GAD and glycine receptor (GlyR), disrupting presynaptic GABAergic inhibition mediated through amphiphysin, an intracellular synaptic protein regulating GABA release.
Postmortem studies of PERM have demonstrated T-lymphocyte infiltration of the central nervous system, suggesting an additional cell-mediated autoimmune component beyond humoral autoantibody effects.
In a prior literature review, 70% of PERM cases were GlyR-antibody-positive, 14% had GAD, DPPX, or anti-amphiphysin antibodies, and 16% had untested or no identified autoimmune antibody.
GlyR-antibody-negative individuals may have a slightly better rate of good neurologic outcome after immunotherapy compared to GlyR-antibody-positive individuals.
About 20% of patients presenting with PERM were found to have an underlying tumor (thymoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, lung, or breast cancer) on further workup, suggesting a paraneoplastic association.
Rituximab is proposed to act in PERM by targeting CD20+ B cells that produce GAD or GlyR autoantibodies.
A prior reported case of GlyR-positive PERM treated with steroids, immunoglobulin, and rituximab did not show significant improvement, contrasting with the substantial response seen in this case.

Relapse of PERM symptoms after initial resolution has been described in the literature, most commonly occurring in patients who were on no maintenance immunotherapy or a decreased immunotherapy dosage.

Spontaneous intracranial hypotension has a slightly higher average incidence in women than in men, with an average age of onset of 40 years.
The most common symptoms of spontaneous intracranial hypotension include orthostatic headache, nausea, neck pain, hearing disturbance, dizziness, and aural fullness.
The cause of cerebrospinal fluid leak in SIH is most commonly a tear in the dural layer surrounding the spinal cord and brain, though in some cases the cause remains unidentified.
MRI of the spine at admission showed extensive extradural cerebrospinal fluid collection extending from the third cervical vertebra to the sacrum, confirming the diagnosis of SIH.

In this patient, three sequential fluoroscopy-guided epidural blood patch procedures (at L1-L2, T10-T11, and T8-T9) ultimately resolved the extradural CSF collection and led to symptomatic improvement, with the patient walking normally by day 57 post-procedure and being discharged on day 118.
Previously published reports show that the success rate of the first epidural blood patch for SIH varies widely, from 13% to 75%.
A recent retrospective study reported that fluoroscopy-guided epidural blood patch for SIH was more effective than a blind approach.
A recent report indicates that 20 mL of blood injected into the epidural space spreads across an average of 4.6 vertebral body intervals.
Ohtonari et al. indicated that the risk of complications from multiple epidural blood patches, as well as the practitioner's stress level, increases significantly with the frequency of the procedure.
Headache of any type was reported by 69% (27/39) of patients with acromegaly, with 51% of the total cohort also being biochemically controlled.
Achieving biochemical control of acromegaly did not significantly affect whether patients experienced headache overall.
54% (21/39) of acromegaly patients had a clinical picture consistent with primary headache.
Among the 21 patients with primary headache, 86% (18/21) met diagnostic criteria for migraine, comprising 67% episodic and 19% chronic migraine.
Migraine prevalence in the overall acromegaly cohort (46%) was higher than the reported prevalence of migraine in the general population.
Tension-type headache was diagnosed in 14% (3/21) of patients with primary headache.

Six patients (15%) had secondary headache attributed to hypothalamic/pituitary hyper- or hyposecretion per ICHD-3 criteria, presenting as bilateral orbital/supraorbital pressure without accompanying autonomic or trigeminal symptoms.
All six patients with secondary headache experienced complete resolution of headache after effective acromegaly treatment (four after surgery, two after medical therapy).
Patients with primary headache had a significantly shorter duration of acromegaly than patients without headache.
The diagnostic delay for acromegaly was significantly shorter in patients with primary headache than in those without headache.
Tumor size (macroadenoma vs microadenoma) did not significantly influence the presence of primary headache.
Cavernous sinus invasion by the pituitary adenoma was not significantly associated with headache presence.
Acromegaly treatment (surgery, radiotherapy, or medical therapy) did not significantly affect the overall course of primary headache.
Biochemical control of acromegaly did not significantly influence the presence of primary headache.
A family history of headache was present in 51% (20/39) of the overall acromegaly cohort, suggesting a possible predisposition to migraine.
Among primary headache patients, 57% (12/21) reported a personal family history of headache.
81% of patients with primary headache used acute medications (NSAIDs or acetaminophen) for attacks, averaging 2.7 pills per month, and none used migraine-specific drugs such as triptans.

A previously reported study found higher plasma concentrations of calcitonin gene-related peptide and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating peptide in pituitary adenoma patients with headache compared to those without, peptides known to be involved in and elevated in migraine.

Prior literature has observed decreased production of interleukin-10 (an anti-inflammatory cytokine) in patients with acromegaly even after effective treatment, suggestive of impaired anti-inflammatory responses that could contribute to migraine susceptibility.

Excessive GH and IGF-1 levels in acromegaly are associated with endothelial progenitor cell dysregulation, altered nitric oxide release, and increased oxidative stress, mechanisms proposed to trigger or aggravate migraine.
One woman with migraine with typical aura reported disappearance of aura episodes after neurosurgery, while non-aura migraine attacks persisted.
38% (8/21) of patients with primary headache reported a slight improvement in headache after acromegaly treatment without complete resolution.

Primary headache in acromegaly patients was mostly bilateral (71%), located in orbital/retro-orbital/frontal regions, with photophobia and phonophobia in 86% and nausea (with vomiting in two cases) in 38%; no cranial autonomic symptoms were observed.

58.1% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis presented with cardiovascular dysautonomia (sustained tachycardia, bradycardia, hypertension, or hypotension not explained by sepsis, fever, or medications).
Patients with poor functional prognosis were significantly older than those with good functional prognosis.
Headache as a prodromal symptom was significantly less frequent among patients with poor functional prognosis than those with good prognosis.
Status epilepticus was significantly more frequent among patients with poor functional prognosis than those with good prognosis.
EEG findings at admission (classified as normal, dysfunction, or epileptic activity) differed significantly between patients with good and poor functional prognosis.
45.8% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis had elevated CPK levels (>223 U/L).
CPK levels did not differ significantly between patients with good and poor functional prognosis.
54.8% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis had CSF pleocytosis (>5 cells/mm3) and 25.8% had hyperproteinorrhachia (>45 mg/dL).
Anti-NMDAR encephalitis was the most frequent definitive diagnosis among patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis, accounting for 19 of 31 cases.

Among 9046 patients seen in the neurological emergency department in 2022, 201 (2.2%) were admitted with suspected infectious or autoimmune encephalitis/encephalopathy, and only 31 (0.3%) ultimately met diagnostic criteria for possible autoimmune encephalitis.
At hospital discharge, 58% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis had good functional prognosis (mRS≤2) while 42% had poor prognosis (mRS≥3), including 2 deaths.
67.7% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis presented with catatonia.
90.3% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis presented with cognitive alterations.
74.2% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis presented with psychotic symptoms.
71% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis presented with abnormal movements (including orolingual dyskinesias).
64.5% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis experienced seizures and 19.4% experienced status epilepticus.
Two patients (6.5%) with possible autoimmune encephalitis had an associated tumor, identified as a mature ovarian teratoma and a solitary pulmonary nodule.

Systemic autoimmune antibody panels (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-beta2 glycoprotein IgG/IgM, lupus anticoagulant, anti-SSA, anti-SSB) were negative in all patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis.
The median time from symptom onset to emergency admission among patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis was 15 days.
The median hospital length of stay for patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis was 45 days.
35.5% of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis had a preceding non-specific respiratory or gastrointestinal infection within 30 days of symptom onset.
Two of 31 patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis (6.5%) had an associated tumor, identified during follow-up as a mature ovarian teratoma and a solitary pulmonary nodule.
Testing for systemic autoimmune disease antibodies was negative in all patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis.
Elevated CPK levels (>223 U/L) were found in 45.8% of patients but did not differ significantly between those with good versus poor functional prognosis.

Among 31 patients meeting criteria for possible autoimmune encephalitis, 19 (61.3%) had CSF anti-NMDAR antibody-confirmed definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis, while 12 (38.7%) were anti-NMDAR antibody-negative.
Headache was present in 41.9% of the overall cohort of patients with possible autoimmune encephalitis, and was notably less frequent among those with poor functional prognosis.

Despite 64.5% of patients having clinical seizures and 19.4% status epilepticus, epileptiform activity on admission EEG was infrequent, likely because antiseizure treatment had often already been started before EEG was obtained.
Metabolic syndrome was commonly observed in patients with migraine, though its impact on migraine pain severity was inconclusive across the nine identified studies.
Patients with spinal pain, fibromyalgia, or general chronic pain who also had metabolic syndrome showed higher pain scores and greater functional limitations than those without metabolic syndrome.

The relationship between metabolic syndrome and chronic pain is proposed to be bidirectional, involving proinflammatory mediators that modulate nociception alongside pain-induced lifestyle changes that affect metabolic function.
Across 28 included studies, metabolic syndrome was found to be prevalent among patients with chronic pain and was associated with worse pain and functional outcomes overall.
Approximately 40% of migraine patients do not respond to monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP or its receptor.
A monoclonal antibody targeting the PAC1 receptor did not outperform placebo in a phase II migraine prophylaxis trial.
Prolonged infusion of VIP triggers migraine attacks in adults with migraine, supporting a role for VPAC1/VPAC2 receptors in migraine induction.
A receptor (MrgB3 in rats, MrgB2 in mice, MrgX2 in humans) expressed on mast cells triggers mast cell activation and represents a fourth PACAP-related receptor pathway.
A proof-of-concept trial found that a PACAP-inhibiting antibody reduced migraine days in patients who had failed two to four prior preventive treatments.
Cluster headache affects approximately 0.1% of the global population and occurs in episodic and chronic forms, with the episodic form more common.
A GWAS in 99 Italian patients with cluster headache found an association between a common ADCYAP1R1 variant and the condition, but this was not replicated in a larger Swedish cohort.
Plasma PACAP levels were significantly lower during the inter-bout phase in patients with episodic cluster headache compared to healthy controls.
Plasma PACAP levels rose significantly during cluster headache attacks compared to the inter-bout phase in the same five individuals.
A double-blind crossover study showed that 20-minute PACAP infusions triggered cluster-like attacks in approximately 50% of patients with active episodic or chronic cluster headache.
PACAP infusions did not trigger cluster headache attacks in patients with episodic cluster headache who were in remission.
PACAP-induced cluster-like attacks were not associated with changes in plasma CGRP, VIP, histamine, or tryptase levels, suggesting PACAP acts via a mast-cell- and CGRP-independent pathway.
PACAP levels fluctuate across the menstrual cycle, with higher concentrations observed during the perimenstrual and periovulatory phases.
Transcranial direct current stimulation was prophylactically effective in menstrually related migraine but did not change serum PACAP-38 levels.
Post-traumatic headache has an estimated lifetime prevalence of approximately 4.7% in men and 2.4% in women following traumatic brain injury.
Intravenous PACAP induced migraine-like headaches in 20 of 21 individuals with persistent post-traumatic headache, closely mimicking their usual headache episodes.
In an open-label trial, erenumab (a CGRP-targeting monoclonal antibody) showed limited effectiveness in 100 individuals with persistent post-traumatic headache.
A phase 2 trial found that monthly fremanezumab injections were not more effective than placebo in preventing persistent post-traumatic headache over 12 weeks.
For headache events meeting full ICHD-3 criteria for migraine without aura ("definite migraine"), symptomatology agreement with clinician-led intake interviews had a median of 55.5%.
For headache events meeting only probable migraine criteria, median agreement with intake symptomatology was lower than for definite migraine, at 41.9%.
For headache events not meeting migraine criteria ("not migraine"), median agreement with intake symptomatology was 39.4%, still substantial despite failing formal ICHD-3 criteria.
Symptom agreement with intake interviews was statistically significantly higher for "definite migraine" events than for both "probable migraine" and "not migraine" events.
Cohen's kappa coefficient for ICHD-3 symptom agreement between intake interviews and headache event registration was 0.48 for definite migraine events, indicating moderate agreement.
Cohen's kappa for probable migraine events was 0.32, indicating only fair agreement between intake and diary-reported ICHD-3 symptoms.
Cohen's kappa for events not meeting migraine criteria was only 0.13, indicating poor agreement between intake and diary-reported ICHD-3 symptoms.
Across the full set of headache events, intraparticipant symptom similarity between headache event pairs (IoU) was low, with a median of 24.4%.
Definite migraine event pairs showed substantially higher ICHD-3 symptom IoU similarity (52.6%) than probable migraine (30.5%) or not-migraine (14.6%) event pairs.
Headache event symptom similarity (IoU) showed a decreasing trend as the time interval between headache event pairs increased, though this trend was not statistically significant within the 95% CI.
Over the course of the 90-day study, more than half of participants (15/27) newly reported at least one ICHD-3 symptom during headache events that had not been reported at intake.
The symptoms most commonly overreported at intake compared with longitudinal registration were vomiting, conjunctival injection, and lacrimation.

Rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and restlessness/agitation - cranial autonomic symptoms classically associated with cluster headache - were newly reported during the longitudinal phase in over one-third of participants who had denied these symptoms during the clinical intake interview.
The majority of longitudinally registered headache events (429/505, over 85%) in patients previously diagnosed with migraine did not meet full ICHD-3 criteria for migraine without aura.
Compliance with the daily electronic diary questionnaire (a proxy for engagement) was moderate, with a median completion rate of 76% and wide interparticipant variability.

Acute migraine medication use was frequent and largely effective in this cohort, with a median per-participant use rate of 87.5% of headache events and median self-reported therapeutic effectiveness of 80%.

The 36 DEGs shared between COVID-19 and SS-KCS datasets were enriched in immune-related biological processes including T-cell activation, leukocyte-mediated immunity, regulation of cell-cell adhesion, and leukocyte activation.
Intersecting the differentially expressed genes from the COVID-19 and SS-KCS datasets identified 36 common DEGs out of 6088 COVID-19 DEmRNAs and 80 SS-KCS DEmRNAs.
WGCNA identified 2413 mRNAs within dark green, dark red, and black modules that significantly correlated with COVID-19 clinical status.
Intersecting the 36 common DEGs with the 2413 COVID-WGCNA genes yielded 10 candidate hub genes: TGFBI, TAP2, IL1R2, CR1, TNFRSF10C, CD28, CCL16, HLA-DRA, CCL22, and IL13.

Among four machine-learning algorithms (RF, SVM, XGB, GLM), the random forest model showed the highest specificity and accuracy for classifying both COVID-19 and SS-KCS samples based on the 10 candidate genes.
Gene importance ranking across the four machine-learning models identified CR1, TNFRSF10C, TAP2, and TGFBI as the top four hub genes in the COVID-19 dataset.
Gene importance ranking identified CR1, IL13, TAP2, and IL1R2 as the top four hub genes in the SS-KCS dataset.
CR1 and TAP2 were the shared top-ranked hub genes across both the COVID-19 and SS-KCS machine-learning models, suggesting a role linking the two diseases.
CR1 expression was higher in COVID-19 patients under 55 years of age compared to older patients, while TAP2 showed no correlation with age.
TAP2 expression showed no correlation with age in the COVID-19 dataset.
Neither CR1 nor TAP2 expression differed significantly between male and female COVID-19 patients.
CR1 was significantly upregulated in COVID-19 patients compared with healthy individuals.
TAP2 expression was higher in healthy individuals than in COVID-19 patients.
CR1 expression was highest in severe COVID-19 cases and lowest in healthy individuals, showing a severity gradient.
TAP2 expression was highest in healthy samples and lowest in mild COVID-19 cases.

CIBERSORT analysis showed that proportions of CD8+ T cells, CD4+ memory resting T cells, activated NK cells, monocytes, M0 and M2 macrophages, and neutrophils significantly differed between COVID-19 and healthy samples.
No significant differences were observed in the proportions of the 22 immune cell types infiltrating the microenvironment between SS-KCS and healthy controls.

CR1 expression was positively correlated with neutrophils, M0 and M2 macrophages, and CD4 memory resting T cells, and negatively correlated with activated NK cells, monocytes, and CD8+ T cells in the COVID-19 microenvironment.
TAP2 exhibited a correlation pattern with immune cell types opposite to that of CR1 in the COVID-19 microenvironment.
In the first explicit analysis of CR1 in Sjögren's syndrome-affected conjunctiva, CR1 expression was significantly higher than in normal controls.
TAP2 upregulation in Sjögren's syndrome observed in this study is consistent with a previously reported finding.
Prior literature reports reduced CR1 levels in patients with autoimmune diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, and paracoccidioidomycosis.
A prior study found decreased CR1 levels in COVID-19 patients in intensive care units, accompanied by hyperactivation of the complement system.
Dams fed a high-methionine diet before and during pregnancy had markedly higher plasma homocysteine levels than control-diet dams.
Offspring of dams with prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia (pHHCY) had significantly higher plasma homocysteine levels than control offspring.
Plasma CGRP concentration was significantly higher in pHHCY rats compared to control rats.

Trigeminal afferents in pHHCY rats required a much lower concentration of the K+ channel blocker 4-AP to significantly increase AP firing than in control rats, and the EC50 for 4-AP-induced excitation was lower in pHHCY.
Baseline trigeminal nerve action potential frequency before ATP application was already higher in pHHCY rats than controls.
ATP application produced a greater relative increase in trigeminal nerve firing rate in pHHCY rats compared to controls, with slower recovery to baseline.
ATP-induced Ca2+ transients in trigeminal ganglion (TG) neurons had larger amplitude and longer duration in pHHCY rats than controls.
ADP-induced Ca2+ transients (metabotropic P2Y receptor activation) in TG neurons did not significantly differ between control and pHHCY groups.
BzATP-induced Ca2+ transients (P2X7 receptor activation) in TG neurons had greater amplitude and duration in pHHCY rats than controls.
ATP-induced Ca2+ transients in satellite glial cells (SGCs) of the TG were larger in amplitude and duration in pHHCY rats than controls.
ADP-induced Ca2+ transients in satellite glial cells were larger in amplitude and duration in pHHCY rats compared to controls.
BzATP-induced Ca2+ transient amplitude (P2X7 activation) in satellite glial cells was larger in pHHCY rats than controls, though duration was not significantly different.
24-hour in vitro incubation of cultured TG neurons in L-homocysteine increased ATP-induced Ca2+ transient amplitude and duration compared to untreated neurons.
24-hour L-homocysteine incubation increased the proportion of TG neurons co-responding to both ATP and the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin, suggesting sensitization of nociceptive neurons.
Baseline mast cell degranulation in the dura mater was substantially higher in pHHCY rats compared to controls, consistent with neurogenic inflammation.
BzATP (P2X7 agonist) application increased dural mast cell degranulation in both groups, but the effect was substantially larger in pHHCY rats than controls.
The proportion of TG neurons responding to ATP was similar between control and pHHCY groups, indicating the sensitization is in response magnitude rather than in the number of responsive cells.

Despite homocysteine's known action on NMDA receptors, prior work by this group found no increased responses to NMDA application in TG neurons or trigeminal afferents of pHHCY rats, contrasting with acute homocysteine's direct excitatory effect via NMDA receptors.
In healthy controls, viewing distance, screen brightness, and ambient light had no significant effect on afterimage latency, validating the fixed experimental setup used in later experiments.
Patients with migraine with aura (MwA) showed significantly longer first-latency afterimage duration than healthy controls.
Second-latency (reactivated) afterimage duration was also significantly longer in MwA patients than in healthy controls.
Patients with migraine without aura (MwoA) did not differ significantly from healthy controls in afterimage duration for either latency measure.
First-latency afterimage duration did not significantly differ between MwA and MwoA patients.
Second-latency (reactivated) afterimage duration was significantly longer in MwA than in MwoA patients.
The proportion of participants who failed to perceive an afterimage at all differed across groups, with healthy controls most often missing the second (reactivated) afterimage.
Migraine patients (both MwA and MwoA) had higher PHQ-9 depression scores than healthy controls, with over 60% of migraine patients showing some depressive symptoms.
Afterimage duration did not correlate with PHQ-9 depression scores in any of the three groups.
Migraine patients (MwA and MwoA) had markedly higher HIT-6 headache-impact scores than healthy controls, corresponding to 'severe impact' versus 'little or no impact'.
Afterimage duration was not associated with HIT-6 headache impact score in any group.
In a second, independent cohort (Experiment 3), MwA patients again showed significantly longer afterimage duration than healthy controls following a black stimulus.
MwA patients also showed significantly longer afterimage duration than healthy controls following a red stimulus.
Stimulus color (red versus black/achromatic) did not significantly affect afterimage duration within either group, suggesting afterimage modulation occurs beyond the retinal level.

Across 10 repeated measurements, MwA patients showed an initial increase then slower decline in afterimage latency (habituation deficit), while healthy controls' latencies declined from the second measurement, though this pattern was not confirmed as statistically significant in the overall four-factor ANOVA.

Prior fMRI literature cited in the discussion found that blood flow in the lateral geniculate nucleus is elevated in patients with migraine with aura, but not in migraine without aura or healthy controls.
Prior literature cited in the discussion indicates cortical hyperexcitability in migraine is predominantly observed in migraine with aura rather than migraine without aura.
A right dorsolateral medullary infarction caused secondary SUNCT syndrome, implicating dysfunction of the trigeminocervical complex in the pathogenesis.
Brain MRI confirmed a subacute right dorsolateral medullary infarction, establishing the diagnosis of secondary SUNCT.
The patient developed intermittent electrical pain in the right posterior head, neck, shoulder and arm, diagnosed as occipital neuralgia occurring concomitantly with the SUNCT episodes.
The patient's occipital neuralgia symptoms responded to treatment with gabapentin.
The patient exhibited classic SUNCT autonomic features including dacryorrhoea, rhinorrhoea and ipsilateral facial oedema alongside brief, frequent trigger-evoked facial pain.

43.5% of the PsA cohort met 2011 ACR fibromyalgia classification criteria, a higher rate of comorbid fibromyalgia than typically reported in PsA (9.3–38.3%) and far higher than the general population (~1.78%).
PsA patients with comorbid fibromyalgia had significantly higher 66-joint tender joint counts than those without fibromyalgia.
PsA patients with comorbid fibromyalgia reported significantly higher patient global disease activity VAS scores than those without fibromyalgia.
PsA patients with comorbid fibromyalgia had significantly higher composite Disease Activity in Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA) scores, likely inflated by the inclusion of pain-related components.
PsA patients with comorbid fibromyalgia had significantly higher Leeds Enthesitis Index (LEI) and BASDAI scores than those without fibromyalgia.
PsA patients with comorbid fibromyalgia had significantly greater prior exposure to antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs/biologics) despite similar disease duration, suggesting relative treatment resistance.

Current overall body pain intensity was slightly but not significantly higher in PsA patients with comorbid fibromyalgia compared to those without, indicating that a global pain rating alone cannot distinguish underlying pain mechanisms in this high-inflammation cohort.

Functional connectivity between the default mode network and the right anterior insula was positively associated with the degree of nociplastic pain (FMness) in PsA, reflecting a reduced anticorrelation between these networks in patients with higher nociplastic pain scores, though this result was only marginally significant.

Whole-brain seed-to-voxel analysis showed that nociplastic pain (FMness) scores were positively correlated with functional connectivity between the right middle insula and left posterior insula and DMN regions including the bilateral parahippocampal gyri and the frontal pole/medial prefrontal cortex.

Functional connectivity of the left posterior insula to the brainstem (pons) and ipsilateral thalamus was positively associated with current overall body pain intensity in PsA, consistent with a somatosensory/nociceptive pathway contribution to pain.
Additional posterior insula connectivity to the middle temporal gyrus, contralateral insula, and cerebellum also correlated with current overall body pain in PsA.
Aside from the DMN-right anterior insula connectivity result, no other ROI-to-ROI connectivity between the six insula seeds and the DMN was significantly associated with nociplastic pain (FMness).
SNP-based heritability of dry eye disease was estimated at 6.0% on the liability scale in European-ancestry MVP participants using LDSC.
A multi-ancestry meta-analysis of MVP GWAS data identified ten independent genome-wide significant loci in nine susceptibility regions for dry eye disease, all novel.
The DED-associated locus near FAM180B showed a stronger protective effect in African-ancestry participants than in European-ancestry participants.
The DED risk locus near BLK is pleiotropically associated with multiple autoimmune diseases including Sjögren's disease, systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis.
The FAM180B locus is also linked to corneal structural traits and glaucoma risk, with the glaucoma risk allele being protective against dry eye disease.
A rare missense variant in SYNGAP1 showed the largest effect size of any dry eye disease GWAS locus.
The MLLT10 locus, the top GWAS hit for dry eye disease, was successfully replicated in the independent GERA cohort using the broad phenotype definition.
The polygenic score for self-rated health was the single strongest predictor of dry eye disease case-control status in European-ancestry MVP participants.

Six polygenic scores, representing major depressive disorder, non-cancer illness count, abnormal appetite, neuroticism, and peripheral nerve disorders, were significantly associated with dry eye disease with consistent effect direction across all four ancestry groups.

A GenomicSEM single-factor model derived from dry eye disease, fibromyalgia, IBS, multisite chronic pain, and migraine showed the latent pain factor accounted for over half of the genetic variance in dry eye disease.
Fibromyalgia had the highest genetic correlation with dry eye disease among all traits tested.
Multisite chronic pain showed the second-highest genetic correlation with dry eye disease.
Gastro-esophageal reflux disease showed substantial genetic correlation with dry eye disease.
Genetic correlation analysis found DED shared substantial genetic overlap with gastro-esophageal reflux disease.
Asthma showed substantial genetic correlation with DED.
IBS showed substantial genetic correlation with DED.
Osteoarthritis showed substantial genetic correlation with DED.
A moderate genetic correlation was found between DED and endometriosis despite the cohort being 90% male, suggesting pleiotropy rather than a causal link.
ADHD showed substantial genetic correlation with DED, second only to PTSD among psychiatric traits.
MDD showed significant genetic correlation with DED.
Broadly defined anxiety showed significant genetic correlation with DED.
Bipolar disorder showed a relatively attenuated genetic correlation with DED compared to other psychiatric traits.
Schizophrenia showed a relatively attenuated genetic correlation with DED compared to other psychiatric traits.
Fatigue was genetically correlated with DED.
Insomnia was genetically correlated with DED.
The personality trait neuroticism was significantly genetically correlated with DED.

The genetic correlation between DED and Sjögren's disease remained essentially unchanged after excluding individuals with a history of SjD diagnosis, indicating the shared genetics are not driven solely by clinically diagnosed SjD cases.
Allergic rhinitis showed a moderate genetic correlation with DED among autoimmune/allergic traits.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis showed a moderate genetic correlation with DED among autoimmune traits.
A GWAS-defined diagnosis of any autoimmune disease showed a modest genetic correlation with DED.
Sleep apnea had the strongest genetic correlation with DED among cardiometabolic traits.
Type 2 diabetes showed genetic correlation with DED, a trait noted to have inflammatory and autoimmune facets.
Triglyceride levels showed a moderate positive genetic correlation with DED.
HDL cholesterol showed a negative genetic correlation with DED, indicating genetic liability for DED tracks with lower HDL.
Dry eye disease showed the highest genetic correlation among autoimmune traits with Sjögren's disease, consistent with dry eye being a defining symptom of that condition.

The genetic correlation between DED and Sjögren's disease remained largely unchanged after excluding individuals with a clinical Sjögren's diagnosis, indicating the correlation is not driven solely by comorbid cases.
DED showed a moderate genetic correlation with allergic rhinitis.
DED showed a moderate genetic correlation with juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
A GWAS of diagnosis of any autoimmune disease showed a modest but significant genetic correlation with DED.
Among cardiometabolic traits, sleep apnea had the strongest genetic correlation with DED.
DED showed a moderate genetic correlation with type 2 diabetes, a condition with inflammatory and autoimmune facets.
DED showed a modest positive genetic correlation with triglyceride levels.
DED showed a negative genetic correlation with HDL cholesterol levels.
Poor self-rated health was the behavioral trait most genetically correlated with DED.
DED was genetically correlated with earlier age of tobacco use, part of an externalizing behavior pattern.
DED was genetically correlated with earlier age of sexual debut, consistent with an externalizing behavior pattern.
DED was negatively genetically correlated with educational attainment.
Time spent watching TV was positively genetically correlated with DED.
Time spent gaming was positively genetically correlated with DED.
General computer usage showed no genetic correlation with DED, contrasting with TV and gaming usage.
Alcohol use measured in drinks per week was negatively genetically correlated with DED.
DED was positively genetically correlated with increased water intake, consistent with prior observational associations.

A single latent factor model of DED, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, multisite chronic pain, and migraine using GenomicSEM fit the data well, supporting a shared chronic pain genetic architecture.
The latent chronic-pain factor loaded strongly onto DED and explained just over half of its genetic variance, suggesting DED may partly reflect a broader multisystemic pain liability.
The latent chronic-pain factor was more strongly genetically correlated with TV usage than DED alone was, suggesting shared underlying liability rather than a causal effect of screen time on DED.
The largest-effect DED risk locus identified was a low-frequency missense variant near SYNGAP1, though its effect size was still modest.
DED GWAS loci implicated plausible disease mechanisms, including autoimmunity (BLK) and neurotransmitter signaling/synaptic plasticity (SYNGAP1, GRIA1, EFNA5).
Overall, seven of the nine genotyped DED GWAS loci showed effect directions in GERA consistent with those observed in MVP, though most individual loci were underpowered for formal replication.
Psilocybin-assisted therapy (two doses of 15 mg and 25 mg) was well tolerated in five fibromyalgia patients, with no serious adverse events.

Treatment-related adverse events occurred on or the day after dosing and were minor to moderate, most commonly headache, followed by diarrhea, stomach ache, and migraine, with headaches resolving within two days.
Blood pressure and heart rate remained within pre-specified safety ranges during dosing sessions and were not associated with cardiovascular symptoms.
Average daily pain severity scores decreased from baseline to end of treatment following psilocybin-assisted therapy.
Sleep disturbance T-scores decreased from baseline to end of treatment following psilocybin-assisted therapy, indicating improved sleep.
Pain interference T-scores decreased from baseline to end of treatment following psilocybin-assisted therapy.
Chronic pain acceptance increased modestly on average, with three participants improving and two showing slight decreases.
FM survey scores improved on average from baseline to end of treatment.
Physical function scores increased (improved) on average from baseline to end of treatment.
Self-reported cognitive abilities improved on average from baseline to end of treatment.
Fatigue scores decreased (improved) on average from baseline to end of treatment.
Anxiety scores decreased (improved) on average from baseline to end of treatment.
There were no substantial changes in depression scores from baseline to end of treatment, possibly reflecting floor effects since participants with severe depression were excluded.
All five participants reported some degree of global improvement on the Patient Global Impression of Change following psilocybin-assisted therapy.
Most participants had a complete mystical-type experience following psilocybin dosing, with the proportion increasing at the higher second dose.
Physical distress and grief were the most commonly reported domains of challenging experiences during dosing sessions.

In a North American survey of people with fibromyalgia, most reported neutral or positive perceptions of psychedelic use, and nearly all who used psychedelics specifically for chronic pain reported improved symptoms.
In a separate randomized placebo-controlled trial in migraine patients, psilocybin produced a significantly greater reduction in weekly migraine days than placebo.
Subcutaneous capsaicin injection into the first trigeminal branch region of the forehead induced ipsilateral parasympathetic autonomic symptoms in nearly all healthy subjects.
Female subjects reported significantly higher pain intensity than male subjects at all measured time points after capsaicin injection.
Among the observed autonomic symptoms, lacrimation was the most common (84% of subjects) while ptosis and nasal congestion were the least common (27% each).
For all autonomic symptoms except ptosis, symptom duration was significantly longer in female than in male subjects.
The frequency of every autonomic symptom was higher in female subjects, and the composite autonomic activation score was significantly higher in females than males.
The autonomic activation score correlated positively with pain intensity one minute after capsaicin injection.
When analysed by sex, the correlation between autonomic score and pain intensity was significant in female subjects but not in male subjects.
Prior studies cited in the discussion found that capsaicin injection into the third trigeminal branch (mandibular region) did not induce autonomic activation, unlike injection into the first branch.

The authors cite their own prior work showing that CGRP release after capsaicin injection into forehead skin is not specific to trigemino-autonomic cephalalgias or migraine, since healthy subjects also release CGRP under this stimulus.

Cited literature indicates that α-CGRP levels increase by about 100% during migraine or cluster headache attacks compared with baseline, versus only about 40% in healthy subjects after capsaicin-induced pain.

Cited epidemiological studies report that 13%-37% of migraine patients show unilateral autonomic symptoms, and these patients tend to have more severe and strictly unilateral pain than other migraine patients.

A cited case report describes a chronic cluster headache patient whose trigeminal nerve sensory root section (denervating cranial vessels and dura) neither stopped attacks nor altered cranial autonomic symptoms, suggesting autonomic activation can occur independently of the trigemino-facial parasympathetic reflex.
A machine learning model using only genetic variant data (108 of 123 known migraine risk loci) predicted new-onset migraine with weak discrimination.
A machine learning model using only general clinical/sociodemographic data predicted new-onset migraine with moderate accuracy, substantially better than genotype alone.
Combining genotype and clinical data in a single model yielded the best predictive performance for new-onset migraine, outperforming either data type alone.
An additive voting-classifier combination of separately trained genotype-only and clinical-only models performed worse than the jointly trained combined model.
The superior performance of the jointly trained combined model versus the additive voting classifier suggests non-additive genotype-phenotype interactions contribute to new-onset migraine.
SHAP analysis identified middle age, being married, and not having paid work as important predictors of new-onset migraine.
A higher number of self-reported gastrointestinal symptoms was an important SHAP-identified predictor of new-onset migraine.
Higher serum cholesterol levels were an important SHAP-identified predictor of new-onset migraine, though the pathophysiological link remains unclear.
Higher non-fasting serum glucose was an important SHAP-identified predictor of new-onset migraine.
Self-reported diabetes was an important SHAP-identified predictor of new-onset migraine, though literature on this association is indeterminate.

Nine of the 20 most important features in the combined predictive model were established migraine-risk genetic variants, but these ranked only 15th to 87th in univariate GWAS significance rather than being the strongest known hits, suggesting importance emerges through interaction with clinical features.

The observed 10-year incidence of new-onset migraine (491/12,995, ~4%) in this older HUNT cohort was lower than reported in other populations, possibly reflecting the relatively high mean age of participants.
Individuals who developed new-onset migraine were younger and more often female than those who remained headache-free.

Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) failed to improve classification accuracy for the imbalanced migraine dataset, instead leading the model to classify synthesized rather than real minority-class data.
The decision tree combined model showed poor probability calibration, with predicted probabilities deviating substantially from observed outcome frequencies.
A meta-analysis of 11 studies (3955 subjects) estimated the overall time between first cluster headache attack and correct diagnosis at 10.43 years.
In a UK cohort, mean diagnostic delay fell markedly from 22.3 years for patients diagnosed 1950-1960 to 2.6 years for those diagnosed 1990-1999.
A Danish cohort showed diagnostic delay decreasing from 25.1 years for onset 1960-1969 to 0.9 years for onset after 2010.
In a Greek cohort, median diagnostic delay decreased from 20 years before 1989 to 1 year after 2010.
In a Serbian cohort, mean diagnostic delay was longest for CH onset before age 20 and shortest for onset after age 40.
In a Danish cohort, mean diagnostic delay was longest for CH onset before age 20 and shortest for onset after age 40, replicating the Serbian finding.
In an Italian cohort, pediatric-onset CH patients had a longer mean diagnostic delay than adult-onset patients.
In an international survey, pediatric-onset CH patients had a longer mean diagnostic delay than adult-onset patients.
Presence of migraine-like features in CH attacks was not associated with a significant difference in diagnostic delay.
Diagnostic delay was significantly longer in patients with refractory chronic CH compared to non-refractory chronic CH.
An earlier UK study reported no significant difference in CH diagnostic delay between men and women, although no data were presented.

A Dutch case series found that photophobia/phonophobia, nausea/vomiting during attacks, episodic CH pattern, alternating attack side, nocturnal attacks, and lower age at onset were each associated with longer diagnostic delay.
The same Dutch study found sex, interictal headache, circadian rhythm, restlessness during attacks, and jaw pain radiation did not influence CH diagnostic delay.
A Belgian Flanders study found lower age of CH onset and attacks not peaking within the first 5 minutes were associated with significantly longer diagnostic delay.
A higher number of autonomic symptoms during CH attacks was associated with a significantly shorter diagnostic delay in the Belgian Flanders study.

A Greek case series found alternating attack side, facial/occipital pain location, photophobia, forehead/facial sweating, physical activity aggravation, and absence of autonomic symptoms were associated with significantly longer diagnostic delay.
In a Danish gamma regression model, CH occurring after 1990 was strongly associated with reduced risk of longer diagnostic delay.
In the same Danish regression model, nocturnal attacks were associated with increased risk of longer diagnostic delay.
The Danish gamma regression model found female sex was not significantly associated with diagnostic delay.
In the Danish gamma regression model, presence of migraine-like features showed a borderline association with longer diagnostic delay.

Synthesizing across the four predictor studies, the review concludes that CH occurrence after 1990-2000 is associated with decreased diagnostic delay, lower age of onset and nocturnal attacks are associated with increased delay, and female sex shows no association.

Considering the mirror effect of absence versus high number of autonomic symptoms reported in separate studies, the review concludes that presence of autonomic symptoms predicts a shorter CH diagnostic delay.
Neurologist diagnostic accuracy for cluster headache varied widely between studies, with one reporting 80% correct diagnosis and another reporting 40% of patients missed by a neurologist.
The authors describe a novel headache syndrome presenting as episodic burning pain localized to a 10-20 cm diameter area on the vertex.
Most patients with the burning vertex headache syndrome were women (16 of 25).
Episodes of the burning vertex headache occurred one to three times weekly or daily, typically lasting under four hours but ranging from one minute to twenty-four hours.
The majority of patients (76%) had associated symptoms including nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, or autonomic features alongside the burning vertex headache.
Common comorbidities among patients with the burning vertex headache syndrome were hypertension, diabetes, and polycystic ovarian disease.
Neurological examination was normal in most patients except for a slight local temperature rise over the affected vertex area in 2 patients.
Two patients treated with greater occipital nerve (GON) block reported reduced frequency and severity of their burning vertex headaches.
The authors propose that the burning vertex headache syndrome may involve small fiber pathways originating from the scalp.

The novel burning vertex headache syndrome does not fully match the diagnostic criteria of other primary headache disorders such as nummular headache, migraine, cluster headache, or tension-type headache.
Treatment responses among patients with burning vertex headache were variable and generally inconsistent, aside from the subset who responded to greater occipital nerve block.
Serum ionized magnesium was low in a greater proportion of chronic daily headache patients with migraine features than in those with tension-type headache.
A higher proportion of chronic migraine patients had elevated calcium/magnesium ratios than chronic tension-type headache patients.
Serum magnesium was significantly lower in migraine (with and without aura) patients than in tension-type headache patients, and lower again in all headache groups than healthy controls.
Percentage of CD8 T-cells was significantly lower in migraineurs without aura than in both tension-type headache patients and healthy controls, which were similar to each other.
The CD4/CD8 ratio was highest in migraine patients and significantly higher than in tension-type headache patients.
Plasma methionine-enkephalin concentrations were elevated in tension-type headache patients compared to migraineurs (with and without aura) and healthy controls.
Platelet methionine-enkephalin levels were higher in migraineurs (with and without aura) than in tension-type headache participants.
Plasma CGRP was significantly higher in chronic migraine patients than in episodic migraine, cluster headache, and healthy control groups.
CGRP levels were similar between episodic migraine and cluster headache, so CGRP failed to differentiate these two headache types.
Plasma VIP was significantly higher in chronic migraine patients than in episodic cluster headache and healthy controls.
VIP levels did not significantly differ between episodic and chronic migraine, so it did not act as a universal biomarker for migraine chronicity/type.
Lymphocyte count was significantly higher in medication overuse headache patients than in episodic migraine patients.
Neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio was higher in medication overuse headache patients than in episodic migraine and healthy controls, suggesting an increased role of immune response in MOH.
In paediatric patients, CGRP levels were higher in migraine patients than in non-migraine headache and non-headache groups, both during and between attacks.
A machine-learning model using complete blood count parameters, their ratios, and demographic data achieved moderate accuracy in distinguishing primary from secondary headaches.
Plasma D-dimer levels were higher in spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage patients than in non-traumatic acute headache patients due to other causes, with high diagnostic accuracy.
APTT was decreased in subarachnoid haemorrhage patients compared to non-SAH acute headache patients, though with lower classification accuracy than D-dimer.

MRI trapezius muscle T2 values were highest in patients with combined migraine and tension-type headache features compared to TTH-only and healthy controls, correlating with headache days and neck pain.
Carotid intima-media thickness did not significantly differ between migraine (ictal/interictal), tension-type headache, and healthy control groups.

An MRI classifier combining structural/functional brain data with clinical presentation distinguished migraine from cluster headache with high accuracy, with reduced left thalamic-cortical functional interaction being the most discriminative feature in cluster headache.
Cluster headache patients had lower frontal grey matter volume than migraineurs and healthy individuals, and lower lateral occipital grey matter volume than migraineurs specifically.
Cluster headache patients showed higher functional connectivity than migraineurs in the working memory network and executive control network.

Both migraine and cluster headache patients showed weaker structural covariance between hypothalamic region volume and frontal/temporal cortical thickness than healthy controls, but this pattern did not distinguish the two headache types.

Several frontal, precuneal, and supramarginal brain regions showed significantly different thickness/volume between migraine and persistent post-traumatic headache patients, with measurements generally lower in PTH than migraine.

Seventeen region pairs showed significant differences in static functional connectivity, and ten in dynamic functional connectivity, between migraine and persistent post-traumatic headache patients, involving somatosensory, insular, hypothalamic, cingulate, and prefrontal areas.
In episodic cluster headache patients, salivary VIP levels significantly increased during the headache attack compared to the interictal period.
Salivary CGRP and substance P levels increased significantly during the ictal period in both migraine and cluster headache patients.
Salivary magnesium concentrations were lower in migraine (with and without aura) than in tension-type headache, with healthy controls showing the highest levels.
In headache-free paediatric patients, visual evoked potential P100 latency and amplitude were significantly higher in migraine patients than in those with tension-type headache or healthy controls.
In a separate paediatric cohort, no significant differences in VEP P100 latency were found among migraine, tension-type headache, and healthy control groups, contradicting an earlier study.

The discussion notes that inflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β, and TNF-α are proposed to be elevated in migraine compared to healthy controls and may serve as future diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers.
Serum IL-6 concentration was higher in patients with new daily persistent headache than in healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 concentration was higher in patients with chronic migraine than in healthy controls.
IL-6 levels did not differ between the NDPH and chronic migraine groups, suggesting a non-specific pain-related elevation rather than a disease-specific biomarker.
Serum IL-8 concentrations did not differ between NDPH, chronic migraine, and healthy controls.
Serum TNF-α concentrations did not differ between NDPH, chronic migraine, and healthy controls.

Of the remaining 27 cytokines/chemokines measured (including Eotaxin, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, IL-1α/β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-7, IL-10, IL-12/23p40, IL-12p70, IL-13, IL-15, IL-16, IL-17A, IP-10, MCP-1/4, MDC, MIP-1α/β, TARC, TNF-β, VEGF-A), concentrations were similar across NDPH, chronic migraine, and healthy control groups, with several cytokines undetectable in a large proportion of participants across all groups.
Within the NDPH group, there was no significant difference in IL-6, IL-8, or TNF-α levels between those with an infectious precipitant to their headache and those without.
A previous study found that CGRP levels strongly correlate with IL-6 levels in patients with migraine, suggesting a possible link between the neuropeptide and cytokine pathways.

IL-6 has previously been reported to be raised in other chronic pain disorders including fibromyalgia, supporting the idea that IL-6 elevation may reflect a non-specific pain response rather than a migraine/NDPH-specific process.

In a previous small study, cerebrospinal fluid TNF-α was elevated above the normal range in the large majority of NDPH, chronic migraine, and post-traumatic headache patients, though serum TNF-α was elevated in only a minority.

Both ultrasound-guided SPG block and GON block significantly improved all headache diary parameters (frequency, duration, intensity, total pain burden) at 1 month compared to sham injection, with no difference between the two active blocks.
HIT-6 total score (headache functional impact) was significantly reduced at 1 month in both SPG and GON block groups compared to sham, with no significant difference between the two active blocks.
MIDAS disability scores were significantly reduced at 3 months in both SPG and GON block groups compared to sham, with no significant difference between the two active blocks.
There was no significant difference in overall efficacy between SPG block and GON block for chronic resistant migraine across headache diary parameters, HIT-6, and MIDAS scores.
Presence of cranial autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, nasal congestion, ear fullness, vertigo) was associated with a significantly better treatment response to SPG block than to GON block.
Among patients with temporal pain, more were good responders to SPG block than GON block (72.7% vs 26.4%), but this difference was not statistically significant.
Among patients with occipital pain, more were good responders to GON block than SPG block (71.4% vs 50%), but this difference was not statistically significant.
Local pain at the injection site lasting 24-48 hours was reported by 90% of all cases across the study, regardless of block type.
Patients in the GON block group experienced transient post-procedural dizziness lasting a few minutes, attributed to positioning during the procedure.
Local bleeding during the procedure occurred in 80% of SPG block cases, controlled by brief minimal compression.
Post-procedural TMJ pain, attributed to maintained mouth opening during injection, occurred in 40% of SPG block cases and resolved with simple analgesics within 48-72 hours.
Facial swelling at the injection site occurred in 30% of SPG block cases, relieved by hot fomentations within 24 hours.

Infusion of CGRP in human provocation studies triggers delayed migraine attacks in susceptible individuals.
Some studies identified elevated CGRP levels in the peripheral blood of both episodic and chronic migraine patients compared to healthy controls.
Other studies found no significant difference in serum CGRP levels between migraine patients and healthy individuals, contradicting reports of elevated interictal CGRP.
VIP demonstrated migraine-inducing properties only after prolonged infusion in provocation studies.

PET and fMRI studies of triggered and spontaneous migraine attacks show stronger functional connectivity between the hypothalamus and sympathetic/parasympathetic-regulating brain areas in the hours preceding a headache.
Structural and functional imaging studies reveal differences in thalamic and thalamo-cortical activity between migraine patients and controls, both during attacks and interictally.
Resting-state fMRI during the interictal phase reveals widespread alterations in brain connectivity of migraine patients involving cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, brainstem, amygdala and cerebellum.

A diffusion tensor imaging study found that mean diffusivity decreased in the spinal trigeminal nucleus, dorsomedial/dorsolateral pons, and midbrain periaqueductal gray/nucleus cuneiform immediately before a migraine attack, and increased again immediately after.
Migraine patients present a poor sleep endophenotype, including poor sleep quality, shorter self-reported sleep duration, poorer sleep health score, and a modestly lower percentage of REM sleep.

An observational study found incident morning migraine attacks were associated with poorer sleep quality and decreased energy the prior day, while increased energy and greater average stress were associated with later-day headache onset.

Non-pharmacologic strategies such as setting routines, relaxation therapies, aerobic exercise, hydration, and avoidance of fasting and stressful situations have proven effective in reducing migraine burden or days.
Small molecule CGRP antagonists (gepants) are indicated for both acute and preventive treatment of migraine, enabling situational prevention during the interictal phase.
Some patients experience more migraine attacks on weekends, possibly due to a sudden shift in sympathetic-parasympathetic balance and adaptation to a more relaxed state.

Preliminary observations suggest that COVID-19 infection may modify brain bioelectrical activity, potentially causing cortical spreading depression and subsequent visual aura via increased neuronal activity, especially in the occipital lobe.

The authors propose a theoretical model in which migraine arises from the combined effects of unstable/depressive mood, unrestful sleep, and sympathetic-parasympathetic imbalance with parasympathetic prevalence, acting through dysfunction of hypothalamic homeostatic networks, producing a low brain energy 'high-risk area' state that precedes migraine attacks.
Increased parasympathetic tone due to altered physiological or emotional homeostasis may activate meningeal nociceptive pathways via the superior salivatory nucleus and sphenopalatine ganglion.
Poor sleep may impair glymphatic flow, leading to accumulation of neuroexcitatory and pro-inflammatory chemicals implicated in migraine development.
The KIT D816V mutation underlies abnormal mast cell growth and accumulation characteristic of systemic mastocytosis and is the target of newer therapies.
Midostaurin, a KIT-D816V-targeting drug, induces major responses or remission in advanced systemic mastocytosis and rapidly improves mediator-related symptoms and quality of life.
Avapritinib, a KIT-D816V-targeting drug, induces major responses or remission in advanced systemic mastocytosis and rapidly improves mediator-related symptoms and quality of life.
Management of mastocytosis includes recognition and prevention of comorbidities such as osteoporosis and anaphylaxis.

Individuals diagnosed with insomnia had more than twice the risk of subsequently developing cutaneous lupus erythematosus compared to non-insomnia controls, and this risk persisted across all sensitivity analyses.
Insomnia was associated with a modest but statistically significant increased risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis compared to non-insomnia controls, persisting across all sensitivity analyses.
Patients with insomnia had a significantly increased risk of subsequently developing Sjögren syndrome compared to non-insomnia controls, a finding that persisted across all sensitivity analyses.
Insomnia was associated with an increased risk of developing autoimmune thyroiditis relative to non-insomnia controls, persisting across all sensitivity analyses.

In the primary analysis, insomnia was associated with increased risk of SLE, ANCA-associated vasculitis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, and type 1 diabetes mellitus, but these associations were not confirmed when psychiatric comorbidity exclusion was applied throughout follow-up (sensitivity analysis S2).

No significant or persistent risk differences were found between insomnia cases and controls for alopecia areata, vitiligo, dermatitis herpetiformis, systemic sclerosis, dermato-/polymyositis, myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, primary biliary cirrhosis, autoimmune hepatitis, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, or pemphigus/pemphigoid diseases.

The authors propose that insomnia-induced disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis leads to dysregulated cortisol secretion, which over time contributes to immune dysregulation and increased susceptibility to autoimmunity.

Chronic sleep impairment is proposed to cause persistent sympathetic activation and catecholamine release, which suppresses regulatory T-cell function while promoting pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF, and IL-17, mediators implicated in autoimmune disease pathogenesis.

When patients with psychiatric disorders and antidepressant use were not excluded from the insomnia cohort, the number of autoimmune diseases significantly associated with insomnia increased from four to nine, suggesting psychiatric comorbidity may confound or contribute to the sleep-autoimmunity relationship.

The authors note that sleep fragmentation and shortened sleep duration increase pro-inflammatory immune activity including sustained activation of the NF-κB pathway, which may contribute to persistence of autoimmune inflammation.
Among the 10 patients, cluster headache preceded SUNHA in 7 cases, SUNHA preceded cluster headache in 1 case, and both started simultaneously in 2 cases.
Of the 8 patients with dedicated trigeminal imaging, half were found to have an ipsilateral neurovascular conflict on MRI review.
Nine of 10 patients reported similar cranial autonomic symptoms occurring during both cluster headache and SUNHA attacks, mostly on the same side and in the same cranial region.
Three of ten patients (30%) received dual diagnoses of trigeminal neuralgia and SUNHA based on temporally separated attacks and prominent cranial autonomic features in the SUNHA episodes.

Microvascular decompression produced a temporary reduction in cluster headache in one patient, suggesting a possible peripheral neurovascular contribution to pathophysiology, though efficacy could not be firmly inferred.

The authors hypothesize that hypothalamic dysfunction, via disinhibition of the hypothalamic-trigeminal pathway and trigeminal nucleus caudalis, may underlie both cluster headache and SUNHA and explain their co-occurrence.

Based on the estimated prevalence of cluster headache and SUNHA, random co-occurrence would be expected in only about 1.19 individuals nationally, supporting a non-coincidental association in this case series.
One patient in the series had an incidental pituitary microadenoma identified on neuroimaging.

Neurological examination revealed abnormalities in 2 of the 10 patients, including mild slowness of speech/motor task execution in one and a unilateral extensor response with vascular white matter lesions in another.
Side-shifting of attacks occurred in 2 of 10 patients: one had shifts limited to cluster headache, and the other had shifts in both cluster headache and SUNHA.
In patients who developed SUNHA after cluster headache onset, the time to onset of SUNHA ranged from 0.5 to 16 years, averaging 5.3 years.
In one patient, both cluster headache and SUNHA spontaneously resolved, with cluster headache resolving after 4.1 years and SUNHA resolving 9.5 years later.
Of the 10 patients, 6 had chronic cluster headache and 4 had episodic cluster headache.
Among 154 artificial stone workers with silicosis, 21.4% were diagnosed with autoimmune diseases or autoimmune serological abnormalities, supporting silica as a trigger of autoimmunity.
The patient's anti-scleroderma-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody was markedly elevated, consistent with systemic sclerosis.
The patient's anti-SS-A (anti-Ro) antibody was markedly elevated, consistent with Sjögren's syndrome.
Antinuclear antibody was strongly positive at high titer with a nucleolar pattern.
Thoracentesis showed a lymphocyte-predominant exudative pleural effusion with markedly elevated LDH.
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid showed an increased lymphocyte fraction with a markedly reduced CD4/CD8 ratio.
Oral corticosteroids (30 mg/day) failed to control the pleuritis, which progressed despite treatment.
Adding cyclosporine (200 mg/day) with increased corticosteroid dose still produced no effect, and the patient's general condition deteriorated, leading to death 18 months after treatment initiation.
Silica inhalation activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1β and driving persistent systemic inflammation implicated in silica-induced autoimmunity and treatment resistance.
Pleuritis is reported to occur in about 5% of systemic sclerosis patients and 1% of Sjögren's syndrome patients, making the coexisting pleuritis in this case unusual.
In an autopsy series of 110 chronic silicosis cases, 35% had pleural effusions, but only 11% of cases were purely silicosis-related, with most attributable to other causes.
MCC950, a selective NLRP3 inhibitor, has been reported to reduce IL-1β release and ameliorate lung inflammation in preclinical silicosis models.
OLT1177, an orally active NLRP3 inhibitor, has shown potential in clinical trials for inflammatory diseases and may be relevant to silica-induced conditions.

The patient's presentation met ASIA diagnostic criteria, with a defined silica adjuvant exposure history plus typical symptoms (fever, chronic fatigue, sicca symptoms), autoantibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, and progressive autoimmune disease.

Six months of anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy significantly reduced headache frequency in migraine patients, with no significant difference in the degree of improvement between those with and without fibromyalgia comorbidity.

Although headache intensity improved with anti-CGRP therapy in all migraine patients, the improvement was significantly smaller in patients with fibromyalgia comorbidity, who retained more intense headache than non-FM patients after treatment.
Migraine-related disability (MIDAS) improved similarly with anti-CGRP therapy in both FM and non-FM groups.
In fibromyalgia-comorbid migraine patients, fibromyalgia-related disability measured by the FIQ improved significantly after 6 months of anti-CGRP therapy.
Somatic pain intensity in fibromyalgia-comorbid patients, measured by the SNRS, improved significantly with anti-CGRP therapy.
Improvement in fibromyalgia disability (FIQ) was significantly correlated with improvement in migraine-related disability (MIDAS) in FM-comorbid patients.
The correlation between improvement in FIQ and reduction in headache frequency showed a similar trend but did not reach statistical significance.
The proportion of patients achieving at least a 50% reduction in headache frequency was similar between FM and non-FM migraine groups.

A significantly greater proportion of fibromyalgia-comorbid migraine patients failed to return for the 6-month follow-up compared to non-FM patients, despite no differences in adverse effects or drug ineffectiveness.
The frequency of medication ineffectiveness at 3 months (leading to discontinuation) did not differ significantly between FM and non-FM migraine groups.

Adverse events with anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies were rare and mild, including transient local injection-site skin reactions and mild constipation with erenumab, with no discontinuations due to adverse effects.
Among chronic migraine patients, the percentage reduction in headache frequency with anti-CGRP therapy was similar between FM and non-FM subgroups.
Episodic and chronic migraine patients with fibromyalgia comorbidity did not differ significantly in the percentage reduction of FIQ scores after anti-CGRP therapy.
A cited study (Korucu et al.) found that serum CGRP levels are higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.

CSF orexin A levels were elevated in chronic migraine and medication-overuse headache patients compared to controls.

Baseline plasma levels of orexin A and orexin B were lower in episodic migraine patients than in controls, with orexin A negatively correlated with weight gain during prophylactic treatment.

In an RCT of nightly filorexant (10 mg) for three months, no difference was observed versus placebo in mean monthly migraine days, in a trial population that was 85% female.

Migraine patients with and without aura showed lower interictal plasma NPY levels compared to controls, with levels increasing significantly during attacks in those with aura and moderately in those without.

Females with chronic migraine had higher NPY levels than episodic migraine patients or healthy controls following a fasting glucose test, along with increased insulin resistance but normal beta-cell function.

NPY signaling in the medial habenula produced analgesic and anxiolytic effects via the Y1 receptor in a mouse migraine model, and NPY levels in trigeminal ganglia fluctuated across the natural estrous cycle, suggesting ovarian steroid regulation.
Intravenous infusion of PACAP38 elicited delayed migraine-like attacks in 65-70% of migraine patients following initial mild headache and heat sensation.
Serum PACAP38 was elevated during migraine headache in adult episodic and chronic migraine patients compared to healthy controls.
Infusion of VIP was no better than placebo at triggering migraine headache in several studies.
In a multicenter RCT, the anti-PAC1 receptor monoclonal antibody AMG301 showed no efficacy in migraine prevention compared to placebo.
In a Phase II RCT in patients with prior treatment failures, the anti-PACAP monoclonal antibody Lu AG09222 produced a significant reduction in mean migraine days compared to placebo.
Migraine patients with and without aura had lower interictal plasma NPY levels than controls, with levels rising during attacks (more in those with aura).
Females with chronic migraine had higher NPY levels than episodic migraine patients or healthy controls after a fasting glucose test, with increased insulin resistance but normal beta-cell function.
NPY modulates migraine-related dural-trigeminovascular nociceptive neurons, likely via Y1 receptor activation.
