Intravenous PACAP38 infusion caused delayed migraine-like attacks in 65-70% of people with migraine.
PACAP38 infusion causes vasodilation of cranial blood vessels and alters plasma VIP and prolactin concentrations without changing inflammatory markers such as TNF.
Serum PACAP38 levels were elevated during migraine headache in adult episodic and chronic migraine patients compared to healthy controls.
Infusion of VIP was no better than placebo at triggering migraine headache in several short-infusion studies.
PACAP38 mediates activation and sensitization of dural-trigeminovascular neurons in rodents, producing periorbital hypersensitivity, a proposed mechanism for cranial-nociceptive migraine symptoms.

PACAP38 or a PAC1 antagonist microinjected into the PVN shifts dural-trigeminovascular neuron responses, and SuS stimulation triggers TNC activation via the cranial parasympathetic projection and alters lacrimal blood flow, effects blocked by VPAC1 and PAC1 antagonists.
AMG301, a monoclonal antibody targeting the PAC1 receptor, showed no efficacy in migraine prevention compared to placebo in a randomized controlled trial.
Longer (2 hour) VIP infusion can trigger migraine in patients, supporting a role for multiple PACAP-family receptors in migraine mechanisms.

Lu AG09222, a monoclonal antibody targeting both PACAP27 and PACAP38, significantly reduced mean migraine days compared to placebo in a Phase II trial of patients with two to four prior treatment failures.
Intranasal oxytocin inhibits central sensitization related to trigeminally-mediated migraine pain and chronicity.
Melatonin levels are reported to decrease during migraine episodes, suggesting a possible protective role that is lost during attacks.
Melatonin supplementation at 3 mg showed positive results in migraine prevention compared with placebo and amitriptyline, whereas 2 mg dosing showed little effect.

Circadian changes in orexin levels and increased orexin in chronic migraine, together with the high prevalence of migraine in narcolepsy (a disorder of altered orexinergic transmission), suggest orexinergic mechanisms link sleep disorders and migraine.

In an acute nitroglycerin rat model, males showed lower Fos expression (neuronal activation marker) in PVN, amygdala, and TNC than freely cycling females, suggesting female rodents are more predisposed to migraine-like neuronal changes.
An estrogen threshold of approximately 45-50 pg/mL has been described below which migraine attacks tend to increase, supporting estrogen's role in migraine prevention strategies.
In rats, high estrogen levels potentiated cortical spreading depression, an effect that was reversed by estrogen withdrawal.

Estrogen receptors alpha and beta are expressed in migraine-relevant brain areas (LC, amygdala, SON, PVN) and trigeminal structures, with males showing lower expression of estrogen receptors in the trigeminal system than females.

Levels of allopregnanolone, a neurosteroid derived from progesterone, are decreased in menstrual-associated and postmenopausal migraine even when serum progesterone levels do not differ from controls.

In rats, progesterone enhanced the effects of capsaicin-evoked dural CGRP release and vasodilation exclusively in males, suggesting a sexually dimorphic role for progesterone in trigeminal sensory processing.
Males with chronic migraine showed decreased levels of testosterone, and androgen use decreased headache attacks in females with menstrual migraine, supporting a protective role of testosterone.
Testosterone showed a neuroprotective effect in familial hemiplegic migraine 1 (FHM1) mice, decreasing susceptibility to cortical spreading depression.
In patients with hyperprolactinemia, 65.2% showed migraine-like symptoms, and dopamine agonist treatment alleviated headache in 75% of cases.

A systematic review found serum prolactin levels are higher in females with migraine compared to healthy controls, with increased serum prolactin associated with higher frequency of migraine attacks in both chronic and episodic migraine.
In contrast to other findings, a decrease in serum prolactin levels was also observed during migraine headache attacks in one study, attributed to heightened dopaminergic system activity.

Direct administration of prolactin onto the dura mater caused prolonged migraine-like behaviors only in female (cycling and ovariectomized) rodents, with prolactin receptor expressed on dural afferents mainly in females, sensitizing CGRP release only in female ex vivo dura; deletion of prolactin receptor from sensory neurons reduced these migraine-related responses.

In a restraint stress migraine model, stress increased serum prolactin in both sexes but more in females; bromocriptine reduced serum prolactin in both sexes but only attenuated stress-induced nociceptive behaviors in female mice.

In a sumatriptan medication overuse headache model, sumatriptan caused down-regulation of prolactin receptor in trigeminal ganglia only in female mice, and only females responded to cabergoline (which inhibits circulating prolactin) with prevention of periorbital allodynia and receptor down-regulation.

Restraint stress activated kappa opioid receptors on tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic neurons resulting in increased circulating prolactin in female mice, representing a mechanistic link between stress-induced hypothalamic activation and female-specific trigeminal nociceptor sensitization.
People with migraine experience increased diurnal cortisol concentration compared to healthy controls, as a manifestation of neuroendocrine dysregulation.
Dexamethasone, a synthetic glucocorticoid, was classified as 'possibly effective' (level C evidence) for the acute treatment of migraine.

In male mice exposed to prolonged restraint stress, elevated corticosterone activated NMDA receptors, triggering microglia proliferation; this was blocked by inhibiting corticosterone synthesis, the glucocorticoid receptor, or the NMDA receptor.

Repeated corticosterone injections in the absence of stress induced facial mechanical hypersensitivity only in female mice, indicating a female-specific effect of corticosterone on stress-like hypersensitivity.
Acute stress reduces estradiol and testosterone levels in the plasma of female rats, while these levels remain unchanged in male rats, indicating sex-specific stress-hormone interactions.

During Ramadan fasting, several studies reported a significant increase in migraine attack frequency in individuals with a history of migraine, particularly during the first week, with frequency decreasing after approximately ten days, partly attributed to insulin resistance onset and dehydration.

Chronic migraine is strongly associated with insulin resistance, with the number of insulin receptors in hypothalamic and brainstem regions supporting a potential role of hyperinsulinemia in chronic migraine pathogenesis.
Hyperinsulinemia is associated with migraine and correlates with elevated nitric oxide stress in both female and male patients.

In male rats, insulin and leptin lowered blood glucose while glucagon raised it, but all three peptides inhibited dural-evoked neuronal firing in the trigeminocervical complex; insulin and leptin reduced TCC pERK1/2 expression while glucagon increased it, and leptin uniquely decreased pERK1/2 in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus.

Direct pharmacological activation of the dorsomedial hypothalamus increased sensitivity to mechanical stimulation in awake animals, confirming its role in modulating hyperalgesic responses linked to stress and pain.

Lu AG09222, a monoclonal antibody targeting both PACAP27 and PACAP38 isoforms, produced a significant reduction in mean migraine days compared to placebo in a Phase II trial in patients with prior treatment failures.
AMG301, a human monoclonal antibody targeting the PAC1 receptor, showed no efficacy in migraine prevention compared to placebo in a multicenter randomized controlled trial.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, the dual-orexin receptor antagonist filorexant (10 mg nightly for three months) showed no difference compared to placebo in mean monthly migraine days, a trial that was 85% female.
In a mouse model of lupus nephritis, human gingival-derived MSCs reduced proteinuria and histological severity of nephritis by suppressing B cell function via the CD39/CD73 axis.
Umbilical-cord-derived MSC injection reduced circulating Th17 cell levels and increased Treg cell levels in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.

Human bone-marrow-derived MSC injections reduced glomerulonephritis, self-reactive antibody production, proteinuria, and mortality in NZM/W F1 lupus-prone mice, partly by hindering follicular Th cell growth.
Autologous bone-marrow-derived MSCs were used to alleviate symptoms in nine patients with severe rheumatoid arthritis.

Allogeneic bone-marrow MSC intravenous infusion was found safe and to have a promising therapeutic effect in active ankylosing spondylitis patients who did not respond to conventional pharmacological drugs.
After receiving umbilical-cord MSC infusion, all ankylosing spondylitis patients in a trial showed pain alleviation and reduction in disease severity/activity scores.
Osteoarthritis affects approximately 10%-15% of the human population and is the most prevalent form of arthritis, disproportionately disabling the elderly.
The circular RNA circ_0005564 was reported to contribute to osteoporosis by raising mRNA levels of osteogenic differentiation markers RUNX2, osteopontin, and osteocalcin.
Bone-marrow-derived MSCs from Sjögren's syndrome patients show impaired immunological activity, which may contribute to disease development.
Umbilical-cord-derived MSCs were shown to considerably boost salivary production, relieve disease manifestations, and reduce inflammatory conditions in Sjögren's syndrome.

Exosomes from labial gland MSCs (LGMSC-Exos) reactivated salivary glands in a spontaneous Sjögren's syndrome mouse model, and co-culture with patient PBMNCs markedly lowered CD38+CD27+CD20-CD19+ plasma cell percentages, an effect attributed to microRNA-125b targeting specific genes in plasma cells.
MSC injection into Crohn's disease strictures produced partial and complete resolution of stricture, though some occlusions were detected on follow-up.
Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain condition affecting 2%-8% of the global population, characterized by generalized pain, cold allodynia, thermal hyperalgesia, fatigue, sleep disorders, and depression.

In a reserpine-induced fibromyalgia rat model, BM-MSC injection (2×10^6 cells) improved behavioral and physical assessments, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and inflammatory mediators, improved cerebral cortex histology, and showed neurogenesis activity compared with untreated FM rats.

MSCs isolated from systemic sclerosis patients show impaired endothelial cell differentiation and higher levels of TGF-β and VEGF compared with MSCs from normal subjects, potentially contributing to fibrosis progression.

A long-term retrospective study with 9 years of follow-up found that all systemic sclerosis patients' skin symptoms and serological indices improved after MSC transplantation, with six deaths that were unrelated to the transplants.

In a HOCl-induced mouse model of systemic sclerosis, MSC-based treatment decreased dermal and pulmonary fibrosis by improving extracellular matrix remodeling, lowering inflammatory cytokines, strengthening antioxidant defenses, and lowering serum anti-Scl-70 autoantibody levels.

In 10 patients with drug-resistant dermatomyositis/polymyositis given allogeneic BM- or UC-MSC IV infusion at 1×10^6 cells/kg, serum creatine kinase levels improved, along with improvements in interstitial lung disease and skin ulcers in some patients; several patients required an additional dose for recurrence.

In dermatomyositis/polymyositis patients receiving UC-MSC infusion (3.5-5.2×10^7 cells) plus glucocorticoids/immunosuppressants, creatine kinase fell more and lung function improved more than in the control (drug-only) group; IFN-γ rose at 6 months while IL-4 fell at 6 months and IL-17 declined at 3 and 6 months post-infusion.

A 9-year long-term retrospective study of MSC IV infusion (1×10^6 cells/kg) in polymyositis/dermatomyositis patients found improvement in symptoms and serological markers, though 11 patients died from causes unrelated to transplantation.
A 35-year-old female with dermatomyositis/polymyositis experienced dramatically better strength at 3-month follow-up after four IV infusions of autologous expanded adipose-derived MSCs.
All patients with Parkinson disease met criteria for postprandial hypotension, while only 69% of patients with MSA did.
The median maximum postprandial decline in systolic blood pressure was larger in PD than in MSA.
The median maximum postprandial decline in diastolic blood pressure was larger in PD than in MSA.
The area under the curve for postprandial SBP was not significantly different between PD and MSA, though numerically higher (less decline) in MSA.
The compounded postprandial decline in DBP (AUC) was significantly greater in PD than in MSA.
Postprandial HR increased significantly (higher AUC) in MSA but not in PD.
The decrease in SBP 30 minutes after meal intake was significantly larger in PD than in MSA.
The decline in DBP at 30 minutes post-meal was not significantly different between PD and MSA.
Supine SBP was significantly higher in PD than in MSA.
The Valsalva ratio was significantly lower in PD than in MSA, indicating greater parasympathetic impairment in PD.
The pressor response during phase IV of the Valsalva maneuver was more blunted in PD than in MSA.
HR within 3 minutes of standing was significantly higher in MSA than PD, though degree of orthostatic hypotension did not differ.
Supine plasma norepinephrine was significantly higher in MSA than in PD.
Supine plasma DHPG (a norepinephrine metabolite) was significantly higher in MSA than in PD.
Upright plasma norepinephrine was significantly higher in MSA than in PD.
Upright plasma DHPG was significantly higher in MSA than in PD.
The increase in plasma norepinephrine from supine to standing was significantly greater in PD than in MSA.
The increase in plasma DHPG from supine to standing was significantly greater in PD than in MSA.
The NE-to-DHPG ratio, reflecting norepinephrine transporter reuptake activity, did not differ significantly between PD and MSA in supine, upright, or change positions.
Myocardial MIBG imaging showed a normal heart-to-mediastinum ratio in MSA but a below-normal ratio in PD, indicating cardiac sympathetic denervation in PD.
In multivariable regression adjusting for age and supine SBP, PD diagnosis remained significantly associated with a greater decline in postprandial DBP AUC compared to MSA.
In the adjusted multivariable analysis, diagnosis group was not significantly associated with AUC for SBP, despite a large effect estimate.
Thirty minutes after the meal challenge, patients with PD had a significantly larger drop in systolic blood pressure from baseline than patients with MSA.
The decline in diastolic blood pressure at 30 minutes post-meal did not differ significantly between PD and MSA groups.
There was no significant difference between PD and MSA in heart rate change 30 minutes after meal consumption.

In univariable regression, diagnosis group (PD vs MSA) showed a borderline significant association with postprandial SBP AUC, while age, BMI, sex, supine SBP, sinus arrhythmia ratio, ∆HR/∆SBP, and Valsalva phase IV HR were not significantly associated.
In the multivariable regression adjusting for age and supine SBP, diagnosis group was not significantly associated with postprandial SBP AUC, though the effect size was large in magnitude.
In the multivariable regression, diagnosis group was not significantly associated with adjusted postprandial HR AUC.

After adjusting for age and supine SBP, PD diagnosis remained significantly associated with a greater fall in postprandial DBP AUC compared with MSA, suggesting PD is an independent risk factor for PPH severity.

A prior study cited by the authors found that administration of levodopa/benserazide twice daily did not contribute to the severity of blood pressure decline in orthostatic and postprandial hypotension.

The authors note that other studies report levodopa and carbidopa have vasodilatory and negative inotropic effects that specifically worsen orthostatic hypotension in PD patients with autonomic failure, and could not rule out their contribution to PPH in this study's PD cohort since 9 of 13 PD patients remained on this treatment.

The authors cite prior work showing that pharmacologically blocking residual sympathetic activity with clonidine and trimethaphan decreases blood pressure in MSA patients, supporting the presence of tonic residual sympathetic regulation of BP in this group.

The authors note that in subjects with healthy autonomic function, postprandial hemodynamic compensation involves a 62% increase in cardiac output, driven by a 17% increase in heart rate and a 41% increase in stroke volume, which counteracts the BP decline from splanchnic blood pooling.
Monthly headache clinic visit frequency increased significantly after the dedicated pediatric headache outpatient clinic was established, compared to the prior 11-year period.
More than half of the pediatric headache clinic patients were diagnosed with migraine.
Primary headache disorders accounted for approximately 60% of cases seen at the clinic.
Secondary headache causes identified in the clinic included adjustment disorder and orthostatic dysregulation.
Orthostatic dysregulation was identified as one of the secondary causes of headache among pediatric patients seen at the headache outpatient clinic.
All patients seen in the headache outpatient clinic were instructed on nonpharmacological lifestyle guidance as an initial management step.
In roughly half of the patients, a combination of nonpharmacological therapy and acute abortive therapy was sufficient to improve their headaches.
Over 80% of patients treated at the headache outpatient clinic ultimately experienced some degree of headache relief.
Migraine and depression are described as predisposing factors for recurrence of transient global amnesia (TGA), which recurs in 2.9-26.3% of cases.
The reported patient with recurrent TGA had a pre-existing history of hypertension and migraine with aura.
During both acute episodes of TGA the patient's activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) was shortened, gradually normalizing over subsequent days/weeks after symptom resolution.
Prothrombin time (PT) was likewise shortened during both acute TGA episodes and normalized after resolution of symptoms.

The patient exhibited markedly elevated blood pressure during the acute phase of each TGA episode, with ambulatory monitoring later showing exceeded but lower BP values than at the acute presentation.

In a case-control study of 206 TGA patients, the right vertebral artery (V4 segment) diameter was significantly narrower than in healthy controls, suggesting vertebral artery hypoplasia as a risk factor for TGA.
Heart rate variability fluctuations were greatest during the first week after a TGA episode and decreased over subsequent time, indicating transient autonomic dysfunction.
Volumetric MRI assessment of 87 TGA patients showed greater atrophy of the anterior ventral cingulate gyrus compared to controls.
In a small perfusion study of 5 TGA patients during the acute phase, no clinically significant ischemia was found, though 4 of 5 patients showed mild oligemia in posterior cerebral artery territory.

Patients with TGA and patent foramen ovale had fewer cardiovascular risk factors and fewer chronic vascular brain changes than controls, suggesting paradoxical microembolism rather than traditional vascular risk as a TGA mechanism in this subgroup.
TGA patients showed greater cerebrospinal fluid biological antioxidant potential (csfBAP) than healthy controls, suggesting oxidative stress involvement in TGA pathogenesis.

The patient's diffusion-weighted MRI performed ~32 hours after symptom onset showed two small hyperintense lesions within the left hippocampus, consistent with the typical CA1-sector DWI findings described in TGA, which resolve within 7-10 days.

The authors propose that a stressful trigger preceding TGA may provoke an acute-phase reaction causing both shortened coagulation times (increased clotting factor activity) and dysregulation of central blood pressure control, suggesting TGA, coagulation disorders, and blood pressure abnormalities may share a common underlying stress-related mechanism.
In a provocation study, administration of amylin was able to trigger migraine attacks, similar to CGRP.
One study identified amylin plasma levels as a potential biomarker for migraine in migraine patients.
Preclinical rodent studies of amylin signalling have reported sex differences relevant to migraine mechanisms.
Some therapies designed to block the CGRP pathway have also been shown to target amylin receptors.

Detailed assessments show children have increased risk of fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and sleep difficulty following SARS-CoV-2 infection, beyond effects attributable to pandemic-related social isolation and stress.
Children with long COVID, similar to adults, develop postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.
Children with long COVID show impaired exercise tolerance as assessed by cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
Children with long COVID exhibit autonomic cardiac dysfunction.
Global estimates project that more than 60 million adults have developed new-onset long COVID.
Large US studies suggest nearly 6 million children are living with long COVID.
A survey of large pediatric cohorts found a 7.7-fold increased odds of school loss in children with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to those without.
Rates of autoimmune disease, thyroid disease, and diabetes mellitus are increased in children in the post-infectious period after SARS-CoV-2, mirroring risks in adults.
One hypothesis proposes that SARS-CoV-2 viral reservoirs persist in both children and adults, with long COVID associated with Spike antigenaemia and correlating hyperinflammation.

SARS-CoV-2 RNA and/or antigen has been detected in the gastrointestinal tract, lymphoid tissue, and brain tissue of both children and adults months to years after acute infection, suggesting persistent viral reservoirs across all ages.
Antiviral clinical trials targeting viral reservoirs in long COVID, using drugs such as nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and remdesivir, have shown negative results to date.
Spike antigenaemia can be detected in the circulation of children with long COVID.
Children with long COVID show neutrophil activation as part of a dysregulated inflammatory response.
Children with long COVID show contraction of the naive and switched B cell compartments.
Children with long COVID show increased regulatory T lymphocytes as part of immune dysregulation.
Children with long COVID show increased inflammatory cytokine profiles.
Children with long COVID show circulating fibrin amyloid microclots.
Long COVID negatively impacts longevity and cardiovascular health.
The Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory is a validated patient-reported outcome that can be used to assess fatigue from young children through adulthood.
A core outcome set for paediatric long COVID has been proposed using a rigorous Delphi consensus process.
By consensus, a transient drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 40 mmHg within 15 seconds of standing is considered abnormal and has been termed 'initial orthostatic hypotension'.

The hypotensive event associated with immediate/initial orthostatic hypotension is typically solitary and brief, spontaneously resolving within 15-30 seconds, with the individual remaining symptom-free until another postural change occurs.
12.1% of patients with post-COVID-19 condition (38 of 314) tested positive for serum antineuronal antibodies.
No significant difference in the prevalence of serum antineuronal antibodies was found between PCC patients and post-infection controls without PCC.
Among seropositive PCC patients, CASPR-2 antibodies were the most prevalent, found in 7 of 38 (18.9%) seropositive individuals.
Neurofascin-186 antibodies were detected in 5 of 38 (13.2%) seropositive PCC patients.
Glycine receptor antibodies were detected in 4 of 38 (10.8%) seropositive PCC patients.
No intrathecal antineuronal autoantibodies were detected in cerebrospinal fluid analyzed in a subset of PCC patients.
Among post-infection controls, two subjects tested seropositive, one with low-titer myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies and another with borderline myelin antibody levels.
CSF analysis performed on a subset of patients showed no intrathecal antineuronal autoantibodies.
None of the seropositive patients met criteria for autoimmune encephalitis, and neurological assessments and brain MRI were unremarkable.
Neuropsychological testing showed a trend toward impairments in attention and executive functions among antibody-seropositive individuals with PCC.
Eptinezumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets and inhibits calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), the mechanism underlying its use for migraine prevention.
Plasma exposure (AUC0–inf and Cmax) after a single weight-based dose of eptinezumab was similar between the 150 mg and 300 mg dose groups in children and adolescents.
The plasma elimination half-life of eptinezumab in children and adolescents was similar to that reported in adults, at a median of 27.5 days for the 150 mg dose and 29.2 days for the 300 mg dose.

During the extension period, repeated eptinezumab dosing at 150 mg or 300 mg every 12 weeks produced similar overlaying plasma concentration-time profiles, with only a minor difference in AUC between dose levels.
In the main trial period, over half of participants experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, with similar incidence in children and adolescents and no serious or severe events.
The most common adverse event associated with eptinezumab infusion in the main trial period was orthostatic hypotension, occurring in three adolescents and resolving the same day.
In the extension period (up to four infusions), 61% of participants had at least one TEAE, with no serious or severe events and no orthostatic hypotension reported.

Two participants (one child, one adolescent) reported suicidal ideation on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale during the main trial period, both with a pre-existing history of psychiatric disorders.
Immunogenicity testing showed only two adolescents (no children) developed low-titer anti-drug antibodies to eptinezumab, none with neutralizing potential, and without associated adverse events.
A single dose of eptinezumab was associated with reductions in migraine-related disability, as measured by PedMIDAS, from baseline to Week 12 in both children and adolescents.
Repeated eptinezumab dosing over the extension period was associated with sustained reductions in PedMIDAS scores through Week 64 in both children and adolescents.

Weight-based dosing (100/150/300 mg) achieved plasma exposures in children and adolescents comparable to those seen with the 300 mg adult dose, as simulated exposures for all body weight groups fell within the 90% confidence interval for adults.
In a companion pediatric population PK analysis of this trial's data, sex was found not to be a significant covariate of eptinezumab exposure.

A retrospective chart review by Zorrilla et al. found that eptinezumab treatment benefited nine of 11 adolescents with chronic migraine or new daily persistent headache, with continued or additional improvement on dose escalation and tolerability across up to four infusions.

In a long-term open-label safety trial of eptinezumab 300 mg in adults with chronic migraine, mean MIDAS disability scores decreased substantially from baseline to Week 12 and remained generally sustained through Week 104.
In the fully adjusted model, N3C patients with the most severe COVID-19 (hospitalized and ventilated) had a 47% higher risk of new-onset autoimmune disease compared to outpatients with mild COVID-19.
In the fully adjusted model, PCORnet patients with the most severe COVID-19 had a 14% higher risk of new-onset autoimmune disease compared to mild outpatients.
In the fully adjusted model, PEDSnet pediatric patients with severe COVID-19 had over 3-fold higher risk of new-onset autoimmune disease compared to asymptomatic infection.

Within N3C, autoimmune disease risk increased progressively with COVID-19 severity, being elevated in the ED-or-hospitalized group and further in the hospitalized-and-ventilated group relative to outpatients.
In contrast to the other networks, PCORnet patients hospitalized without ventilation had an 18% lower risk of new autoimmune disease compared to outpatients.
Children with moderate COVID-19 had a 2-fold increase in risk of new autoimmune disease after full adjustment, in addition to those with severe infection.

After excluding patients with any prior autoimmune disease, the association of COVID-19 severity with new autoimmune disease risk persisted but slightly attenuated for the ED and hospitalized groups in N3C.
Among PEDSnet children excluding prior autoimmune disease, moderate and severe COVID-19 remained strongly associated with new-onset autoimmune disease.
In the sensitivity analysis, N3C and PCORnet patients hospitalized with ventilation had an elevated but statistically non-significant risk of new autoimmune disease compared to outpatients.
Stratifying the fully adjusted models by sex did not reveal any significant difference in the COVID-19 severity/autoimmune disease association between males and females in any of the three networks.
